### Past Meets the Present

The **Past Meets the Present** feature boxes help you link the chapter to today.  
They ask you to see how ideas from the past connect to the modern world.  
They also ask why a historical issue still matters now.

---

### Names, spellings, and dates

This book is a global history.  
We try to respect world cultures by using names close to their original language.

Experts chose these spellings using current research.  

For Chinese names, the text uses the **pinyin** system.  
It does not use the older **Wade-Giles** system.  
We use pinyin because it is the system used by the People’s Republic of China.  
It also matches the sounds of Mandarin Chinese more closely.

For languages that use the Latin alphabet, we keep accent marks in names.  
Examples include **Hernán Cortés** and **Napoléon Bonaparte**.

For names translated from languages like Chinese and Arabic, we avoid accents and apostrophes when possible.  
We only use them when they help pronunciation and make the text easier to read.

For events, places, and other historical terms, we usually use the most common English form.

All dates use the **Gregorian calendar**, which is the international standard civil calendar.  
We use **BCE** for dates before the Common Era.  
We use **CE** for dates in the Common Era.

---

### Why maps matter in world history

World history also requires strong geography skills.  
You might think maps are simple and objective.  
You might think they just show where things are.

For most of history, that was not true.  
Maps are often debated as historical evidence.  
This is because mapmakers usually showed the world from their own point of view.  
They did not make maps in a neutral way.

Many civilizations placed themselves at the center of the world they knew.

Maps have also been used to support conquest and control.  
During the Age of Exploration, the Pope divided inhabited lands that were new to Europeans.  
He then granted those lands to Spain and Portugal.  
Centuries later, in Berlin, Germany, European diplomats drew borders on a map of Africa.  
They divided territory among colonial powers.

History might look different if the maps that survived were made by Indigenous peoples.

Even after people learned more about the size of the world, maps were still often inaccurate.  
Many maps showed Europe as larger than it really is.  
They showed parts of the Global South as smaller than they really are.  
This includes Latin America, Africa, and parts of Asia and Oceania.

---

### Contested territories

Maps can also be difficult because some places are claimed by more than one government.  
This happened in the past, and it still happens today.

Two examples are **Crimea** and **Taiwan**.  
Crimea is claimed by both Russia and Ukraine.  
Taiwan claims independence, while China says Taiwan is part of China.

This text will point out these contested regions when they appear.  
This will help you understand how complex geography can be.

chapter_key: How Farming Changed the Human Experience
text:
The example of the Indigenous people of Australia shows that not everyone adopted agriculture when they encountered it. This can seem strange today. Our world depends on agriculture. But we are far removed from the difficult transition many of our ancestors faced.

One major cost was the loss of leisure time. Researchers who study modern hunter-gatherers find that they often need about 20 hours per week to get enough food. Similar agricultural societies spend 30 hours or more on farming. This leaves less time for rest, sharing knowledge, and enjoyable activities. These studies also show that women lost the most leisure time. Women in farming societies often did more hard labor than hunter-gatherer women in similar environments.

Large farming communities also faced new risks. They were more vulnerable to epidemic diseases. This was common in places where large amounts of human and animal waste built up. Farmers were also more dependent on the weather. Crops needed enough water, but not too much. Unlike hunter-gatherers, farmers could not easily move to better conditions.

Farmers also ate a less varied diet. Their food often came from one or two staple crops, usually starchy carbohydrates. Farmers did have domesticated animals. But Neolithic communities ate much less meat than hunter-gatherers did. Depending on a narrow range of foods could cause vitamin and mineral deficiencies.

Agriculture also brought clear benefits. It supported much larger populations. More people meant more workers to produce food. It also meant more people to defend the settlement. When agriculture worked well, it produced a steady food supply. It could also create a surplus that could be stored.

As humans began leaving hunter-gatherer life around 12,000 years ago, they also moved away from the egalitarianism it encouraged. Agriculture required specialization in a way hunting and gathering did not. Farming a wheat field, for example, required a family to focus on that work and related chores. This left little time for the wide range of tasks common in hunter-gatherer life.

As agriculture became more advanced, some farmers became more successful than others. Tools like plows, and domesticated animals to pull them, increased production. Some farmers produced surpluses. This allowed them to build wealth through property and land. They passed this wealth, and the higher status that came with it, to their descendants. This strengthened social divisions between the wealthy and everyone else. When food was plentiful, not everyone had to farm. Some people became artisans or traders. They could generate even more wealth.

Some people specialized so much that they no longer focused on food production at all. They became traders, stoneworkers, religious leaders, and other elites. Those with great wealth could become leaders. They could command armies and make rules for society. Those without wealth faced hard labor if they were lucky. If they were not, they could face bondage.

Agriculture also created new divisions based on sex. In many hunter-gatherer societies, women commonly gathered and men commonly hunted. In many agricultural societies, men typically worked in the fields. The need for strength to control the plow likely helped drive this change. Women were pushed into domestic work. They prepared food, made pottery, and wove cloth. Because men were less tied to the home, they had more chances to become leaders. They also had duties women usually did not, including dangerous work like fighting and dying to defend the settlement.

In the home, women did difficult and time-consuming work like milling grain. At first, people used mortars and pestles. As farming output grew, larger stone tools were used. Using these mills required long hours. Women often had to kneel and bend over millstones. Wool from domesticated sheep was also processed at home. It was spun into thread and woven into cloth. These tasks came on top of giving birth, raising children, and preparing food.

Agriculture also strongly shaped religion. Greater specialization allowed priestly classes to form in many places. These religious elites claimed authority by interpreting the supernatural world. This ability was highly valued. Because of it, they could control material and human resources. They used these resources to build monuments and perform carefully organized rituals.

Religions also became more complex and changed in character. Before agriculture, many societies practiced forms of animism. They saw spiritual meaning in many ordinary things and animals. They often tried to connect with the supernatural through shamanic and other rituals. After the Neolithic Revolution, many communities focused more on agricultural fertility. They emphasized deities who could help humans by supporting fertility. These beliefs also reinforced the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth.

Like the people of Mesopotamia, Ancient Egyptians were polytheists.  
They worshipped many gods.  
These gods controlled the forces of nature.

Re was the god of the sun.  
Isis was the earth goddess of fertility.  
Osiris was linked to the Nile.

The most important event of the Egyptian year was the Nile’s yearly flood.  
Egyptians explained this flood with the myth of Osiris.

In the myth, Osiris was murdered by his brother Seth.  
Seth was the god of the desert wind.  
Osiris was then brought back to life by his loyal wife, Isis.

This story matched what people saw in nature.  
In summer, the Nile was at its lowest level.  
At the same time, the hot desert wind was blowing.  
This was linked to Seth.  
Later, the Nile flooded its banks.  
It brought life-giving water to the land.  
This was seen as Osiris being “resurrected,” with Isis bringing fertility.

text:
The end of the third millennium BCE was a major turning point in Mesopotamia.  
It was also a time of disorder.

Invaders came from the north, east, and west.  
They put heavy pressure on the rulers of the Third Dynasty of Ur.  
This was the last Sumerian dynasty.

One of the biggest threats came from nomadic peoples.  
They lived in the desert regions of Syria.  
These raiders were called the Amorites.

Amorite raids became a serious problem.  
Around 2034 BCE, Shu-Sin, the ruler of Ur, built a wall to stop them.  
The wall was about 170 miles long.  
It ran from the Euphrates River to the Tigris River.

The plan did not work.  
During the reign of Shu-Sin’s son, Ibbi-Sin, the Amorites broke through the wall.  
They began attacking cities.

Soon, another enemy joined them.  
The Elamites came from the east.

Raids grew more frequent and more intense.  
City after city fell.  
The Third Dynasty of Ur collapsed.

By about 2004 BCE, Ibbi-Sin’s empire was almost gone.  
Only the city of Ur remained.

In that same year, Ur was attacked and looted.  
The Elamites and other groups sacked the city.

After this, the Amorites spread across Mesopotamia.  
They founded strong cities of their own.

They adopted local religious traditions.  
They also adopted local customs.  
They used the Akkadian language.

They also took on the region’s political culture of rivalry.  
Two Amorite cities became especially important: Isin and Larsa.  
These cities fought for supremacy.

This competition pushed innovation and expansion.  
It was similar to what had happened earlier with the first city, Ur.

## The Yayoi Period: Farming and New Society

The next phase of Japan’s prehistory is called the **Yayoi** period.  
It is known for a major change: **the move into agriculture**.

### New migrants and new crops
Around **300 BCE**, new migrants arrived.  
They came from groups in **northern Asia**.  
They settled first on **Kyushu**, Japan’s southern island.

They brought knowledge of farming.  
They grew **barley** and **buckwheat**.  
Later, they also grew **rice**.

Over time, the Yayoi people **overwhelmed and replaced the Jōmon**.

### Farming technology and population growth
The Yayoi built large **storehouses** for grain.  
They also **domesticated horses and dogs**.

As Yayoi culture spread, people learned to reshape the land for farming.  
They built **irrigation canals**, **wells**, and **pits**.

Agriculture brought more stability.  
It also supported population growth.  
By the first centuries of the common era, the Yayoi population may have reached **more than 500,000**.

## More contact with Korea and China
The Yayoi period was a turning point.  
From this time on, **Korea, China, and Japan** had more regular contact.

This was partly because of the Bronze Age economy.  
**Copper was scarce in Japan.**  
So the Yayoi had to **import** much of it.

This period also marks the start of **written records** about Japan.

## Trade and the first written descriptions
The **Han** conquests and the building of garrisons on the Korean peninsula increased trade.  
Through Korea, Japan received new goods and ideas.  
These included **bronze mirrors**, **iron weapons**, and **agricultural practices**.

The **Han dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE)** sent occasional envoys to Japan.  
Later, the kingdom of **Cao Wei (220–265 CE)** also sent envoys.  
The Han called Japan the **Wa kingdom**.

These envoys left the **first written records** about Yayoi life.  
Their reports show society and politics changing slowly.

At first, Yayoi communities were mostly communal.  
People shared **wooden tools** and **public spaces**.  
Even with more food and more goods, life stayed cooperative for a time.

Later, some places became more valuable for farming.  
This led to competition.  
Competition led to more warfare.  
Over time, **states emerged** to organize defense.

## Dual rule and Queen Himiko
Chinese records describe a distinctive system of **dual governance**.  
In this system, **male and female rulers shared power**.  
This appeared in early Japanese states near the end of the Yayoi era.

One famous ruler was **Queen Himiko**.  
She ruled in the **early third century**.  
She paid tribute to the Chinese emperor.  
In return, China recognized her as an ally.  
She was given a **golden seal**.

Himiko ruled alongside her **younger brother**.  
He managed the administration of her realm.

Cao Wei records say Himiko fought a neighboring king.  
They also say she supported her authority through spiritual power.  
This included **elaborate burials**, **divination**, and other sacred rituals.

Through this kind of specialization, women could hold political power.  
This may connect to older Jōmon traditions.  
Jōmon **dogu** figurines often show women as deities.  
These figures were linked to **fertility and safety**.

## A more stratified society and body art
Chinese envoys also described a more stratified society.  
It included **aristocratic families**, **merchants**, **skilled divers and fishers**, **farmers**, and other commoners.

Warfare was constant.  
Because of this, palaces often looked like **garrisons**.  
Even so, **granaries and markets** were busy and full.

These early Japanese did not yet have a written script.  
But the Yayoi developed another kind of “writing.”  
They used **tattoos** on the body.  
Tattoo patterns showed **rank**, **status**, and **family**.

But the Yayoi developed another kind of “writing.”

They used tattoos on the body.

text:
Records from Queen Himiko’s time show that political power was becoming more concentrated. Control over land was shifting toward a loose confederation of states and powerful families. This time is called the Yamato era. It included the building of tombs for dead royals like Himiko. These royals were buried with many treasures. Human sacrifices were also included to accompany them in the afterlife.

The Yamato era may have begun because the climate changed and Japan faced constant turmoil. Many people lost hope. They abandoned older deities who seemed unable to protect them. New gods then rose in importance. These gods were linked to imported technology, especially mirrors from China and Korea. Powerful rulers and a new military class, shaped by warfare, connected themselves to these new gods. Most importantly, they linked themselves to Amaterasu, the female Sun goddess. Amaterasu soon became the ancestral figurehead of the imperial household. Yamato kings gained more power by making alliances. They managed trade. They gave symbolic gifts. They also led ceremonies meant to create a shared culture across Japan.

Women still held political influence. They did so as co-rulers of kingdoms or as heads of households. They used knowledge of sorcery. They used items such as mirrors. They often showed success through gold jewelry and earrings. Many spiritual practices came from earlier Chinese dynasties, including the Shang dynasty. During Queen Himiko’s burial, Chinese envoys reported a Japanese practice of divination. People heated bones and read the cracks. They used this to predict harvests and the outcomes of wars. Other burial practices were more native to Japan. One example was water purification. These practices later shaped religions such as Shintoism. Later, new foreign religions also arrived, including Buddhism. Women such as Empress Suiko used Buddhism politically. Suiko ruled in the early seventh century CE. She tried to preserve women’s role in politics. She emphasized piety, serious study of sutras, and the building of shrines and temples.

Large keyhole-shaped tombs became especially important. Control over burial rituals helped Yamato rulers gain power. Their influence stretched from western Honshu to northern Kyushu. Building these tombs required many laborers. It also required skilled artisans, including blacksmiths. The tombs displayed Yamato wealth and strong organization. These same skills were later used to build capital cities. These cities had large markets. They also had highways leading to the countryside and to coastal ports.

To centralize power, kings began issuing law codes. One example is Prince Shotoku’s Seventeen Article Constitution in 604. This document stressed law as the basis of rule. It also supported a bureaucracy to help rulers govern. It included Confucian values. These features show Yamato reliance on Chinese culture for ideas and inspiration. Using a Chinese model of imperial statecraft, the Yamato also strengthened rule through mythology and jeweled regalia. This raised kings to a godlike status. Over time, it transformed them into emperors. Later legal codes continued this process. The Kiyomihara Codes of 689 organized monasteries. They created a judiciary. They also managed relations between the king’s advisors and vassals. These developments helped shape Japan’s culture and political system in the later Nara and Heian periods.

North of Yamato lands lived another group. They descended from early Jōmon foragers. These people had lived through, and resisted, the spread of Yayoi settled agriculture. They continued to forage and hunt. They kept their own spiritual beliefs. They rejected the Yamato cultural sphere. They also rejected Yamato borrowings from China, including Buddhism, Confucianism, and the idea of large states ruled by kings and emperors. While the imperial courts in Nara and Heian built stronger ties with China’s Tang dynasty, these northern people followed a different path. Their world was shaped by contact with smaller northern Asian cultures. One example is the Satsumon people of Hokkaido.

Over time, relations between north and south worsened. Nara and Heian elites called the northerners Emishi, meaning “barbarians.” The Emishi survived from the seventh to the eleventh century. They endured repeated attempts by southern emperors and militarists to subjugate them. They resisted through war. They moved into remote areas. They also used other forms of evasion. Still, southern Japanese culture steadily moved north. By the end of the ninth century, the remaining Emishi groups were subdued.

Indian culture, religion, and art changed forever because of Buddha Sakyamuni. He lived around 563 BCE. He was born into a royal family near India’s eastern border with Nepal. He is also known as Siddartha or Gautama.

Sakyamuni lived in luxury in his family’s palace. Then he had an awakening. After that, he left the palace. He began a spiritual journey that lasted the rest of his life. People later called him the Buddha. “Buddha” means “enlightened.” His teachings offered an alternative to the dominant Brahmanist values of his time.

Buddhism looks closely at human suffering. It also examines desire, envy, decadence, and death. It offers a way out of an endless cycle of misery. This path begins with the Four Noble Truths. The Four Noble Truths lead to the Eightfold Path.

The Four Noble Truths say that pain and disappointment are unavoidable in life. They also teach that suffering can be overcome. This happens by focusing on spiritual matters through the Eightfold Path. Buddha taught people how to think, speak, and act with respect for all life. He also taught many other practices. Over time, followers can reach an enlightened salvation called *nirvana*.

Nirvana is a state of ultimate peace. It comes from the extinction of all desire. It also involves transcending the person’s very being. Without nirvana, the soul is reincarnated after death. It is reborn into a new life. That new life again includes suffering, misery, and the search for enlightenment.

Buddha and his followers challenged the status quo in ancient India. Buddha criticized the Brahmans. He questioned their authority. He also questioned their dependence on ritualism. Later teachers, missionaries, and lay Buddhists continued this challenge. They used his teachings to attack the Brahmanist-based caste system.

Many women were drawn to Buddhism. Buddhism promoted the idea that women could achieve enlightenment. It offered this opportunity on an equal basis with men.

Before Buddhism, Brahmanist teachings supported a strict gender system. In the first centuries of the common era, this system described women’s genitalia as foul. Because of this, women were excluded from public rituals and worship. Buddhism did not treat women as spiritually unclean. It promised women higher status. It also offered greater participation in the community’s spiritual life.

Lower-caste people were also drawn to Buddhism. This was true despite their inherited class. Both women and lower castes found more independence and freedom in Buddhism. However, women often found Buddhism patriarchal as well. Monasteries were separated into male and female spheres. Male monks and female nuns lived in segregated communities. Women held lower positions. They also had fewer privileges.

Buddhism never replaced Brahmanism as India’s dominant religion. In later centuries, Buddhism was influenced by Brahmanism. It incorporated deities such as Shiva. It also incorporated concepts such as karma. Over time, the boundaries between the two religions blurred. This helped Brahmanists and Buddhists coexist. It also allowed cooperation.

Buddhism began in a society dominated by Brahmanism. Many Buddhist teachings and practices, such as meditation, show Brahmanist influence. At the same time, Brahmanism was influenced by Buddhism. Buddhism was popular with certain classes in India. Because of this, Brahmanism changed over several centuries. This change happened roughly between 400 BCE and 200 CE.

During this period, Brahmanism became more devotional. It allowed individuals to communicate directly with the gods. People did not rely only on Brahman priests. Worship became more personal and private. It often centered on prayer and songs in the home. In this way, Brahmanism developed into Hinduism.

Hinduism kept the caste system. It also kept belief in the Vedas. At the same time, it offered guidance for ordinary followers. It taught them how to live moral and fulfilling lives. A central text of Hinduism became the *Bhagavad Gita*. It was finished around 300 CE. It taught that commoners, not only Brahmans, could live exemplary moral lives. It emphasized abandoning bodily desires. It also emphasized seeking inner peace.

Both Buddhism and Hinduism were diverse. They branched into hundreds of schools of thought and sects. These were often adaptable to local contexts. As Buddhism became more institutionalized, it lost some of its early character. It was no longer mainly a path of liberation for the lowly of India. Instead, it gained support from elites. Elite patronage helped make Buddhism Asia’s most influential inspiration for monumental architecture and high art.

Buddhism spread across Asia. Millions adopted it in China, Korea, Thailand, and Japan. Many communities in Southeast Asia also adopted it.

Religious life in Rome was varied and diverse. In the first century CE, Christians became part of this landscape. Their relationship with traditional Roman religion was often tense. Early Christians were not one unified group. Still, they often stood out because they refused to take part in some traditional rituals.

Christians usually disapproved of animal sacrifice. They also rejected worship of the emperor. Instead, they focused on prayer and meetings in house churches. Purpose-built churches and basilicas appeared in Rome only in the late third and fourth centuries. Regular gatherings for worship helped Christians form a shared community identity.

Christians also held communal meals. They called each other “brother” and “sister.” They practiced baptism. Baptism differed across the empire, but it focused on cleansing the spirit. It was performed by church leaders, especially bishops or deacons.

Roman officials often worried less about Christian beliefs themselves. They worried more about what Christian practices meant for Roman authority. Officials sometimes called Christians “atheists” because they refused animal sacrifice. At times, Christians were singled out for punishment.

The earliest recorded violence happened under Nero. In 64 CE, a fire broke out in Rome. Nero chose to punish Christians for the fire. Over the next two centuries, local authorities struggled with how to deal with Christian groups.

One example comes from Pliny the Younger. He was a provincial governor in Asia Minor in the early second century. He wrote letters to Emperor Trajan asking what to do about Christians. Pliny said he arrested and questioned people he suspected were Christian. Trajan told him not to hunt for Christians. But Trajan also said that if Christians were caught and refused to renounce their faith, they should be punished.

Later, persecution became more formal. The Edict of Caracalla in 212 extended citizenship across the empire. It also seems to have made everyone responsible for making sacrifices on behalf of the Roman state. In 250, Emperor Decius called for universal sacrifice. After that, it became a crime for Christians across the empire not to sacrifice to the emperor. Torture and death were likely punishments.

This period of persecution ended under Emperor Constantine. After a civil war, Constantine won in 312. He said the Christian God gave him victory. He claimed he saw a vision of a cross in the sky. In 313, he issued the Edict of Milan. It supported religious toleration. Christianity was no longer illegal. Most traditional Roman religious practices could continue.

Constantine also founded Constantinople as a new capital of the empire. He decorated the city with images of himself and religious iconography.

The Roman Empire controlled both its cultural borders and its physical borders.

Romans defended the frontier with an army.  
They also argued constantly about citizenship, or *civitas*.  
They debated who should receive it.

To have *civitas* at birth, a person had to be the child of two citizens.

Citizenship gave important rights.  
It gave voting rights.  
It gave the right to serve in the military.  
It gave the right to run for public office.  
It gave certain marriage and property rights.  
It also gave other legal benefits.

It was not always clear how much non-Romans were blocked from these rights.

Romans placed foreigners into different groups.  
One group was free provincials, called *peregrini*.  
They were not Roman citizens.  
Other groups included army recruits.  
Another group included people living beyond the Roman border.

Foreignness was not fixed.  
A person could move from one group to another.  
The definitions also changed over time.

People could gain citizenship in other ways, not only by birth.

Enslaved people who were manumitted often received citizenship.  
Allied fighters in times of conflict were also likely to receive it.

Romans sometimes granted “Latin Rights.”  
This was a limited form of citizenship.  
It was often given to existing communities after Rome took control of them.

In 212 CE, Emperor Caracalla issued an edict.  
It extended citizenship to all free people in the Roman Empire.

The effects of this edict are not clear.  
Caracalla was accused of having an ulterior motive.  
The surviving text also seems to exclude a group.  
This group may have been stigmatized foreigners or freed people.

Even after the edict, differences in status and ethnicity continued among Romans.

A person could also lose citizenship privileges.

Exile and expulsion were common punishments for criminals.

The poet Ovid lived during the reign of Augustus.  
In several works, he mourned his own exile.  
He was sent to a city on the Black Sea.

The reason for Ovid’s banishment is unclear.  
He seems to have angered the emperor.  
He referred to “a poem and an error” (*carmen et error*) as the cause.

Some people chose exile voluntarily.  
They did this to avoid harsher punishment from Rome.  
This was especially true when the death penalty was possible.

Over time, there were different levels of exile.  
A person might lose their property.  
Or a person might later be allowed to return to Rome.

Rome could also expel whole groups from the city.

In 19 CE, Jewish people were expelled.  
Followers of Isis were also expelled.

Later, under Emperors Nero and Domitian, other groups were expelled.  
These included astrologers, philosophers, and actors.

People who settled in the resource-rich Pacific Northwest formed complex hunter-gatherer societies. They adapted closely to the region’s abundant marine life.

They likely reached the area by following caribou, which they hunted. After settling in the dense forests, they learned to live on many animals. These included beaver, elk, seals, birds, sea lions, and salmon. They also ate many other kinds of fish.

Salmon were a key resource. In the fall, salmon swam upstream to spawn. They were so numerous that people could catch them easily. They used traps, simple dams, or spears. They ate the fish right away or dried them for later.

Halibut was also important. People of the Pacific Northwest made it a staple food.

The land also provided materials for tools. People made harpoons from bone. These harpoons helped them hunt large marine mammals, including whales. They polished local rocks into woodworking tools. With these tools, they carved dugout canoes from trees.

They also developed advanced woodcarving. They used it to create art. They made special fishhooks from bone and wood. They used certain kinds of tree bark to make cloth and baskets.

Because resources were so abundant, these groups could build wealth more easily than many other hunter-gatherers. Their societies became complex. Wealth and social status were linked.

Archaeological evidence supports this. A few burial sites from around 2000 BCE suggest that wealth already shaped social differences. In the graves of very wealthy people, archaeologists found carved antler tools. They also found objects made from shells. Over time, wealthy graves included even more items. These objects showed higher social status.

There is also evidence that some areas had high population density. This was possible because food was plentiful. People could also store and save food supplies.

In the wide Great Plains, in the center of North America, settlers hunted large herds of bison. The bison grazed on the short grasses that grew there.

Unlike the animals hunted by the Clovis people, bison could adapt to a warming climate. They survived and spread across the plains.

The people who followed the bison lived a seminomadic life. They moved often and owned few belongings. Because of this, their society had less social stratification than the societies of the Pacific Northwest.

Bison hunting was dangerous. Hunters had to keep their distance. They did not want to startle the animals. They also did not want the bison to become fearful of humans.

Archaeological sites in central Canada, Texas, Montana, Wyoming, and Colorado show that by 8000 BCE, hunters used a cliff-driving method. They drove bison herds over cliffs to their deaths. This could kill or injure many animals at once, sometimes hundreds. Afterward, hunters processed the carcasses. They used the meat, bones, and hides.

Hunters also used other methods. One method was to corner a herd. This let hunters get close enough to use spears.

Plains peoples hunted more than bison. They also hunted antelope and deer. They hunted small animals too, such as rabbits and birds.

Bird hunting sometimes used decoys. Hunters made decoys with feathers. The decoys helped hunters get close enough to kill the birds.

Animal hides were useful for clothing. Soft hides, like rabbit hides, could be stitched together. People used plant materials for stitching.

People also gathered edible plants. These included seeds, berries, nuts, acorns, and tubers. Tubers included yampa and biscuit-root. People dug them up with digging sticks.

People carried and stored food in containers. They used coiled baskets made from plants. They also used bags made from leather.

East of the Great Plains are the wetter, greener Eastern Woodlands.  
This region stretches from the Mississippi River basin to the Atlantic coast.

People who lived there found many plants and animals to use for food and other needs.  
The region had many rivers and lakes.  
These provided fresh water.  
They also encouraged people to settle along the shores.

Oxbow lakes were also important.  
These are U-shaped pools that formed as river courses stabilized in warmer conditions.  
Oxbow lakes were good places to hunt and fish.  
People hunted and fished for catfish, deer, birds, rabbits, and many other animals.

People also ate many plants.  
They gathered nuts from oak, chestnut, and beech trees.  
Near the coast, they could also use saltwater marine life.

In this region, people did not need to move as often.  
Settlements could last longer.  
Around 6500 BCE, populations began to rise.

People also built large earthworks.  
These were built in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Florida.

The oldest known earthwork is Watson Brake in northern Louisiana.  
It dates to about 3900 BCE.  
It includes several human-made earth mounds.  
Some mounds are as high as twenty-five feet.  
They are arranged in a circular formation.

Archaeologists think Watson Brake was likely used by hunter-gatherers.  
They believe it was used on a seasonal basis.

No burial remains have been found at Watson Brake.  
However, large cemeteries from the same period have been found in other woodland areas.  
These include sites in Illinois and Tennessee.

Some of these sites contain the remains of more than one hundred individuals.  
Some people were buried with personal items.  
These items include weapons and art.

These cemeteries show that populations were rising.  
They also show that people were living in one place more often.

chapter_key: Early Cultures of the American Southwest
text:
Far west of the mound-building cultures, a different tradition grew in the dry Southwest.

People there began testing maize very early. This started as early as the third millennium BCE. Some groups planted maize in small plots along riverbanks. They used it to add to a hunter-gatherer way of life.

We do not know exactly how maize traveled from southern Mexico to the American Southwest. There must have been occasional contact. Farmers in the south likely met hunter-gatherers farther north. For many centuries, maize stayed a small part of life in the Southwest. Most people still relied on hunting and gathering. The dry climate may have forced people to move often. That may have made farming less useful at first.

Some of the earliest proof of maize farming dates to about 2250 BCE. This evidence comes from what is now northwestern New Mexico.

By about 1200 BCE, groups at Las Capas made major advances. Las Capas was near the Santa Cruz River, close to modern Tucson, Arizona. These people built a complex irrigation system to grow maize. They dug canals to carry river water into their fields.

They built oval-shaped homes near their fields. They also dug pits to roast the maize they grew. Over time, the homes became more complex. They were arranged in rings around courtyards.

Even at Las Capas, maize was still only one part of life. People continued to hunt and gather most of their food. They gathered goosefoot and piñons. They hunted rabbits, bison, and deer.

By about 500 BCE, people also began growing beans. This added more variety to their diet. Beans encouraged greater reliance on maize. The two foods work well together for nutrition. Beans provide lysine, an amino acid that maize lacks. Beans also add nitrogen to the soil. This helps the soil stay fertile longer.

Even with beans, fully settled farming communities did not appear until around 200 CE. After that, the region changed quickly. This transformation led to the Anasazi, also called the Ancestral Pueblo societies.

chapter_key: The Last Great Empires of Antiquity
text:
In the sixth and seventh centuries, the Byzantines and the Sasanians fought for a long time. This was their longest period of ongoing conflict. There were some peaceful periods. There were even times when they were allies. But most of the time, their relationship was defined by war.

Khosrow I was a very skilled military leader. He stopped several invasions by nomadic peoples into the Sasanian Empire. In 532, he made peace with the Byzantines. But the peace did not last. Khosrow moved west into Byzantine territory. At the same time, Justinian was busy trying to reconquer Italy.

A long war lasted from 541 to 557. During this war, the Sasanians took parts of Byzantine-controlled land. These included Armenia and Syria. A truce was signed in 557. It ended in 565, when Justinian died. After that, fighting began again.

Khosrow II was the last Sasanian king to fight a long war with the Byzantines. At first, he had a friendly relationship with them. He had regained his throne from a rival with help from the Byzantine emperor Maurice. But then Maurice was murdered. Khosrow used this as a reason to invade Byzantine territory in 602.

The Sasanians again took Armenia and Syria. This time they went further. They took Palestine and Egypt. By 619, they had even reached Libya. The Byzantines fought back successfully. They recovered all the territory they had lost. Because of this, Khosrow II was removed from power in 628.

Even with all this fighting, the two empires shared some court rituals. They also exchanged culture and ideas. People from each empire were present at the other’s court. They communicated often through embassies. This continued even during wartime.

Court rituals included gift exchanges. They also included processions and games. Both empires used similar symbols to show power. They treated their capital cities as centers of authority. These were Constantinople and Ctesiphon. They also connected themselves to past imperial glory. They created art to show that their rule was legitimate. Each empire accepted the other as a legitimate rival state. At the same time, both competed for universal power.

During this period of near-constant war, both empires used smaller states as proxies. Armenians were Christians, and there were religious rivalries. Even so, Armenians often asked the Sasanians for help. The Byzantines also played different nomadic groups against each other.

Over time, both great empires became less powerful across their territories. Their geographic strength slowly shrank. States on the edges of the empires became more important.

Their geographic strength slowly shrank.

States on the edges of the empires became more important.

text:
East Africa was an important part of the Indian Ocean trade network. This network linked East Africa with the Middle East, China, and East and Southeast Asia.

At first, trade in East Africa focused on the Red Sea. Egypt had been ruled by the Hellenistic world and later by Rome. This made trade with Greece and Rome especially important and profitable.

East Africa traded luxury goods with the Roman Empire. These goods included ivory, furs, and spices such as frankincense and myrrh.

After the Roman Empire collapsed, other groups took over more of this trade. Many of these traders came from places like Arabia.

Over time, new trading ports appeared farther down the east coast of Africa. At the same time, Bantu-speaking Africans moved into the region.

A new and advanced culture developed on the Swahili coast. It expanded its role in Indian Ocean trade. It built powerful city-states. It also traded with the African interior.

After Mongke Khan died in 1259, a civil war began. Hulagu Khan had to manage several conflicts at the same time.

The biggest danger was war with the Golden Horde. The Golden Horde was led by Berke, Batu’s younger brother. Berke had converted to Islam. He was deeply upset by Hulagu’s destruction of Baghdad. He was also upset by the murder of the caliph.

Hulagu and Berke also argued about tribute. They disagreed over who should receive tribute from areas where Hulagu had restored stability.

Hulagu and Berke supported different sides in the civil war to succeed Mongke. Their war lasted almost four years. It ended only when both men died in 1265. After that, their successors focused on other goals.

For decades, the Il-Khanate faced repeated conflict. It fought the Golden Horde and the Mamluks of Egypt. Sometimes the Seljuks from Anatolia joined these enemies. Sometimes the Chagatai khans joined them too.

Defending against these attacks used most of the Il-Khanate’s effort and resources. This problem grew worse because of periodic civil wars over succession. Because of this, further expansion was not possible.

The Il-Khans struggled to hold the Tigris-Euphrates basin. They could not take the Nile delta. They also could not take the Levant, including lands holy to the Abrahamic religions. These areas stayed beyond their control.

Most people in the Il-Khanate had become Muslim centuries earlier. Because the Il-Khans had to focus on defense, they left much of government to religious scholars. These scholars were called the *ulama*. This strengthened traditional Islamic law and custom.

Ghazan Khan ruled from 1295 to 1304. He strongly favored Islam. His brother Oljaitu took the Muslim name Khodabandeh. Oljaitu promoted Shia Islam. This helped deepen Shia influence in what is now eastern Iraq and Iran.

Even so, conflict with Muslim neighbors continued. The Il-Khanate still tried to take more resources for itself. It did this at its neighbors’ expense.

The economy recovered slowly from the destruction caused by Hulagu’s attack. Frequent wars kept damaging irrigation systems and city infrastructure.

There were long-term labor shortages in the first generations after the conquest. Many people had been murdered. Many had been enslaved. Many had been relocated. Many also emigrated to nearby Islamic lands.

Ghazan’s reign prepared the way for a generation of prosperity and cultural growth. This was greater than in the unstable periods before and after his rule. The center of this prosperity was east of Baghdad and the Tigris-Euphrates basin. It was focused around Maragha and Tabriz in modern Iran.

The Il-Khanate rulers tried to follow the dream of Chinggis and Ogedei Khan. They wanted a world united by trade. They negotiated trade deals, especially with Venice and Genoa in Italy. They also kept secure trade with Mongolian China.

This prosperity did not solve the danger of succession struggles. In 1335, the son of Ghazan died without an heir. The Il-Khanate fell into a civil war. It never recovered from that war.

After 1335, several men claimed to be *il-khan*. None of them controlled more than a fraction of the lands Hulagu had conquered.

- **the Mamluks of Egypt**

This problem grew worse because of **periodic civil wars over succession**. Because of this, further expansion was not possible.

Frequent wars kept damaging:
- irrigation systems
- city infrastructure

Many people had been:
- murdered
- enslaved
- relocated

This prosperity did not solve the danger of succession struggles.

text:
Turan Shah did not live long enough to enjoy his success.

The wandering Turks in his army had become mamluks. They were the backbone of his forces. They believed the ransom money from the crusaders would be used against them. They feared Turan Shah would replace them with more traditional mamluks from Africa.

To protect their position, they overthrew Turan Shah. They also wanted control of the ransom money.

Turan Shah’s stepmother was Shajar al-Durr. She was the surviving widow of al-Salih. She briefly took the throne. But the mamluks would not follow a female sultan. They forced her to marry their leader, Izz al-Din Aybak. They also forced her to give up the throne in his favor.

Historians see Aybak’s rise as a turning point. It ended the Ayyubid dynasty. It began the Egyptian Mamluk dynasty.

The Ayyubids left important marks on the Islamic Levant. They restored Sunni Islam as the leading form of Islam. This came after over two hundred years of Shia Fatimid rule. They built new madrasas in Aleppo, Cairo, and Damascus. Madrasas were Muslim schools of learning. They often focused on studying the Quran.

While Christians and Muslims fought each other, Hulagu Khan prepared to expand Mongol rule. His troops had looted Baghdad. Their supply routes were secure. They moved north to lands better for the huge herds the army needed.

Hulagu decided that Syria and Egypt would be his next targets. These areas were under Mamluk control. He demanded that the Mamluk sultan become his vassal and pay tribute. The sultan refused.

In 1259, Hulagu attacked the Mamluks. First, he secured cooperation, or at least noninterference, from Islamic forces in Anatolia. He also secured cooperation from crusader forces in the region. At first, he succeeded. He took Aleppo. Aleppo was destroyed, like Baghdad. He also took Damascus. Damascus surrendered without conditions and was mostly spared.

Hulagu did not stay long. In early 1260, he learned he was needed at a *kurultai* in Karakorum.

Hulagu seems to have underestimated the Mamluks. He withdrew possibly 90 percent of his forces as he returned to Karakorum. Even so, he ordered Kitbuqa to invade Egypt. Kitbuqa was one of his top generals. He was also a Nestorian Christian. Hulagu gave him twenty thousand troops.

Kitbuqa’s army gained extra support. Christian Armenians joined him. Some remaining crusaders also joined him.

In the fall of 1260, the Mamluks attacked at Ain Jalut. They defeated the Mongols decisively. They killed Kitbuqa and most of his force.

This loss was small compared with Hulagu’s total forces. But it mattered. It helped protect parts of the Islamic world that the Mongols had not conquered.

Soon, Hulagu faced other threats. He had to defend his lands from other Mongols. The Golden Horde was a major enemy.

Meanwhile, the Mamluks pushed back their enemies. They freed Syria and Palestine from the Mongols. They also freed these areas from the remaining crusaders. They gave some support to the Golden Horde in its conflicts with the Il-Khanate.

## turan shah’s short rule

turan shah did not live long enough to enjoy his success.


---

## the mamluks overthrow turan shah

the wandering turks in his army had become mamluks.  
they were the backbone of his forces.

they feared two things:

- the ransom money from the crusaders would be used against them  
- turan shah would replace them with more traditional mamluks from africa

to protect their position, they overthrew turan shah.  
they also wanted control of the ransom money.


---

## shajar al-durr and the rise of aybak

turan shah’s stepmother was shajar al-durr.  
she was the surviving widow of al-salih.

she briefly took the throne.  
but the mamluks would not follow a female sultan.

they forced her to marry their leader, **izz al-din aybak**.  
they also forced her to give up the throne in his favor.

historians see aybak’s rise as a turning point:

- it ended the ayyubid dynasty  
- it began the egyptian mamluk dynasty  


---

the ayyubids left important marks on the islamic levant.

they restored sunni islam as the leading form of islam.  
this came after over two hundred years of shia fatimid rule.

they built new madrasas in:

- aleppo  
- cairo  
- damascus  

madrasas were muslim schools of learning.  
they often focused on studying the quran.


---

his troops had looted baghdad.  
their supply routes were secure.

they moved north to lands better for the huge herds the army needed.

hulagu decided that syria and egypt would be his next targets.  
these areas were under mamluk control.

he demanded that the mamluk sultan:

- pay tribute

at first, he succeeded:

chapter_key: The Black Death in Asia and North Africa
text:
Chinese records do not give an exact date for the Black Death’s arrival in China.  
They first mention a deadly epidemic in the years 1331 to 1334.  

Accounts from the Chinese Imperial Maritime Customs Service were compiled in the late 1800s.  
These accounts suggest that about thirteen million people died in this outbreak.  

For people in China, the disaster may have seemed like a warning.  
It could have looked like the Yuan dynasty had lost the Mandate of Heaven.  
Epidemics, droughts, and other disasters were often seen as signs of divine anger.  
They could be taken as proof that a ruler no longer had divine support.  

After devastating China, the plague spread west.  
It moved along trade routes by land and by sea.  
These routes allowed it to reach much of the Middle East.  

The Il-Khanate depended heavily on Silk Road trade networks.  
This made it especially vulnerable when the plague disrupted trade communities.  
At the same time, the Il-Khanate was in a long conflict with the Golden Horde to the north.  
The Il-Khanate was already weakened by invasion, internal disputes, and the death of its ruler.  
Abu Sa’id Bahadur Khan died in 1335, possibly from plague.  

After Abu Sa’id’s death, Mongol rule in the Il-Khanate weakened further.  
The plague damaged trade and reduced the population.  
This made the decline worse.  

Tabriz in Iran had long been a major trade center.  
By the 1340s, it was largely abandoned.  
Foreign merchants fled suddenly.  
Commerce collapsed.  
To understand the shock, imagine modern trade cities like New York, Tokyo, London, or Hong Kong.  
Imagine them suddenly becoming ruined and empty ghost towns.  

The fall of Tabriz stunned people at the time.  
But few cities were spared.  
Infected fleas traveled easily with trade caravans.  
They moved across Central Asia and into the Middle East.  

Death rates across the Middle East were high.  
Much of what we know comes from records about the Mamluk Empire (1250–1517).  
The Mamluk Empire lost about one-third of its population.  

The Mamluk rulers were based in Cairo.  
Trade routes in the Nile delta were hit especially hard.  

In Egypt, the plague was made worse by local famines.  
These famines disrupted farming.  
Many rural peasants went to big cities like Cairo and Alexandria.  
They looked for work as unskilled wage laborers.  
Crowded city life increased their risk of catching the plague.  

Nomads in the region had long avoided settled areas when strange diseases appeared.  
Many escaped by retreating into the desert.  

In 1347, some of Cairo’s Mamluk elite fled to rural areas north of the city.  
Most stayed in Cairo.  
They wanted to protect their citadel from rival attacks.  
By staying, they exposed themselves to the plague.  
Many of them died.  

Islamic scholars wrote treatises in the 1340s.  
These texts help us understand Muslim responses to the plague.  
They served as chronicles of the epidemic.  
They also offered medical guidance and advice on proper behavior.  

Doctors could not define the disease.  
They also could not cure it.  
So many texts explained the plague in religious terms.  
They used the Quran and religious law for guidance.  

These writings often said the plague was not contagious.  
They told people not to flee.  
They described the plague as a chance for martyrdom for faithful Muslims.  
They also described it as a warning from God to infidels.  

Other Arab writers described the plague as an apocalyptic disaster.  
They linked it to a breach in the gate that separated humanity from Gog and Magog.  
In tradition, Gog and Magog were evil forces that threatened the faithful.  

Even with this apocalyptic language, the Muslim response was usually different from some other regions.  
It generally lacked the doomsday predictions and persecution of minorities seen in Christian Europe.  
Many people likely fled anyway, despite the treatises.  
But writers often stressed a collective and controlled response.  
They emphasized resignation and acceptance of God’s will.  

Many industries in Mamluk cities declined sharply during the plague.  
At the same time, construction increased.  
More madrasas, mosques, and tombs were built.  
For survivors, these buildings expressed gratitude.  
Artisans who worked on them were often paid very well.  

One other group also did well.  
Spice merchants prospered.  
Egypt remained an important depot in the international spice trade.  

Still, agriculture and many other trades collapsed.  
The Mamluks’ golden age ended abruptly in 1341.  
The Mamluks continued to rule until 1517.  
But fierce internal clashes and ethnic rivalries caused major instability.  
This instability eventually led to the empire’s collapse.

The Mamluks’ golden age ended abruptly in **1341**.

Beginning around 1800 BCE, centuries of trade between the Indus Valley and Mesopotamia ended.

The civilization declined, likely in stages.

Around 2000 BCE, the Indus River floodplain shifted dramatically.  
This created dry riverbeds where water had once flowed.  
Some cities had been built near these rivers.

Changes in seasonal wind and rainfall may have caused these effects.  
In South Asia, this seasonal pattern is called the **monsoon**.  
If water became less reliable, people would have struggled.  
They needed water for drinking and for irrigation.  
Without secure water, city populations would likely fall.

Another theory focuses on long-term environmental damage.  
Centuries of urban growth and rising population may have degraded the land.  
This could have made the region less suitable for large human populations.

Other ideas also exist.  
Some scholars suggest tectonic activity changed river courses.  
Others suggest epidemic disease reduced the population.

Before these environmental explanations became common, many people supported a different view.  
For many years, the main idea was that the Indus Valley civilization was destroyed by conquest.

This view is called the Aryan invasion theory.  
It says nomadic Indo-European speakers, who called themselves Aryans, conquered the region.  
The Aryans were Sanskrit-speaking nomadic pastoralists.  
They raised cattle and horses.

Some Aryans began migrating from the Eurasian Steppe around 3500 BCE.  
This steppe lay north of the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea.  
Over time, different groups spread into Europe, Anatolia, and Iran.

It was produced sometime between 1500 and 1000 BCE in northwestern India.

It describes deities and other religious topics.  
It aims to explain the origin of the universe and the nature of the divine.

Some parts also describe the arrival of the Aryans.  
These passages describe attacks on walled cities and forts.

This evidence gives some support to the conquest claim.

More than one cause may have contributed.

Environmental degradation likely had an effect.  
Years of resource use and high population density could damage the land.  
Climate change and disease could have made the situation worse.  
If the region was already weakened, it would be more vulnerable to raids.  
Groups like the Aryans could have taken advantage of that weakness.

However it happened, by around 1500 BCE the social and political systems had broken down.  
The sophisticated culture of the Indus Valley civilization collapsed.

People abandoned the architectural styles of the great cities.  
They also stopped using the writing system.

chapter_key: The Nomadic Culture of the Steppes
text:
The eastern half of the Eurasian Steppe is sometimes called the **Inner Asian Steppe**.  
Today it has wide grasslands, mountains, and deserts.  
Most of this land is not good for farming.  
Few people live there.

Climate change shaped the region’s history.  
In Mongolia, rainfall once supported herds of sheep, camels, goats, and horses.  
When the climate cooled, the grasslands could shrink.  
Nomads then had to travel to find new pastures.  
Drought could also push them into crisis.  
If nearby societies would not trade, nomads often raided farms and cities to survive.

Scholars now think that around **1500 BCE**, the climate became colder and drier.  
This may have forced many people to stop farming.  
They turned instead to herding livestock.  
Herding required people to move often.  
They had to find fresh grass and protect animals from predators.  
This need led to cultural change.  
People became skilled at horseback riding.

As herders, many steppe peoples ate a lot of meat and dairy.  
They also made goods from animal flesh and furs.  
They could trade these goods in farming villages.  
They spoke languages not related to Chinese, such as **Turkic** or **Mongolic**.  
A few groups, such as the **Jie**, may have spoken **Indo-European** languages.

Because climate made pastoral life difficult, steppe peoples stayed in constant contact with farming civilizations.  
This included the Chinese.  
Chinese societies often saw nomads and their herds as a danger to their livelihoods.  
For centuries, Chinese and Koreans tried to build physical and cultural barriers.  
They wanted separation from “foreign” steppe groups.  
Even so, ethnic and ancestral lines were not fixed.  
They were porous between nomads and their neighbors.

During raids, steppe peoples took prizes.  
These included silk, lacquerware, grain, and war captives.  
Chieftains gave these goods to loyal supporters.  
Supporters then honored leaders with titles.  
One title was *chanyu*, or **khan**.  
This meant a supreme leader with spiritual and military authority.

Khans gained more power through horses.  
They could command thousands of horses.  
In an age of cavalry warfare, this mattered greatly.

Steppe tribal confederations also controlled the **Silk Roads**.  
These were trade routes for luxury goods.  
They connected China with parts of central Asia, India, and the Middle East.  
For mobile societies, manufactured and luxury goods had huge value.  
They mattered for daily life, status, and politics.

**Silk** was especially prized.  
It was light, which helped in hot summers.  
It was also soft, which made it good for lining beds.  
Generals and khans who collected large amounts of silk used it to show power.  
Other luxury goods, such as wine, had similar importance.

Most nomadic groups lived in small family units.  
They also lived in a **clan**.  
A clan was several families sharing one camp.  
They herded or hunted together.  
Clans followed a chieftain.  
The chieftain was chosen for skill as a mounted warrior.

Compared with many ancient cultures, steppe societies were more egalitarian.  
Differences in role and status between men and women were less strict than in cities and farming settlements.  
Archaeology supports this.  
Female skeletons from the **Xiongnu**, **Xianbei**, and **Turkic** peoples show signs of horseback riding.  
They also show evidence of combat skills, such as archery.  
These women may have inspired later stories.  
One example is the legend of **Mulan**, which began circulating in Chinese society in the sixth century.

A mobile life limited how much wealth people could own.  
It also limited how much they could display wealth.  
Large buildings and elaborate clothing were harder to maintain.  
This may help explain why written scripts were less common.  
At the same time, steppe cultures often adopted new technologies, goods, and ideas from neighbors.

Steppe peoples were pioneers in domesticating the horse.  
This gave them a major military advantage.  
Riding and hunting trained people for war.  
They started both at a young age.  
Hunting was central to nomadic life.  
It was also part of rituals.  
These rituals marked progress from child to adult.  
They could also mark a rise in social rank.

The steppes touched both Europe and Asia.  
They formed a bridge between the two.  
From this bridge, new developments spread across Asia.  
These included the chariot and cavalry warfare.  
Chariots and mounted warriors helped create large confederations.  
These confederations became serious military threats.

Campaigns led by steppe conquerors changed regional history.  
One example is **Modun**, who came to power in **209 BCE**.  
Such campaigns marked a turning point.  
They reshaped relations between the Inner Asian Steppe and China.  
They also affected the growing Silk Roads as major routes of exchange in the ancient world.

Periods of conquest helped the Roman economy in several ways. Romans wanted to control natural resources. They also wanted wealth from the lands they conquered. The money from conquest helped Rome feed its people. It also helped Rome pay its troops.

In early Rome, the army was made of volunteers. These volunteers were called up only during war. By the time of the empire, the army had changed. It became a permanent, professional force.

The Roman **legion** was the main unit of the army. Its structure changed over time. A legion had about five thousand soldiers. It was led by a legate. A legion also included craftspeople. It also included people who helped with building projects.

After the reforms of Augustus, there were twenty-eight legions. They were placed across the provinces and along the frontier. Each legion had a number. Many also had nicknames. The nicknames came from where they were formed or where they served. Legions could move around the empire. For example, the First German legion might be stationed in Spain.

Soldiers served for sixteen years. Later, the term was raised to twenty years. Soldiers were paid a set amount at the end of their service. Soldiers and military staff received a large share of the wealth taken in war. Sometimes they were also promised land taken during Rome’s conflicts.

Many wars were meant to gain resources and money. Rome’s grain supply grew greatly after it conquered Egypt in the first century BCE. Earlier in Rome’s history, conquest of Sicily and Sardinia also expanded the grain supply. People captured in war were often sold in Roman slave markets. Enslaved and freed people did much of Rome’s work. Their labor was the backbone of Roman industry. Because of this, enslaved people also supported the economy.

This system had trade-offs. As the Roman army grew, it became more expensive. As the frontier expanded, conflict also became more costly. Earlier, soldiers might fight only part of the year. In the imperial period, fighting on the frontier became common. Campaigns could last for months. Some wars may have seemed endless.

Distance also raised costs. Campaigns far from the city of Rome were expensive. Paying and supplying the army required huge resources. This pressure encouraged further conquest. Over time, this situation strained the Roman military.

Continuous war also harmed society. Romans were proud of their military strength. Still, the loss of life and property was a heavy burden. War abroad disrupted regional markets that Italy depended on. For example, a break in the grain supply in 190 CE caused famine and riots in the city of Rome. Elites benefited most from conquest. People in the lower classes likely carried more of the negative effects.

After the Carolingian Empire collapsed, Europe became unstable.  
This created tension between secular rulers and the Christian Church.

Under German law, lords controlled everything on their land.  
This control included churches and monasteries.

Lords also controlled church appointments.  
They could choose abbots and bishops.

Many lords wanted loyal church leaders.  
So they appointed family members.  
Some lords sold church offices to the highest bidder.

This caused serious problems.  
People with no religious calling could become church leaders.  
Some did not even know basic Christian teaching.

Even the pope could be treated this way.  
The pope is the bishop of Rome.  
At times, the papal office could be bought and sold.

Many people were disgusted by this.  
A reform movement began.  
Its goal was to remove secular control from the church.

This movement is often linked to the monastery of Cluny in France.  
Cluny gained independence from a local aristocrat.  
Other monasteries in France wanted the same rights and protections.  
This created the **Cluniac reform** movement.

Over time, the movement spread beyond monasteries.  
More clergy joined it.  
They wanted the church to choose bishops without interference from lords.  
Eventually, this push for independence reached the top of the church.  
It reached the bishop of Rome.

Popes and reformers began to change church practices.  
They condemned the sale of church offices.  
They called this sin **simony**.

They also said bishops should be elected by clergy.  
A lord should not control the election.  
Clergy who bought an office, or had one bought for them, could be removed.

Reformers also wanted to stop church offices from becoming family property.  
They did not want a church position treated like a fief.  
They did not want it passed to an officeholder’s children.

So priests were told to be celibate.  
They were forbidden to marry.

Celibacy was not new in the Catholic Church.  
But reforming monks and popes enforced it more strongly than before.

These reforms created conflict with European rulers.  
The church responded with a serious threat.  
A king who tried to appoint a bishop could be excommunicated.  
A king who demanded a bribe could also be excommunicated.

Excommunication meant being placed outside the church.  
It meant exclusion from communion and the sacraments.  
The goal was to pressure the person to change.

Excommunication could weaken a king.  
It could threaten his rule.  
It could even encourage rebellion.

Reformers also wanted a more Christian society.  
They tried to define what kinds of war were acceptable.

The church argued that Christian soldiers should follow a moral code.  
This was especially aimed at knights.

For example, knights should not loot monasteries.  
They should not hold clergy for ransom.  
They should protect the church.  
They should protect women and the defenseless.

They should also follow declared truces.  
They should not fight on holy days like Easter.

These ideas helped shape **chivalry**.  
Chivalry was a code meant to Christianize knightly violence and behavior.

In practice, chivalry did not stop violence.  
It was only one part of a wider, secular interest in knightly culture.  
Still, images of Christian knights became useful to popes.  
They helped popes justify directing Europe’s warriors against people seen as enemies of the church, and therefore of God.

The reform movement gave the church more moral prestige.  
But it also increased tensions between eastern and western Christianity.

In the Middle Ages, five ancient Christian centers were seen as most prestigious:  
Jerusalem, Antioch, Alexandria, Rome, and Constantinople.

Each center was led by a bishop called a “patriarch.”  
By the tenth century, only Rome and Constantinople were not under Muslim rule.

Rome and Constantinople shared many beliefs.  
But language and culture pushed them apart.

In the west, the church used Latin.  
It insisted clergy should be celibate.  
It also taught that the pope was the final authority for the whole church.

In the east, the church used Greek.  
It allowed priests to marry.  
Tradition still said bishops should be unmarried.  
The eastern church also believed other patriarchs had authority equal to the pope.

The reform movement made these divisions sharper.  
It did not intend to do this, but it happened.

In 1054, the pope sent representatives to Constantinople.  
They went to discuss differences between east and west.

The pope’s chief representative thought the patriarch was not cooperating.  
He also felt the patriarch did not recognize the embassy.  
So he issued a letter excommunicating the patriarch and his followers.

Soon after, the patriarch responded.  
He issued a letter excommunicating the pope’s representatives.

This event is called the **Great Schism of 1054**.  
After it, the eastern church became known as the Eastern Orthodox Church.  
The western church became known as the Catholic Church.

The Great Schism was not the only cause of division.  
Tensions had been growing for a long time.  
But the schism made the split clear.

It also showed that Christianity was developing differently in different regions.  
After this, popes hoped to reunite the churches under papal authority.  
They wanted the Orthodox Church to accept their reforms.

Orthodox bishops might accept the pope as “first among equals.”  
But the papacy insisted on being the supreme authority in the church.

these regions were **less economically developed** than the il-khanate.

people in these areas lived in many different ways, and power was **less centralized** than under the il-khans.

because of this, the region avoided breaking into civil war.  
this lasted until **outside forces intervened**, more than a generation after the il-khanate fell.


---

### founding leaders and rule

**batu** and **berke** were the horde’s founding leaders.

they created a capital to store tribute, as their grandfather had done.  
but they mostly traveled with their armies.

their rule relied on movement and force:

- they **raided neighbors**  
- they **defended against attacks**  


---

### peoples of the golden horde

the golden horde ruled many different peoples.

**turkish groups** included the **kipchaks**.  
the kipchaks were **seminomads**, similar to the mongols.

the horde also ruled **settled slavic peasants**, many living in small towns.


---

### how the horde governed

#### indirect rule over turkish groups

the mongols ruled many turkish groups **indirectly**.

local leaders were allowed to:

- enforce the **yassa**  
- collect **taxes**  
- conscript **labor and soldiers**  

mongol officials in the capital:

- received and distributed **tribute**  
- heard **appeals** about local decisions  


#### more direct rule over the rus and other slavs

the rus and other slavic peoples were ruled **more directly**.

mongol overseers were assigned to each local ruler.  
their job was to:

- make sure **taxes were paid**  
- help prevent **rebellion**  


---

### religion in the golden horde

**berke** was the first ruler and khan of the golden horde to adopt **islam**.

not all later khans were muslim.  
even so, islam kept gaining followers among the horde’s mongols.

in **1313**, **uzbeg** made islam the **official religion** of the golden horde.

however, he did **not** remove the yassa tax exemption for other religions.  
uzbeg’s support of islam strengthened islamic communities across horde lands.


---

### the orthodox church under horde rule

horde rule also strengthened the **orthodox church** in slavic regions.

the church came to represent **rus national identity**.  
people turned to christianity to distinguish themselves from the mongols.  
they may also have used it to resist mongol rule in subtle ways.

under the **yassa**, religious institutions and their leaders had **tax and service exemptions**.  
these exemptions were greater than what the church received from rus nobles.

because of this, church landholdings **grew** under the horde.


---

### why church landholdings grew

this growth may have happened through **donations**.

people may have donated land to support the church’s growing role.  
the church provided:

- **spiritual comfort**  
- a **sense of identity**  

growth may also have come through **fraud**.

some elites could avoid mongol taxes and duties by donating land.  
then they became church officials in charge of that land.

by the late **fifteenth century**, mongol rule collapsed.  
by then, the russian orthodox church owned about **one-third of the arable land** in areas once ruled by rus nobles.


---

### trade and the pax mongolica

the golden horde benefited from the **pax mongolica**, and it also helped create that prosperity.

direct european trade was under **horde control**.

goods entering the mongol world in the east often passed through horde lands:

- some goods were made by the **rus**  
- others were brought by **italian merchants** from europe  

in either case, they almost certainly entered through the golden horde.  
this gave the horde the **first chance to buy** them.

the **yam system** helped goods move across the empire.  
it continued for **hundreds of years** after mongol rule faded.


---

## the chagatai khanate

### location and conflict

the chagatai khanate lay in the middle of mongol territory.  
because of this, conflict with other mongol states was hard to avoid.  
conflict with kublai’s yuan dynasty was also likely.

at different times, other mongol states supported usurpers against chagatai khans:

- sometimes they acted **alone**  
- sometimes they acted **together**  

most of these efforts did not succeed in the long term.  
but they kept the khanate **unstable**.

by the mid-fourteenth century, it broke into **smaller states**.


---

### conflict beyond the mongol world

chagatai rulers also fought outside the mongol world.

some raided the **delhi sultanate**.  
on a couple of occasions, they tried to **conquer** it.

these attempts failed.  
they weakened the chagatai regime, which invited more challenges and more instability.


---

### the chagatai khanate and islam

the chagatai khanate’s most important long-term impact involved **islam**.  
it helped secure islam’s hold over **western central asia**.

central asia had long been religiously diverse.  
merchants of many faiths traveled its trade routes.

the region helped spread:

- **buddhism** from india  
- **islam** beyond the caliphate’s borders  
- forms of **christianity** (asian versions, different from catholic and orthodox christianity in europe)  


---

### tarmashirin and legal change

**tarmashirin** was the last ruler of the unified chagatai khanate.

he introduced policies that **favored islam** over other faiths.

he replaced the **yassa** with **sharia** (islamic religious law).  
sharia was **more restrictive**.

this change angered many non-muslim communities.  
even so, islamic law remained in place in chagatai lands afterward.

this continued even after the khanate broke into small, warring states.

He also had to pay the pope tribute.

Even if the king wrote them, nobles, clergy, and wealthy commoners had to agree.

Edward I called his first Parliament in 1275.

---

Other areas were part of the Islamic Almohad Caliphate.

Enslaved people lived very different lives across the empire. Their daily life depended on age and gender. It also depended on where they lived. Some lived in the countryside. Others lived in towns and cities.

Enslaved people did many kinds of work. Some did unskilled labor. Some worked as artisans. Some helped merchants and shopkeepers. Many were trained as teachers, doctors, musicians, and actors. Others helped build public works, such as bridges and roads. Some even served as imperial administrators.

City life could bring some advantages. Household work, especially, could be less harsh. It could help people avoid the brutal labor found in mines, quarries, and *latifundia* across the empire. On these large estates, more than one hundred enslaved people might work. Their hard lives showed in their poor clothing. It also showed in cruel treatment. Many could not save money to buy their freedom.

Even so, enslaved people in any setting could be punished at any moment. Slaveholders feared conspiracy and rebellion. This fear created a culture of uncertainty, coercion, and submission. Violence was always a threat. Enslaved people could be whipped, beaten, or tortured. They were also often sexually abused.

In Petronius’s *Satyricon*, a novel from the first century CE, the freedman Trimalchio describes what he did while enslaved. He says: “Still, I was my master’s favorite for fourteen years. No disgrace in obeying your master’s orders. Well, I used to amuse my mistress too. You know what I mean; I say no more, I am not a conceited man.”

Enslaved people were denied official marriage rights. But they could still form families and have children. This often happened in cities. Slaveholders could also interfere in these relationships for their own purposes.

Islam means “submission [to the one God].”
