## Sources and early history

Islam’s origins and early decades can be hard to study.  
Much of what we know comes from Muslim sources.  
These sources often assume the reader already believes.  
So they may leave out details that historians want.

Many people in this period were illiterate.  
They did not write history as events happened.  
Because of this, we have less evidence outside religious scripture.

Arabs strongly valued remembering the past.  
But they mainly passed information through memorization and oral recitation.  
Poetry was an important memory aid.  
It helped people preserve and transmit material across generations.

Written history for future readers was often seen as less important.  
Oral tradition was a “living performance” of knowledge.

This focus on oral transmission was not unique.  
Early Judaism was also passed down orally before being written much later.  
Historians also struggle to reconstruct early Christianity.  
Very little writing from the time survives.

Epic poetry as a way to preserve the past also has precedents elsewhere.  
In the Mediterranean world, this includes *The Iliad* and *The Odyssey*, linked to Homer.  
In the ancient Indian world, it includes the *Mahabharata*.

## Core beliefs and the Five Pillars

Islam’s founding centers on Mecca, worship of one God, and the leadership of prophets.  
The one God is called Allah.  
Muslims do not see Allah as a different god from the God of Judaism and Christianity.  
“Allah” is simply the Arabic word meaning “the one God.”

Arabic-speaking Christians in the Middle East also use the word “Allah.”  
They use it to refer to the God of the Christian Bible.

The first and most important of the Five Pillars of Islam is the **shahada**.  
This is the profession of faith.  
To embrace Islam, a person must accept this creed:  
“There is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of God.”

Muslims recognize Muhammad as the final prophet.  
They place him in a long line of prophets.  
This line includes Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus.

Muhammad was divinely chosen.  
He is not worshipped as a God.  
He is not worshipped as a relative of God.

Other pillars of Islam also resemble practices in other religions.  
These include fasting, charity, and daily prayer.

For Muslims, these practices are defined in specific ways:

- Daily prayer, facing the holy mosque in Mecca  
- Almsgiving, giving money and goods to the community and to people in need  
- Fasting (if able) during Ramadan, the holy month when the Quran was first revealed to Muhammad  
- The pilgrimage to Mecca, the **hajj**, at least once (if able)  
  - This pilgrimage recalls key moments in the life of Abraham and his family’s arrival in Arabia  
  - It includes circling the Kaaba, the house of God, in prayer

## Islam and earlier monotheistic faiths

Muslims have long believed Islam is not a new faith invented in the seventh century.  
They see Muhammad’s message in the early 600s as a corrective.  
It corrects earlier monotheistic religions.

From this perspective, Islam is the same faith as Judaism and Christianity.  
All three worship the same God.  
All three recognize God’s guidance through prophets.

Muslims also recognize Jewish and Christian scriptures as originally given by God.  
But they believe these scriptures were corrupted over time.  
So Islam presents itself as a purer form of the same tradition.  
It also presents itself as directly connected to Judaism and Christianity.

All three traditions share a lineage through Abraham.  
Each lists Abraham as an ancestor.  
Because of this, many modern scholars call Judaism, Christianity, and Islam the **Abrahamic faiths**.

## What was uniquely Arabian

Islam was influenced by other monotheistic worship in the region.  
But it also had features that were uniquely Arab or Arabian.

One key feature was the setting.  
Judaism and Christianity focus heavily on the land of modern Israel and Palestine.  
In contrast, much of Islam’s formation as a distinct religion took place in western Arabia.  
This region is called the Hijaz.  
Islam’s holiest sites are there.  
The founder’s life was spent almost entirely there.

Islam is also firmly connected to Arabic.  
Arabic is the indigenous language of the region.  
It is central to Islam’s holiest scriptures.  
It is also tied to cultural practices, like using Arabic poetry to record the past.

Pre-Islamic Arabian society was organized by tribes.  
This tribal structure shaped the first decades of Islam and the states it inspired.  
It created a social hierarchy.  
For much of Islam’s first century, conversion was often very difficult.  
In many cases, a person could not convert unless an Arab tribe first accepted them as a member.

In this way, conversion was linked to older Arab customs.  
A convert did not need a specific ethnicity or bloodline.  
But the convert did need to adopt the cultural traditions and markers of Arabian tribal society.

For early believers, it likely seemed that the one God had chosen the peoples of western Arabia.  
Their traditions may have seemed specially recognized.  
So adopting these features could be seen as required to be among the “chosen” people.

Most influential of all was belief in Muhammad’s leadership and message.  
Muslims believed God chose him as the final prophet.  
He was an Arab man of the early seventh century.  
He came from the Hijaz in western Arabia.

Scholars still debate how agriculture began in Africa. Even so, most agree it started in three main regions. These regions were the Nile River in Egypt, the eastern Sahara in Sudan, and the great bend of the Niger River in West Africa.

## Agriculture in Egypt and North Africa
The oldest evidence of agriculture in Africa is in Egypt. It is found along the Nile River valley. Sometime after 7000 BCE, farming knowledge reached Egypt. This knowledge likely came from southwest Asia.

People brought new crops and animals. They domesticated wheat and barley. They also domesticated sheep, goats, and cattle. These methods changed the region. They helped set Egypt on the path to greatness.

Over the next few thousand years, farming spread west across North Africa. It reached Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco.

## Agriculture in the grasslands south of the Sahara
South of the Sahara, agriculture developed independently. This process may have begun as early as 9000 BCE. The Nilo-Saharan people started using grain-collecting and grinding methods. They learned these methods from northern neighbors. They used them on local tropical grasses. These grasses included sorghum and pearl millet from the Nile region.

These changes were possible because the Sahara was much wetter for a long time. This wet phase began around 11,000 BCE. During this time, monsoon-like weather brought heavy rains. The Sahara had lakes and rich plant life. The land had grasses and acacia forests. Many kinds of wildlife lived there.

By around 8000 BCE, the Nilo-Saharans had domesticated wild cattle. These cattle came from the Red Sea hills. They also began making pottery. They used pottery to store and cook grains.

By as early as 6000 BCE, gathering wild grains began to change. It started to become deliberate domestication. Over the next few thousand years, the Nilo-Saharans domesticated more plants. These included watermelons, cotton, and gourds.

## Agriculture in West Africa: the Niger River bend
Agriculture also developed independently in West Africa. This happened far west of the Nilo-Saharans. It took place in the bend of the Niger River.

The Niger-Congo peoples gradually domesticated yams. This likely began around the same time that eastern Sahara peoples were adopting agriculture. The process was probably piecemeal.

By 3000 BCE, Niger-Congo peoples were actively farming. They cleared land using stone tools. They planted yams, oil palm, peas, and groundnuts.

Over the next couple thousand years, they domesticated a special African variety of rice. They grew it in the wetlands of the Niger River region.

## Metallurgy and the growth of farming
Farming grew even more with advances in metalworking. Bronze reached Egypt from the Near East and the Eastern Mediterranean. This happened a little before 3000 BCE.

From Egypt, bronze technology spread. It moved west across North Africa. It also moved south up the Nile into sub-Saharan Africa.

Bronze was much harder than earlier farming materials. This made farming more productive. Wooden plows could only scratch the soil. Bronze-bladed plows were different. When pulled by oxen, they could dig deep. They could also turn over large amounts of earth.

## Iron in Egypt and the Near East
Iron objects were not unknown in Egypt during the Bronze Age. An iron dagger was placed in Pharaoh Tutankhamun’s tomb in 1323 BCE. Archaeologists have also found several hundred iron objects. These come from sites around the Near East and Eastern Mediterranean. Many date to centuries before the Iron Age began.

Most early iron objects were ornamental. They included items like iron jewelry. After about 1000 BCE, iron tools began to outnumber bronze tools across the Near East.

Iron was harder to produce than bronze. Early iron objects were often weaker than bronze. That is why many early items were decorative.

During the Late Bronze Age Collapse (1200–1100 BCE), tin became hard to obtain. This pushed people to experiment more with iron. By about 900 BCE, many blacksmiths in the Near East could make iron tools. These tools were much stronger than bronze.

In Egypt, evidence of advanced ironworking dates to the seventh century BCE. This technology was introduced from other parts of the Near East.

## Ironworking in sub-Saharan Africa
For many years, historians thought ironworking spread from Egypt to the rest of Africa. Today, the main view is different. Most scholars now think ironworking developed independently in sub-Saharan Africa.

Many scholars also think iron smelting in sub-Saharan Africa came earlier than its introduction into Egypt. It may have predated it by a few centuries. The earliest evidence is from about 1000 BCE. It comes from Central Africa. This includes modern Chad, the Central African Republic, and South Sudan.

From there, the technology seems to have spread west. It reached the Niger River area. By 500 BCE, the Nok culture of West Africa was using iron.

## The Nok and the spread of iron
The Nok lived near where the Benue and Niger Rivers meet. This is in present-day Nigeria. At first, the Nok used iron to make jewelry. Later, they used it for farming tools and weapons.

Iron tools were tough and durable. They helped people clear forests. They helped aerate land. They also helped dig trench-based irrigation systems. Because of this usefulness, more groups adopted iron.

Over the next several centuries, ironworking spread across West Africa. Later it spread much farther.

Iron was especially important for migrating Bantus. They used iron tools to clear trees. They expanded prehistoric irrigation systems. They dug deeper furrows. They supported these furrows with embankments. This helped create Iron Age farms.

As they moved, they spread ironworking across equatorial and subequatorial Africa.

text:
The Yuan dynasty kept some Song policies. One example was rotating officeholders.  
But the Yuan ruled very differently from earlier Chinese dynasties.

## A new class system
Kublai Khan made a major change.  
He replaced the Confucian class system.  
The old system was based on economic roles.  
The new system was based on ethnicity.

There were four main classes.

1. **Mongols** were at the top.  
2. **Non-Chinese people** were next.  
   These included Europeans.  
   They also included steppe peoples such as the **Jurchen, Tangut, and Khitan**.  
3. **Han Chinese in the north** came next.  
   These were Han people who had been ruled by the **Jin**.  
4. **Song Chinese in the south** were at the bottom.

Mongols could not marry people from the bottom two classes.

The government recorded each family’s class in census records.  
The census also listed the head of household’s occupation.  
Sometimes the state assigned an occupation.  
This happened when there was a shortage of certain kinds of labor.

## Different rules for different peoples
The Yuan followed a Khitan idea.  
This idea was to rule different groups in different ways.

More Mongols became literate over time.  
Kublai was the first Mongol great khan who could read.  
Even so, the mandarin written exam system fell into disuse.

Mongols were subject to the **yassa**.  
The next two classes were also subject to the yassa.  
They were ruled by administrators.  
These administrators were appointed by the chief local Mongol administrator or by the emperor.

The **Song Chinese** were in the lowest class.  
They were governed by two administrators.  
One was Chinese.  
One was Mongol or non-Chinese.  
Both were appointed by the emperor.  
The Chinese administrator was supervised by the other administrator.  
He was also responsible to him.

Officials in these jobs were rotated regularly.  
This prevented them from building a local power base.

## “Hostage bureaucrats” and Marco Polo
Some non-Chinese administrators over the Song did not plan to work for the Yuan.  
They came to seek favors from the emperor.  
A common favor was the right to trade.  
In exchange, the emperors required them to do administrative work.

Europeans learned about Yuan China’s riches through one of these officials.  
This was **Marco Polo**.  
He was a young merchant.  
He traveled with a Venetian trade caravan.  
Several family members traveled with him.  
They spent almost **twenty-five years** in Mongol lands.  
He later wrote a popular account of their experiences.

The Polos were the most famous of these “hostage bureaucrats.”  
They served for about **twenty years**.  
Most such bureaucrats were not Europeans.  
Most were **Muslim traders** from other parts of the Mongol Empire.

Even if these officials did their jobs well, they were unlikely to bond with local people.  
They were also unlikely to build a power base.  
This reduced the chance they could challenge imperial authority.

## The exam system returns, with quotas
After Kublai died in **1294**, problems in his system became clearer.

In **1315**, his great-grandson **Buyantu** brought back the mandarin exam system.  
The new exams matched the “dual” administration.

Non-Chinese people took different exams than Chinese people.  
Their exams were also shorter.  
Also, **25 to 50 percent** of those who passed had to be non-Chinese.

This quota mattered even more because of population size.  
Yuan censuses said **Song Chinese were more than 90 percent** of the population.

Because the exams differed and because of the quota, it was easier for Mongols and non-Chinese to pass.  
It was harder for Chinese people to pass.

## Wealth on the surface, stagnation underneath
Travelers described Yuan China as very wealthy.  
Marco Polo did this.  
So did the North African Muslim traveler **Ibn Battuta**, though less so.

But economic growth did not truly rise.  
At best, it stagnated.  
Consumer purchasing power fell.  
This was due to **inflation** and **heavy taxation**.

Paper currency was a major cause of inflation.  
In theory, paper money could be exchanged for metal or silk.

Guns spread through societies in Europe, Asia, and Africa. This change helped bring an end to some nomadic cultures.

For many centuries before this, nomadic societies played an important role in world history. They often helped cause major historical change.

Around 1500 BCE, mounted Indo-Europeans arrived on the Indian subcontinent. Life there changed greatly. Their sacred texts were the Vedas. The Vedas became the foundation for Hinduism. Their social organization helped form the Hindu caste system. Their language, Sanskrit, became a sacred language in both Hinduism and Buddhism.

Nomadic tribes from central Asia also helped set in motion changes that contributed to the fall of the Roman Empire. In the fourth and fifth centuries CE, the Huns lived in central Asia, the Caucasus, and eastern Europe. They moved westward. They attacked and conquered Germanic tribes on the borders of the Roman Empire. These tribes included the Goths, the Visigoths, and others. Many fled into Roman territory. This movement destabilized the empire.

In East Asia, mounted nomads had a similar effect on China. Over many centuries, different tribes traded with and attacked Han Chinese settlements. These tribes included the Xiongnu and the Jurchen.

During the Qin dynasty (c. 221 BCE), China began building a wall. The goal was to protect settled areas from roaming riders. The wall did not fully work. It covered only parts of the border between Chinese-settled lands and nomadic lands. Because of this, Chinese emperors sometimes paid tribute to aggressive tribes. This tribute included gifts and Chinese princesses. This also shows that women’s status was treated as secondary to the needs and decisions of men, even when the women were of high social rank.

In the early modern era, more nomadic societies began to settle down. Firearms used by settled societies threatened the survival of nomadic ways of life. As firearms improved, guns and artillery became more accurate. They could shoot farther and faster. Mounted archers could not compete.

Still, guns alone do not fully explain the decline of nomadic life. Early firearms were heavy and awkward. They were hard to use from horseback. Later, firearms became lighter. Nomads could have adopted them. Some did. The Plains Indians of North America, for example, adopted firearms.

Not all nomads were mounted warriors. Some were, such as the Mongols and Arab Bedouins. The Huns and the Xiongnu were also mounted warriors, and they troubled the Han dynasty. But many nomadic groups did not ride horses. Many did not form armies. The Sami reindeer herders of Scandinavia and Russia were not traditionally warriors. The Gaddi shepherds of the Himalaya were also not traditionally warriors.

Also, settled societies had mounted warriors too. In medieval Europe, knights fought on horseback. European knights disappeared after gunpowder and firearms became widespread. Even so, it took centuries after firearms were developed for mounted warriors to disappear from armies. In World War I, European and U.S. forces still used cavalry.

Because of this, it may be more accurate to say gunpowder made cavalry obsolete. This is different from saying gunpowder made nomads disappear. Mounted warriors are now a thing of the past. But nomadic societies still exist in many parts of the world, though in smaller numbers. Many modern Mongols and Arab Bedouin, for example, still live nomadically.

Firearms did help force many nomads to adapt. They faced new military, political, and social realities. These pressures often pushed them toward settling down. But guns were mainly a *tool* that modern states used. Guns were not the main *reason* nomadic groups declined.

Modern states fought nomads for many reasons. Settled people often feared nomads. This was especially true when nomads fought them. It was also true when nomads competed with them for natural resources.

The North American Plains Indians are one example. Settled people feared Plains mounted warriors. Settled people also wanted the land the Plains tribes used. Plains tribes claimed large hunting grounds. As long as they did, colonizing farmers, ranchers, and miners could not use the resources of the American West as they wished.

Modern nation-states also created permanent borders. They did not want nomads crossing borders freely. They saw this as a threat to national security and sovereignty. They often forced nomads to settle. States also found it easier to tax people who stayed in one place.

Industrialization created more pressure. Nomads needed grasslands and water for their herds. But private lands were fenced. Water sources were polluted. Grasslands were grazed by animals owned by commercial livestock businesses. These businesses produced meat for city populations. At the same time, settled life became more comfortable. Many nomads chose to leave nomadic life behind.

In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, climate change has made nomadic life harder. Droughts and more severe weather threaten grasslands and water sources. For nomadic pastoralists, lack of grass is disastrous.

Climate also mattered in earlier history. Soldiers of the Mamluk Sultanate used early cannons at the Battle of Ain Jalut. Cannons were not the main reason they won. The Mongol force was much smaller than usual. The Levant’s arid climate could not provide enough grass. Mongol warriors traveled with thousands of horses, often five or six per person. Because there was not enough grass, the Mongols had to field a smaller army.

Today, more nomad homelands face desertification and harsh winter temperatures. This may become the final blow for the world’s few remaining nomadic societies.

## Guns and the decline of some nomadic ways of life

Guns spread through societies in **Europe, Asia, and Africa**.  
This change helped bring an end to some nomadic cultures.

---

## Nomads and major historical change

For many centuries, nomadic societies played an important role in world history.  
They often helped cause major historical change.

### Indo-Europeans in South Asia

Around **1500 BCE**, mounted **Indo-Europeans** arrived on the Indian subcontinent.  
Life there changed greatly.

Their sacred texts were the **Vedas**.  
The Vedas became the foundation for **Hinduism**.

Their social organization helped form the **Hindu caste system**.

Their language, **Sanskrit**, became a sacred language in both **Hinduism** and **Buddhism**.

### Nomads and the fall of Rome

Nomadic tribes from **Central Asia** also helped set in motion changes that contributed to the fall of the **Roman Empire**.

In the **fourth and fifth centuries CE**, the **Huns** lived in **Central Asia**, the **Caucasus**, and **Eastern Europe**.  
They moved westward.

They attacked and conquered Germanic tribes on the borders of the Roman Empire.  
These tribes included the **Goths**, the **Visigoths**, and others.

Many fled into Roman territory.  
This movement destabilized the empire.

### Nomads and China

In **East Asia**, mounted nomads had a similar effect on **China**.  
Over many centuries, different tribes traded with and attacked **Han Chinese** settlements.  
These tribes included the **Xiongnu** and the **Jurchen**.

---

## The Great Wall and tribute

During the **Qin dynasty (c. 221 BCE)**, China began building a wall.  
The goal was to protect settled areas from roaming riders.

The wall did not fully work.  
It covered only parts of the border between Chinese-settled lands and nomadic lands.

Because of this, Chinese emperors sometimes paid **tribute** to aggressive tribes.  
This tribute included gifts and Chinese princesses.

This also shows that women’s status was treated as secondary to the needs and decisions of men, even when the women were of high social rank.

---

## Firearms and the early modern shift

In the **early modern era**, more nomadic societies began to settle down.

Firearms used by settled societies threatened the survival of nomadic ways of life.  
As firearms improved, guns and artillery became more accurate.  
They could shoot farther and faster.

Mounted archers could not compete.

---

## Why guns were not the whole story

Guns alone do not fully explain the decline of nomadic life.

Early firearms were heavy and awkward.  
They were hard to use from horseback.

Later, firearms became lighter.  
Nomads could have adopted them. Some did.

The **Plains Indians** of **North America**, for example, adopted firearms.

---

## Not all nomads were mounted warriors

Not all nomads were mounted warriors.

Some were, such as the **Mongols** and **Arab Bedouins**.  
The **Huns** and the **Xiongnu** were also mounted warriors, and they troubled the **Han dynasty**.

But many nomadic groups did not ride horses.  
Many did not form armies.

The **Sami** reindeer herders of **Scandinavia** and **Russia** were not traditionally warriors.

The **Gaddi** shepherds of the **Himalaya** were also not traditionally warriors.

---

## Settled societies also used cavalry

Settled societies had mounted warriors too.

In medieval **Europe**, **knights** fought on horseback.  
European knights disappeared after gunpowder and firearms became widespread.

Even so, it took centuries after firearms were developed for mounted warriors to disappear from armies.  
In **World War I**, European and U.S. forces still used cavalry.

---

## A clearer claim: cavalry became obsolete

Because of this, it may be more accurate to say: **gunpowder made cavalry obsolete**.

This is different from saying: **gunpowder made nomads disappear**.

Mounted warriors are now a thing of the past.  
But nomadic societies still exist in many parts of the world, though in smaller numbers.

Many modern **Mongols** and **Arab Bedouin**, for example, still live nomadically.

---

## Guns as a tool of modern states

Firearms did help force many nomads to adapt.  
They faced new military, political, and social realities.  
These pressures often pushed them toward settling down.

But guns were mainly a **tool** that modern states used.  
Guns were not the main **reason** nomadic groups declined.

---

## Why modern states fought nomads

Modern states fought nomads for many reasons.

Settled people often feared nomads.  
This was especially true when nomads fought them.

It was also true when nomads competed with them for natural resources.

### Example: the North American Plains

The **North American Plains Indians** are one example.

Settled people feared Plains mounted warriors.  
Settled people also wanted the land the Plains tribes used.

Plains tribes claimed large hunting grounds.  
As long as they did, colonizing farmers, ranchers, and miners could not use the resources of the **American West** as they wished.

---

## Borders, taxes, and control

Modern nation-states also created permanent borders.

They did not want nomads crossing borders freely.  
They saw this as a threat to national security and sovereignty.

They often forced nomads to settle.

States also found it easier to tax people who stayed in one place.

---

## Industrialization and shrinking pasturelands

Industrialization created more pressure.

Nomads needed grasslands and water for their herds.  
But private lands were fenced. Water sources were polluted.

Grasslands were grazed by animals owned by commercial livestock businesses.  
These businesses produced meat for city populations.

At the same time, settled life became more comfortable.  
Many nomads chose to leave nomadic life behind.

---

## Climate change and the future of nomadic life

In the **twentieth and twenty-first centuries**, climate change has made nomadic life harder.

Droughts and more severe weather threaten grasslands and water sources.  
For nomadic pastoralists, lack of grass is disastrous.

### Climate also mattered in earlier history

Climate also mattered in earlier history.

Soldiers of the **Mamluk Sultanate** used early cannons at the **Battle of Ain Jalut**.  
Cannons were not the main reason they won.

The Mongol force was much smaller than usual.  
The **Levant’s** arid climate could not provide enough grass.

Mongol warriors traveled with thousands of horses, often **five or six per person**.  
Because there was not enough grass, the Mongols had to field a smaller army.

---

## Closing thought

Today, more nomad homelands face desertification and harsh winter temperatures.

This may become the final blow for the world’s few remaining nomadic societies.

Under Askia the Great, the Songhai Empire flourished.  
Religious scholars and poets came to cities like Timbuktu and Djenné.  
Islam was practiced more widely.  

The state began major building projects.  
It built canals to improve farming and increase food production.  
Trade across the Sahara also grew stronger.  

As Askia grew older, his personal power weakened.  
He depended more on palace officials to run the empire.  
This upset his family.  
They became angry about the influence of his head chamberlain, Ali Fulan.  

In 1528, Askia’s sons rebelled.  
They removed him from power.  
They made one brother, Musa, king.  

Askia Musa’s rule did not begin peacefully.  
Civil war broke out.  
Musa fought his relatives to keep the throne.  
Dozens of his family members were killed.  

In 1531, Musa was killed by his brothers.  
This made the crisis worse.  
The state became even more unstable.  

After that, one ruler after another failed to govern well.  
The ruling class and the military fought for control.  
Political chaos spread.  

The central government stopped working effectively.  
Songhai grew weaker.  
Outside powers saw a chance to step in.  
They wanted control of the profitable trans-Saharan trade in salt and gold.  
Morocco’s Saadi dynasty was especially interested.  

In 1578, the Saadi defeated a Portuguese invasion.  
But the victory cost a great deal of money.  
The imperial treasury was drained.  

To avoid bankruptcy, Sultan Ahmad I al-Mansur Saadi looked for new resources.  
At the same time, Songhai became calmer again.  
Stability returned under Askia Ishaq II, who began ruling in 1588.  

This recovery did not last long.  
In 1591, the Saadi invaded Songhai.  

Songhai had more soldiers.  
But the Saadi had a major advantage.  
They had many guns, ammunition, and cannons.  
These were supplied by Queen Elizabeth I of England.  
She hoped Morocco would become an ally against Spain.  

The Saadi army also included many Spanish Muslims.  
In 1502, Spain’s monarchs ordered all Muslims in Spain to convert to Christianity.  
Many Muslims fled Spain as a result.  

Songhai was outmatched.  
Its larger army lost at the Battle of Tondibi.  
Askia Ishaq II was killed.  

After the battle, the Saadi commander moved against key cities and trade centers.  
He was Judar Pasha, an enslaved Spanish eunuch.  

The Saadi attacked Djenné, Gao, and Timbuktu.  
They looted and destroyed these cities.  
They burned them to the ground.  

To secure their victory, the invaders filled in wells.  
They also destroyed crop fields.  
They spared very few people, including women and children.  

After this destruction, Songhai’s power no longer worked in practice.  
Ten years later, the empire was shattered.  
Its provinces broke apart into smaller kingdoms and territories.

Efforts to silence Martin Luther failed.  
A new form of Christianity, called Protestantism, spread through the German-speaking lands.  
By the end of the 1500s, it was firmly established in western and central Europe.  

Many rulers welcomed the new religion.  
It gave them a reason to reject the pope’s authority.  
Luther urged the German princes to do this.  

The Catholic Holy Roman emperor Charles V (also Charles I of Spain) strongly opposed Protestantism.  
Still, the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 changed the situation.  
It gave Lutheran rulers in the empire the right to make Lutheranism the official religion in their lands.  
A ruler’s subjects had to follow the church the ruler chose.  

Many rulers in northern Germany became Lutheran.  
In Austria and Bavaria, in the south, the Roman Catholic Church kept its power.  
No other religions were allowed under this agreement.  

In Switzerland, Luther’s reform ideas also spread.  
In Zurich, they were taken up by Ulrich (Huldrych) Zwingli.  
Zwingli had been a priest.  
He called for more radical changes than Luther did.  

Zwingli rejected the Catholic teaching of transubstantiation.  
This teaching said Jesus was physically present in the communion wine and wafer during every Mass.  
Even Luther did not reject it as strongly as Zwingli did.  

Zwingli also preached against fasting before major religious holidays.  
He wanted religious images removed from churches.  
He banned organs from churches.  
He closed monasteries and convents.  
He had the Bible printed in German instead of Latin.  
He called for an end to clerical celibacy.  
He said the Bible never mentioned purgatory.  

Zwingli was killed in 1531.  
He died during a conflict between Catholic and Protestant areas of Switzerland.  

One person inspired by Zwingli was Konrad Grebel, a Swiss merchant.  
Grebel focused on baptism.  
He believed baptism should happen in adulthood.  
He thought a person must be old enough to choose to renounce sin.  

Grebel felt Zwingli was reforming Zurich too slowly.  
So Grebel started his own movement in 1524.  
It was called the Swiss Brethren.  

The Swiss Brethren was one of several Anabaptist churches.  
Anabaptists rejected infant baptism.  
They supported adult baptism instead.  
These churches formed in the 1500s, mainly in central Europe and the Low Countries.  

Most Catholics and most Protestants practiced infant baptism.  
They believed baptism removed the stain of original sin, the sin of Adam and Eve.  
Anabaptists disagreed.  
They believed only adults could truly renounce sin and declare faith.  
So, only adults could make a conscious choice to become Christian.  

But baptism was supposed to happen only once.  
So adult baptism for someone baptized as a baby meant rebaptism.  
That violated a key Catholic rule.  

Other Anabaptist movements included the Hutterites, the Mennonites, and the Amish.  
The Amish split from the larger Mennonite movement in the 1600s.  
Anabaptist groups also supported separating church and state.  
They also tended to be pacifists.  

Many European rulers feared Anabaptists.  
Anabaptists often refused to hold public office.  
They often refused to serve in the army.  
They also rejected the right of secular rulers to control religion.  
Because of this, they were often attacked violently.  

Another major center of Protestant thought was Geneva.  
Geneva is in what is now Switzerland.  
Its religious leader was John Calvin.  

Calvin was raised Catholic in France.  
He became Protestant either before or shortly after he fled to Switzerland.  
He fled to escape persecution for his beliefs.  

Calvin agreed with Luther on many points.  
But they differed in one crucial way.  
Calvin taught predestination.  

Predestination said God had already decided who would be saved after death.  
It also said God had already decided who would go to hell.  
No one could know for sure whether they were saved or damned.  
There was nothing a person could do to guarantee salvation.  

Calvinists accepted this teaching.  
Even so, they tried to live very moral lives.  
They emphasized hard work and piety.  
They looked for reassurance in their own behavior.  
They hoped that living like the saved meant they were saved.  

Calvinists rejected many activities as ungodly.  
They rejected dancing.  
They rejected public drunkenness.  
They rejected gambling.  
They rejected obscene speech.  
These could be punished by a special tribunal called the Consistory.

It gained followers in the Netherlands, who formed the Dutch Reformed Church.  
It gained followers in Scotland, where the Presbyterian Church formed.  
It gained followers in France, where followers were called Huguenots.

Joint stock companies helped England fund colonization after the failure at Roanoke Island.  
The English monarchy could not provide enough money.

A joint stock company was like a modern corporation.  
It raised money by selling shares to investors.  
The company used the shared money to run its projects, including colonies in the Americas.

Shareholders had limited liability.  
They were not legally responsible for the company’s actions.  
They could not lose more than what they invested.  
If the company succeeded, they could earn large profits.

This mix of low risk and high possible reward attracted England’s growing merchant class.  
Beginning in the early 1600s, these companies raised huge sums of money.

England supported colonization for religious and political reasons.  
But private investors often pushed colonies toward making profits.

In 1606, the Virginia Company received a charter.  
It was named for Queen Elizabeth.  
She was called the “virgin queen” because she never married.

The Virginia Company sent 144 men and boys to North America.  
In 1607, they founded Jamestown.  
It was named for the new king, James I.  
Jamestown was on the banks of the Chesapeake Bay in what is now Virginia.

Many settlers were younger sons of elite families.  
In England, older brothers usually inherited property.  
Many other settlers were artisans, like goldsmiths and jewelers.  
Most were not used to the hard physical labor needed to build a colony.

The Jamestown settlers followed mercantilism.  
Mercantilism said the world’s wealth, measured in gold and silver, was limited.  
If one nation gained wealth, another nation lost wealth.

Mercantilist nations expected colonies to export raw materials to the home country.  
They especially wanted precious metals like gold and silver.  
Colonies were also expected to buy goods from the home country.

The English government hoped the Virginia Company would find gold.  
Gold would improve England’s trade balance and increase national wealth.  
Many settlers also hoped to find gold.  
They wanted to get rich without hard work or hardship.

They did not find gold.  
There was little mineral wealth in the region.

Instead, they found suffering.  
They faced bad weather, starvation, and disease.  
They also faced internal political disputes.  
They fought military conflicts with the Powhatan tribe, named after its chief.

The Powhatans came to hate the newcomers.  
The newcomers brought disease and violence to their homeland.

Many colonists died in the winter of 1609–1610.  
This period was called “the starving time.”  
By May 1610, fewer than 100 colonists remained.  
The colony almost failed.  
It had not made a profit for the Virginia Company.

Virginia colonists did find success with tobacco.  
Tobacco required hard work in difficult conditions.  
But by 1614, Jamestown exported tobacco to Europe.  
This brought profits to the Virginia Company.

Smoking dried tobacco leaves became popular in Europe.  
The leaves were highly addictive.

Like the Spanish, English colonists struggled to farm using only their own labor.  
They relied heavily on indentured servants.

Indentured servants were European immigrants.  
They usually agreed to work four to seven years.  
In return, they received transportation to the colony.  
They also hoped for a new life after their service ended.

In the 1600s, up to 100,000 people came as indentured servants.  
Most were poor men in their twenties.

Many indentured servants died.  
They died from disease, exposure, and overwork.  
Those who survived often became comfortable and respected settlers.  
A lucky few became wealthy planters.

In 1619, the first Africans arrived in Virginia.  
At first, they had the same chances as European immigrants.  
They could earn freedom and build wealth.

But their condition quickly worsened.  
This followed a larger trend.  
The Spanish and Portuguese had brought the first Africans to the Americas a century earlier.

By the mid-1600s, new policies were developing in the Americas.  
These policies bound Africans to servitude for life.  
This was different from European indentured servants.  
European servants regained freedom after their term ended.

Virginia colonists wanted a permanent labor force.  
This was also true in Mexico, South America, and the Caribbean.  
It was often hard to recruit enough indentured servants from Europe.

Forcing other Europeans to work would have caused too much resistance.  
At the same time, Virginia had a growing underclass of poor White former servants.

text:
Europeans were sometimes hurt by their own success.  
Economic imperialism could create colonies that became strong.  
Some colonies then formed independent nations.  
In one case, thirteen former colonies formed a new country.  
That country later became richer and more powerful than the empire it left.

The British colonies in North America began in the early 1600s.  
At first, they were small and struggled to survive.  
By the mid-1700s, they had more than two million people.  
They mostly governed themselves.  
They also had a strong commercial economy.

British mercantilist policies threatened this growth.  
In the late 1600s, England passed the Navigation Acts.  
These laws aimed to increase England’s profit from the colonies.  
They also aimed to keep colonial resources away from other European powers.  
They also tried to stop smuggling.

The Navigation Act of 1660 listed certain colonial goods.  
These goods could be sold only in England or in English colonies.  
This meant English merchants controlled the market.  
They paid colonists what they thought the goods were worth.  
Colonists could not sell to Dutch, French, Spanish, or other merchants.  
Those other merchants might have paid more.

The listed products included furs, tobacco, and sugar.  
These were goods that many Europeans wanted.  
The list also included rice, ginger, cotton, and indigo.  
It included other plants used to make dye as well.  
English textile makers needed cotton and dyestuffs.

To protect English interests even more, Parliament passed the Exportation Act of 1660.  
This law prohibited the export of English wool.

The laws also controlled “naval stores.”  
These were materials used to build and maintain ships for trade and war.  
They could be sent only to England.  
They included masts.  
They included hemp, used to make rope.  
They included pine tree pitch, used to seal ships and make them watertight.  
They included pine tree sap, used to make turpentine.

When these colonial products reached England, they were heavily taxed.  
The tax money went to the English government.  
It did not go to the colonies that produced the goods.

The Navigation Act of 1663 created another rule.  
Goods going to the colonies from outside the British Empire had to go to England first.  
In England, they were taxed.  
Only then could they be shipped to the colonies.  
This raised prices for colonists.  
Foreign shippers passed the cost of English taxes on to them.

By the end of the 1600s, Parliament added more limits.  
It began to stop colonists from making certain goods.  
These were goods also made in England.  
The goal was to prevent colonists from underselling English merchants.

Colonists could not sell goods made from wool or iron.  
They could not sell them in England.  
They could not sell them to other English colonies.  
By the mid-1700s, they also could not export beaver hats.

Beaver hats were a popular fashion in Europe.  
The English colonies were active in the fur trade.  
Parliament allowed colonists to export only unfinished furs.  
Colonists could not export the finished hats.  
Finished hats would have sold for higher prices.  
This limited how much wealth settlers could gain.

After the French and Indian War, tensions grew.  
British colonists reacted with hostility to new actions by Parliament.  
They believed these actions unfairly limited their economic opportunities.

Many colonists wanted to move west of the Appalachian Mountains.  
They wanted farms on the rich land of the Ohio Valley.  
In New England, families were large.  
Over time, parents struggled to provide enough land for their children.  
In the southern colonies, tobacco farming used up soil.  
New fertile land was always needed.

Many colonies claimed land west of the Appalachians.  
But the French had taken this land.  
It was also home to many Native American allies of the French.  
After Britain defeated the French and their Indigenous allies, colonists expected to take the land.

The British government did not allow this.  
It wanted to avoid angering the tribes of the Ohio Valley.  
It also wanted to avoid costly new wars.  
So it prohibited settlement west of the Appalachians.  
Many colonists were dismayed and angry.  
Many had fought alongside British troops in the war.

Britain also kept troops in North America.  
The goal was to keep peace with Native Americans.  
Britain also needed to repay war debts.  
The troops policed the frontier.  
They regulated colonial trade.  
They collected taxes.

Paying for the army led Britain to seek more money.  
It tried to impose new taxes on colonists.  
It also tried to enforce existing taxes more strictly.

Colonists often used smuggling to evade trade restrictions.  
Britain responded with new legal rules.  
Smugglers had to be tried in admiralty courts.  
These courts did not have juries.  
Many colonists believed this violated the English Bill of Rights.

In 1774, Parliament made another decision that angered colonists.  
It gave control of the Ohio Valley to the province of Quebec.  
It allowed Quebec to keep French civil law.  
It also extended religious toleration to Roman Catholics there.  
Most British colonists were Protestant, and many were outraged.

This decision came alongside another that interfered with colonial self-government.  
Colonists had practiced self-government for about 150 years.  
More and more, they saw Britain as hostile to their interests.

Resentment grew into violence in 1775.  
In 1776, the colonists declared independence.

text:
Europeans were sometimes hurt by their own success.

Economic imperialism could create colonies that became strong.  
Some colonies then formed independent nations.

In one case, **thirteen former colonies** formed a new country.  
That country later became **richer and more powerful** than the empire it left.

---

## British colonies in North America

The British colonies in North America began in the early 1600s.

At first, they were small and struggled to survive.  
By the mid-1700s, they had **more than two million people**.

They mostly governed themselves.  
They also had a **strong commercial economy**.

---

## Britain tries to control colonial trade

British mercantilist policies threatened colonial growth.

In the late 1600s, England passed the **Navigation Acts**. These laws aimed to:

- increase England’s profit from the colonies  
- keep colonial resources away from other European powers  
- stop smuggling  

---

## The Navigation Act of 1660: “listed goods”

The Navigation Act of 1660 listed certain colonial goods.

These goods could be sold only in England or in English colonies.  
This meant **English merchants controlled the market**.

Colonists could not sell to Dutch, French, Spanish, or other merchants.  
Those merchants might have paid more.

**Listed products included:**

- furs  
- tobacco  
- sugar  
- rice  
- ginger  
- cotton  
- indigo  
- other dye plants (dyestuffs)

English textile makers especially needed **cotton and dyestuffs**.

---

## More protection for English business

To protect English interests even more, Parliament passed the **Exportation Act of 1660**.  
This law prohibited the export of **English wool**.

---

## “Naval stores” and shipbuilding materials

The laws also controlled **naval stores**.  
These were materials used to build and maintain ships for trade and war.

They could be sent only to England, including:

- masts  
- hemp (for rope)  
- pine tree pitch (to seal ships)  
- pine tree sap (to make turpentine)

---

## Taxes and who benefited

When colonial products reached England, they were **heavily taxed**.

The tax money went to the English government.  
It did **not** go to the colonies that produced the goods.

---

## The Navigation Act of 1663: goods must go through England

The Navigation Act of 1663 added another rule:

Goods going to the colonies from outside the British Empire had to go to England first.  
In England, they were taxed.  
Only then could they be shipped to the colonies.

This raised prices for colonists.  
Foreign shippers passed the cost of English taxes on to them.

---

## Limits on colonial manufacturing

By the end of the 1600s, Parliament added more limits.  
It began to stop colonists from making certain goods also made in England.

The goal was to prevent colonists from **underselling English merchants**.

Colonists could not sell goods made from **wool or iron**:

- not in England  
- not to other English colonies  

By the mid-1700s, they also could not export **beaver hats**.

---

## The beaver hat example

Beaver hats were a popular fashion in Europe.  
The English colonies were active in the fur trade.

Parliament allowed colonists to export only **unfinished furs**.  
Colonists could not export **finished hats**.

Finished hats would have sold for higher prices.  
This limited how much wealth settlers could gain.

---

## After the French and Indian War: rising tensions

After the French and Indian War, tensions grew.

British colonists reacted with hostility to new actions by Parliament.  
They believed these actions **unfairly limited** their economic opportunities.

---

## Pressure to move west

Many colonists wanted to move west of the Appalachian Mountains.  
They wanted farms on the rich land of the Ohio Valley.

Reasons included:

- In New England, families were large, and land was harder to divide among children.  
- In the southern colonies, tobacco farming used up soil, so new fertile land was needed.  

Many colonies claimed land west of the Appalachians.  
But the French had taken this land.  
It was also home to many Native American allies of the French.

After Britain defeated the French and their Indigenous allies, colonists expected to take the land.

---

## Britain blocks western settlement

The British government did not allow settlement west of the Appalachians.

It wanted to:

- avoid angering tribes of the Ohio Valley  
- avoid costly new wars  

Many colonists were dismayed and angry.  
Many had fought alongside British troops in the war.

---

## British troops, debt, and taxes

Britain kept troops in North America to help keep peace with Native Americans.

Britain also needed to repay war debts.  
The troops:

- policed the frontier  
- regulated colonial trade  
- collected taxes  

Paying for the army led Britain to seek more money.  
It tried to impose **new taxes** on colonists.  
It also tried to enforce existing taxes more strictly.

---

## Smuggling and admiralty courts

Colonists often used smuggling to evade trade restrictions.

Britain responded with new legal rules.  
Smugglers had to be tried in **admiralty courts**.

These courts did not have juries.  
Many colonists believed this violated the **English Bill of Rights**.

---

## 1774: Quebec and colonial anger

In **1774**, Parliament made another decision that angered colonists.

It gave control of the Ohio Valley to the province of **Quebec**.  
It allowed Quebec to keep **French civil law**.  
It also extended religious toleration to **Roman Catholics** there.

Most British colonists were Protestant, and many were outraged.

---

## Self-government and the break with Britain

This decision came alongside another that interfered with colonial self-government.

Colonists had practiced self-government for about **150 years**.  
More and more, they saw Britain as hostile to their interests.

Resentment grew into violence in **1775**.  
In **1776**, the colonists declared independence.

Conversation and debate in public life were closely tied to the growing print culture of the Enlightenment.

In late-seventeenth-century French cities, literacy was limited. About 30 percent of men could read. About 14 percent of women could read. By the mid-eighteenth century, literacy had risen. About 48 percent of men could read. About 27 percent of women could read.

As literacy rose, printed material spread quickly. More books, pamphlets, newspapers, and political cartoons appeared. Print helped standardize spelling and systems of knowledge. It also helped ideas travel farther. News, opinions, poetry, political philosophy, scientific texts, and many other kinds of information could reach more people than speech alone.

This print world supported the “Republic of Letters.” The Republic of Letters was a long-distance community of writers. In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, they wrote to each other across Europe and the Atlantic. They sent handwritten letters and published works of many kinds. This created an important international exchange of ideas.

The Republic of Letters was not based on living in the same place. It was based on shared ideas spread through print. Any literate person, anywhere in Europe or the Atlantic world, could belong. Members treated each other as intellectual equals. They exchanged ideas freely. This was like a political republic, where citizens were, in theory, free and equal.

Some members were famous. They included Voltaire, Benjamin Franklin, and Catherine the Great.

Members came from many countries. They spoke many languages. Because of this, much of their writing was in Latin. At the time, Latin was the universal language of scholarship in multilingual Europe. Other writing required skilled translators. This language barrier made it hard for most people to take part directly in Enlightenment print culture.

Print culture was widespread, but its direct impact on the general public was limited. Many artisans, peasants, and tradespeople still could not read. Literacy rose fastest among the urban elite, especially wealthy merchants and aristocrats. But for people lower in the social and economic hierarchy, literacy stayed well below 20 percent. This was especially true in rural areas.

The Enlightenment supported democratic ideas about sharing knowledge, at least in theory. In practice, participation was limited. People needed enough wealth and leisure time to read and write. Books were very expensive. Most people could not afford them. Even cheap pamphlets cost too much for many eighteenth-century laborers and peasants.

In the second half of the eighteenth century, lending libraries appeared. They increased access to printed materials. But only select academics and government officials could borrow books. By the end of the century, reading clubs became more common. Members paid an annual fee. In return, they could access books and periodicals. These clubs helped expand the reading public. They also helped raise literacy among the middle class.

The U.S. Declaration of Independence (1776) and France’s Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) said that all men were created equal.  
In practice, these ideas mainly applied to White men of European descent.  
In Europe and the United States, women and enslaved people were usually left out.

The rights described as belonging to “all men” were the rights that mattered most to free White men.  
These included property rights, freedom of expression, and the right to take part in government.  
Only the most radical people in the United States and France argued that women should have the same rights as men.  
Only a few also argued that people of different races should be equal to White people in rights and social status.

Even so, these documents helped inspire a slave revolt in Saint-Domingue.  
This revolt became one of the most important effects of the French Revolution in the Americas.

Saint-Domingue was a French colony on the western side of the Caribbean island of Hispaniola.  
France founded it in the mid-1600s.  
It soon became the most profitable colony in the Americas.  
This wealth came mostly from the labor of enslaved Africans.  
They were forced to work on sugar, coffee, and indigo plantations.

In 1791, freed and enslaved Africans and other islanders of African descent rebelled.  
Two key leaders were Toussaint Louverture and Jean-Jacques Dessalines.  
Both men had been born enslaved on local plantations.

The revolt grew into a full revolution.  
It led to independence from France.  
In 1804, the new free republic of Haiti was declared.

The Haitian Revolution was unusual.  
It was not led by White colonists of European descent seeking political representation and more economic freedom.  
That had been the pattern in the British colonies of North America.  
In Saint-Domingue, the fight was led by people at the lowest levels of the social hierarchy.

The rebellion in Haiti had two main goals.  
It also involved two different meanings of liberation.

For free Black people and mixed-race elites, freedom meant ending colonialism.  
It meant independence from French rule.

For enslaved Black people, liberation was more basic.  
It meant an end to plantation abuse.  
It meant an end to slavery.

By January 1804, Black revolutionaries had won through successful guerrilla tactics.  
They defeated a French army that was already weakened by yellow fever.  
This victory created the Haitian nation.

Haiti became the second liberated territory in the Western Hemisphere.  
It also became the second republican system there.

After the uprising in Haiti, political elites in the Americas feared its influence.  
They worried it would inspire other slave rebellions.  
They feared that American Indians, free and enslaved Africans, and people of mixed-racial ancestry might start violent independence movements.

Because of this fear, the creole aristocracy hesitated.  
They were less willing to copy the liberty-seeking Anglo-American colonists.  
Support for independence from their parent countries weakened rather than grew.

Instead, events in the Iberian Peninsula led to the break between Spain and Portugal and their colonies.

During the Napoleonic Era (1803–1814), Portugal and Spain took different sides.  
They were involved in the wider war between France and other European nations.  
These nations had united against Napoléon Bonaparte, the emperor of the French.

Portugal kept its long-standing alliance with Great Britain.  
Britain was an enemy of Napoléon.  
Spain, in contrast, was a French ally.

Since the War of Spanish Succession (1701–1714), Spain had been ruled by the House of Bourbon.  
At this time, King Carlos IV followed a disastrous policy of war with England.

British naval blockades disrupted trade between Spain and its colonies.  
In 1806, British soldiers attacked Buenos Aires.  
Buenos Aires was in the Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata (present-day Argentina).  
Local forces defeated the British.

Still, the attack revealed something important.  
It showed Spanish American colonists that Spain was vulnerable.  
It also showed that Spain could not reliably protect them.

In 1807, Napoléon created the Continental System.  
It was also called the Continental Blockade.  
It required all European ports to close to English shipping.

Portugal did not follow this policy.  
Portugal continued to trade with Britain, one of its oldest allies.  
Britain could not be defeated if it could still trade in Europe through Portugal.

To force Portugal to comply, France would have to invade Portugal.  
France could do this only by marching through Spain.

By then, Spain was a vulnerable French satellite.  
Napoléon easily got permission from the Spanish Crown to invade Portugal by land.  
As a result, Spanish subjects suffered heavy taxation, war, and occupation.

Popular anger grew against these pro-French policies.  
Carlos IV faced pressure to abdicate.  
He stepped down in favor of his son, Fernando.

Napoléon then intervened.  
He detained both Carlos and Fernando.  
He forced both men to give up their claims to the Spanish throne.  
He installed his brother, Joseph Bonaparte, as king of Spain.

Napoléon’s plan did not fully work.  
In early 1808, most people in Spain rejected Joseph Bonaparte.  
Creole royalists and some republicans in the colonies also rebelled.

The rebellion began in Madrid.  
It quickly spread to other cities across the Iberian Peninsula.

This conflict became the Peninsular War (1808–1814).  
British, Spanish, and Portuguese forces fought together.  
They fought against the French.

## Equality in revolutionary documents

The **U.S. Declaration of Independence (1776)** and **France’s Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789)** said that **all men were created equal**.

In practice, these ideas mainly applied to **white men of European descent**. In Europe and the United States, **women** and **enslaved people** were usually left out.

---

## Whose rights counted most

The rights described as belonging to “all men” were the rights that mattered most to **free white men**. These included:

- **property rights**
- **freedom of expression**
- **the right to take part in government**

Only the most radical people in the United States and France argued that **women should have the same rights as men**.

Only a few also argued that **people of different races** should be equal to white people in rights and social status.

---

## How these ideas helped spark revolution in Saint-Domingue

Even so, these documents helped inspire a **slave revolt in Saint-Domingue**. This revolt became one of the most important effects of the French Revolution in the Americas.

---

## Saint-Domingue: a wealthy colony built on slavery

**Saint-Domingue** was a French colony on the western side of the Caribbean island of **Hispaniola**. France founded it in the **mid-1600s**.

It soon became the **most profitable colony in the Americas**. This wealth came mostly from the labor of **enslaved Africans**.

Enslaved people were forced to work on plantations that produced:

- **sugar**
- **coffee**
- **indigo**

---

## The revolt begins (1791)

In **1791**, freed and enslaved Africans and other islanders of African descent rebelled.

Two key leaders were:

- **Toussaint Louverture**
- **Jean-Jacques Dessalines**

Both men had been born enslaved on local plantations.

## From revolt to independence (1804)

The revolt grew into a full revolution. It led to independence from France.

In **1804**, the new free republic of **Haiti** was declared.

## Why the Haitian Revolution was different

The Haitian Revolution was unusual.

It was **not** led by white colonists of European descent seeking political representation and more economic freedom. That had been the pattern in the British colonies of North America.

In Saint-Domingue, the fight was led by people at the **lowest levels of the social hierarchy**.

---

## Two goals, two meanings of liberation

The rebellion in Haiti had two main goals. It also involved two different meanings of liberation.

For **free Black people and mixed-race elites**, freedom meant ending colonialism. It meant **independence from French rule**.

For **enslaved Black people**, liberation was more basic. It meant an end to **plantation abuse** and an end to **slavery**.

---

## Victory and the creation of Haiti

By **January 1804**, Black revolutionaries had won through successful **guerrilla tactics**. They defeated a French army that was already weakened by **yellow fever**.

This victory created the Haitian nation.

Haiti became the **second liberated territory** in the Western Hemisphere. It also became the **second republican system** there.

---

## Fear of Haitian influence in the Americas

After the uprising in Haiti, political elites in the Americas feared its influence. They worried it would inspire other slave rebellions.

They feared that:

- American Indians  
- free and enslaved Africans  
- people of mixed-racial ancestry  

might start violent independence movements.

Because of this fear, the **creole aristocracy** hesitated. They were less willing to copy the liberty-seeking Anglo-American colonists.

Support for independence from their parent countries **weakened rather than grew**.

## The Napoleonic era and shifting alliances (1803–1814)

During the Napoleonic era (**1803–1814**), Portugal and Spain took different sides in the wider war between France and other European nations.

These nations had united against **Napoléon Bonaparte**, the emperor of the French.

**Portugal** kept its long-standing alliance with **Great Britain**. Britain was an enemy of Napoléon.

**Spain**, in contrast, was a **French ally**.

---

## Spain’s weakness and colonial insecurity

Since the **War of Spanish Succession (1701–1714)**, Spain had been ruled by the **House of Bourbon**. At this time, King **Carlos IV** followed a disastrous policy of war with England.

British naval blockades disrupted trade between Spain and its colonies.

In **1806**, British soldiers attacked **Buenos Aires**, in the Viceroyalty of **Río de la Plata** (present-day Argentina). Local forces defeated the British.

Still, the attack revealed something important:

- Spain was **vulnerable**
- Spain could not reliably **protect** its colonists

---

## The Continental System and pressure on Portugal (1807)

In **1807**, Napoléon created the **Continental System**, also called the continental blockade. It required all European ports to close to English shipping.

Portugal did not follow this policy. Portugal continued to trade with Britain, one of its oldest allies.

Britain could not be defeated if it could still trade in Europe through Portugal.

To force Portugal to comply, France would have to invade Portugal. France could do this only by marching through Spain.

---

## French intervention in Spain and a crisis of monarchy

By then, Spain was a vulnerable French satellite. Napoléon easily got permission from the Spanish crown to invade Portugal by land.

As a result, Spanish subjects suffered heavy taxation, war, and occupation.

Popular anger grew against these pro-French policies. Carlos IV faced pressure to abdicate. He stepped down in favor of his son, **Fernando**.

Napoléon then intervened:

- he detained both Carlos and Fernando  
- he forced both men to give up their claims to the Spanish throne  
- he installed his brother, **Joseph Bonaparte**, as king of Spain  

---

## Rebellion and the Peninsular War (1808–1814)

Napoléon’s plan did not fully work.

In early **1808**, most people in Spain rejected Joseph Bonaparte. Creole royalists and some republicans in the colonies also rebelled.

The rebellion began in Madrid. It quickly spread to other cities across the Iberian Peninsula.

This conflict became the **Peninsular War (1808–1814)**. British, Spanish, and Portuguese forces fought together against the French.

The nations of Latin America also became export economies. After they gained independence from Spain and Portugal, they wanted to industrialize. But they faced many obstacles.

In the early nineteenth century, some countries did build industry.

- Brazil imported steam engines. It built facilities to refine sugar, process coffee, and make textiles.  
- Paraguay built an iron foundry. It also started a steamship line.  
- Chile opened coal mines. It built sawmills and flour mills.  
- Many countries built rail lines.

Even so, Latin America did not become heavily industrialized. Development followed a different path.

Independence was part of the problem. Under Spanish and Portuguese rule, merchants disliked trade restrictions. But those rules also taxed foreign goods. That made imported products more expensive. It protected local handicraft industries.

After independence, merchants could trade with any country. Goods from Europe and the United States flooded Latin American markets. Like India and Egypt, Latin American countries found they could not make manufactured goods as cheaply as imports. They also could not produce enough to meet demand at home. Brazilians and Chileans watched their silver flow overseas instead of being spent locally.

Latin Americans soon saw that cash crops brought more success than manufacturing. Sugar and coffee had supported the colonial economy. They were still in high demand. Later in the nineteenth century, Brazil also produced rubber for the same reason. The region used its abundant land and large agricultural workforce to supply raw materials to industrialized nations.

These choices made sense to planters and politicians. But they also locked former Spanish and Portuguese colonies into exporting raw materials. Raw materials sold for less than the finished products made from them.

Latin America sold large amounts of cash crops to the United States and Europe. This enriched the planter class. But earnings from exports never exceeded, or even equaled, what Latin America paid for imports.

This imbalance harmed society.

- Wealthy plantation owners and urban professionals could buy factory-made goods.  
- Agricultural laborers could not. This widened the class divide.

Industrial improvements also brought problems. Mines and railroads were often funded by European and U.S. banks. Much equipment, such as steam engines and other machinery, was imported from Europe. This left less money at home for domestic projects like roads and telegraph lines.

Regional wars also disrupted industrialization. From 1864 to 1870, Paraguay fought Uruguay, Brazil, and Argentina in the War of the Triple Alliance. By the end of the war, fighting and infectious diseases had killed much of Paraguay’s population.

Many forces, together, made industrialization largely unsuccessful. Latin America remained mainly an exporter of cash crops. Railroads were built, but they were usually short lines. They linked the interior to the coast to move raw materials for export. National rail networks did not develop like they did in the United States and Europe. Electrification happened only in major cities.

Under Spanish and Portuguese rule, merchants disliked trade restrictions. However, those rules also **taxed foreign goods**, which made imports more expensive. This helped protect local handicraft industries.

After independence, merchants could trade with any country. Goods from Europe and the United States **flooded local markets**.

Like India and Egypt, many Latin American countries could not make manufactured goods as cheaply as imports. They also could not produce enough to meet demand at home. Brazilians and Chileans watched their **silver flow overseas** instead of being spent locally.

---

## The shift to cash crops

Latin Americans soon saw that **cash crops** brought more success than manufacturing.

- Sugar and coffee had supported the colonial economy and stayed in high demand.  
- Later in the 1800s, Brazil also produced **rubber** for the same reason.

The region used its abundant land and large agricultural workforce to supply **raw materials** to industrialized nations.

These choices made sense to planters and politicians. But they also locked former colonies into exporting raw materials. **Raw materials sold for less than the finished products** made from them.

---

## Economic imbalance and social impact

Latin America sold large amounts of cash crops to the United States and Europe. This enriched the **planter class**.

But export earnings never exceeded, or even equaled, what Latin America paid for imports.

This imbalance harmed society:

- Wealthy plantation owners and urban professionals could buy factory-made goods.  
- Agricultural laborers could not.  
- This **widened the class divide**.

---

## Foreign funding and imported equipment

Industrial improvements also brought problems:

- Mines and railroads were often funded by **European and U.S. banks**.  
- Much equipment (steam engines and other machinery) was **imported from Europe**.

This left less money at home for domestic projects like roads and telegraph lines.

---

## War and disruption

Regional wars also disrupted industrialization.

From **1864 to 1870**, Paraguay fought Uruguay, Brazil, and Argentina in the **War of the Triple Alliance**. By the end of the war, fighting and infectious diseases had killed much of Paraguay’s population.

---

## Long-term result

Many forces together made industrialization largely unsuccessful. Latin America remained mainly an exporter of **cash crops**.

Railroads were built, but they were usually short lines. They linked the interior to the coast to move raw materials for export. **National rail networks** did not develop like they did in the United States and Europe.

Electrification happened only in **major cities**.

The Cold War between the West and the East was fought in many ways.  
Both sides used many strategies.

## Aid and influence
The United States and the Soviet Union gave aid and technical help to countries in Latin America, Asia, and Africa.  
Many of these countries had been European colonies until the end of World War II.

The United States hoped this aid would stop the spread of communism.  
It wanted to remove economic reasons for countries to align with the Soviet Union.

Communism appealed to many poor people.  
It promised that a nation’s wealth would support all citizens.  
In the Soviet system, people were provided with jobs, housing, education, health care, and public transportation.  
The standard of living was lower than in the West.  
Still, for people facing hunger and homelessness, and who saw no way to improve their lives, communism seemed like a good alternative.

## Propaganda and media
Both sides used propaganda.  
They used literature, images, and films.  
The goal was to build support for their own policies and ideology.  
They also tried to damage the other side’s credibility and prestige.

In 1950, the U.S.-funded Radio Free Europe began broadcasting news to Eastern Bloc countries.  
In 1953, Radio Liberty began broadcasting to the Soviet Union.

Radio Free Europe and the Free Europe Committee also printed leaflets and posters.  
The Free Europe Committee was an organization of American business executives and lawyers.  
It was established by the U.S. government.  
These materials praised life in democratic, capitalist countries.  
They were dropped from weather balloons over East Germany, Poland, Czechoslovakia, and Hungary.

## Soviet messaging and its appeal
Soviet propaganda stressed the USSR’s desire for world peace.  
It praised communist ideals.  
It promoted a classless society where people were treated equally, regardless of race or gender.

This message appealed strongly to people in Latin America, Africa, and Asia.  
Some African Americans were also attracted to these promises.  
They faced racism and segregation in the United States.  
Opponents of the U.S. civil rights movement often denounced it as communist in nature.

## Sports and culture
Sometimes propaganda appeared through sports.  
Each side used athletes to show the superiority of its system.  
Swimmers, runners, weightlifters, and gymnasts were part of this effort.  
Sports and news broadcasts closely tracked Olympic medal counts for U.S. and Soviet athletes.

At other times, the two sides used cultural exchanges.  
Soviet ballet dancers toured the United States.  
American jazz musicians and symphony orchestras visited Eastern Bloc countries.

## Technology and the space race
Both sides highlighted their technology and ingenuity.

In 1959, there was an exhibition in Moscow.  
U.S. vice president Richard Nixon showed Soviet premier Nikita Khrushchev American technology.  
He used a model kitchen to do this.  
Khrushchev responded by asking if American families also had machines to save them the effort of putting food in their mouths and swallowing it.

The two countries also competed in space.  
In 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, the first satellite.  
This was a serious blow to U.S. pride.

In response, in 1958 President Dwight D. Eisenhower asked Congress to create an agency to explore space.  
The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) was established that year.

In 1961, the Soviet Union sent the first astronaut into space.  
In 1969, the United States put the first humans on the surface of the moon.

## Espionage and covert action
Espionage was another major tool.

The United States used the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA).  
The CIA was formed in 1947.  
The USSR used the KGB.

These agencies watched the other nation.  
They also planned, supported, and carried out sabotage.  
They also carried out assassinations of people seen as enemies.

The CIA and the KGB also stirred discontent in foreign nations.  
They trained fighting forces.  
They encouraged revolution and insurgency.  
Their goal was to topple foreign governments.  
They wanted to install leaders friendly to their own country.

For example, in 1961 the CIA trained Cuban insurgents.  
The goal was to overthrow Cuba’s communist government under Fidel Castro.  
Similarly, the KGB helped Vietnamese communists.  
These communists tried to defeat the government of South Vietnam during the Vietnam War.

## Nuclear weapons and deterrence
The most dangerous competition was the stockpiling of nuclear weapons.  
This was also the main way each side tried to restrain the other.

In 1949, the Soviet Union detonated an atomic bomb.  
This ended the U.S. monopoly on nuclear weapons.

In 1952, the United States developed the hydrogen bomb.  
Some atomic scientists who had worked on the Manhattan Project opposed this step.  
The United States tested the hydrogen bomb at the Pacific atoll of Eniwetok in 1952.  
This weapon was one thousand times more powerful than the bomb dropped on Hiroshima.

Once the United States developed this weapon, the Soviet Union felt it needed to do the same.

## Missiles, shelters, and MAD
In the 1950s, both countries developed intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs).  
Now nuclear warheads could be launched from within a country’s own territory.  
They could also be launched from satellite nations.  
An air force that could intercept bombers was no longer enough to prevent nuclear attack.

Both the Western and Eastern Blocs prepared for possible war.  
They built shelters to protect citizens in the event of nuclear war.  
However, neither side believed it could truly win.

Both the United States and the USSR came to believe survival depended on retaliation.  
They wanted the ability to strike back with overwhelming destruction.  
The idea was to make the other side afraid to launch the first bomb.  
In the United States, this policy was called “mutually assured destruction” (MAD).

If nuclear weapons failed to prevent conflict, both sides were also ready for conventional war.  
During the Cold War, they built large military forces.  
They also spent billions of dollars on battleships, submarines, and fighter jets.
