chapter_key: Decolonization in Africa in the Shadow of the Cold War
text:
After World War II, many people in Africa wanted to end Western control.  
They wanted the right to govern themselves.

In 1941, the United Kingdom and the United States signed the Atlantic Charter.  
It promised self-determination for all peoples.  
African countries wanted that promise to become real.

In October 1945, the Fifth Pan-African Congress met in Manchester, England.  
Delegates came from African colonies in Europe’s empires.  
Others came from the Caribbean, the United States, India, Sri Lanka, and Central America.  
They called for an end to colonialism.

## European powers resist change

European colonial powers did not agree.  
World War II had damaged their economies.  
Some believed they needed Africa’s resources and markets to rebuild.

Britain’s colony of Gold Coast (Ghana) received a new constitution in 1946.  
It showed Britain wanted to keep control.  
Africans could elect more members of a Legislative Council.  
But the council could only advise.  
Real power stayed with the appointed governor.

## Ghana wins independence

In August 1947, Ghanaians formed the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC).  
The UGCC demanded self-government.  
Kwame Nkrumah was one of its founding members.

In January 1948, Nkrumah and another UGCC member spoke to Ghanaian ex-service members.  
Many people were angry about unemployment and inflation.  
They planned to petition the governor.

A few days later, riots broke out.  
The government blamed the UGCC.  
It arrested several members, including Nkrumah.

In 1949, Nkrumah formed a new party.  
It was called the Convention People’s Party.  
In January 1950, he called for a general strike.  
He wanted Britain to allow a new constitution to be drafted.

He was jailed again.  
He was still in prison when he won election in 1951.  
This was the first election in Africa with universal suffrage.

Nkrumah became Ghana’s prime minister.  
On March 6, 1957, Ghana became independent.

## Kenya and the Mau Mau uprising

After Ghana, other British colonies also gained independence.

In 1944, the Kenya African Union (KAU) was founded.  
It called for liberation from British rule.  
In 1947, Jomo Kenyatta became its leader.

Britain did not want to grant Kenya independence.  
Many White settlers owned profitable coffee plantations.  
They controlled more land than Black Africans did.

In 1952, the Kenya Land and Freedom Army began fighting.  
People commonly called it the Mau Mau.

The Mau Mau was a nationalist movement among the Kikuyu people.  
It supported violence to reach its goal.  
It attacked civilians, both White and Black.  
Some victims were burned to death.  
Others were killed with machetes.  
Africans loyal to the British government were also targeted.

Britain responded harshly.  
It banned all Kenyan political parties, including the KAU.  
Thousands of people were sent to internment camps.  
Whole villages were forced to move to new areas.  
Officials said this was to protect them from the Mau Mau.  
British forces also killed innocent civilians.

By 1956, the uprising was mostly ended.  
In 1960, Britain began talks about independence.  
Kenya became independent in 1963.  
Kenyatta became prime minister.

## French colonies and violent संघर्ष for independence

Nationalism also grew in French colonies.  
France tried moderate reforms at first.

In 1946, France proposed major reforms in its African colonies.  
It ended forced labor.  
It ended racially discriminatory practices.  
It allowed some self-rule.  
But it did not offer independence.

Many people demanded full independence.  
They fought for it.

From 1947 to 1949, the Malagasy Revolt took place in Madagascar.  
It cost thousands of lives.

In Cameroon, violence ended colonialism in 1957.

In Algeria, war lasted from 1954 to 1962.  
France granted independence in 1962.  
More than one million people of European descent left Algeria.

## The Belgian Congo and Cold War conflict

In the Belgian Congo (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), Cold War tensions increased violence.

In 1960, Belgium promised independence in thirty years.  
Nationalist groups rejected this.  
They wanted independence immediately.  
These groups included the Congolese National Movement and the Alliance of Bakongo.

Black Congolese protested.  
Many protests turned into riots.  
People refused to pay taxes.

Many White residents formed citizens’ militias.  
They attacked Black residents.

Belgium saw how strong the nationalist movement was.  
It agreed to independence on June 30, 1960.

### Mutiny and foreign involvement

Independence did not end violence.

A few days after independence, Émile Janssens spoke to Black troops.  
He was the White commander of the *Force Publique*, the security force.  
He made clear that White officers would stay in charge.

Soldiers mutinied.

Patrice Lamumba was prime minister.  
He led the Congolese National Movement.  
He replaced Janssens with a Black commander.  
The force was renamed the National Congolese Army.  
Lamumba promoted Black soldiers.

The mutiny continued.  
White people were attacked across the country.  
Belgian forces invaded to protect them.

During the chaos, Katanga province seceded.  
Katanga was mineral-rich.  
It declared itself independent.

Lamumba asked the United Nations for help.  
The UN had sent peacekeepers to restore order.  
Lamumba wanted the UN to end Katanga’s secession.  
The UN refused.  
It said secession was an internal political matter.

Lamumba then asked the United States for help.  
The United States refused.

Lamumba then turned to the Soviet Union.  
The Soviet Union sent weapons and military advisers.  
In Western eyes, this made Lamumba look like a communist.

Colonel Joseph-Désiré Mobutu (Mobutu Sese Seko) led the security force.  
He used the chaos to act.  
He put Lamumba under house arrest.  
He placed Joseph Kasa-Vubu in charge.  
Kasa-Vubu led the Alliance of Bakongo.

Lamumba was later killed by Katangese troops.  
The CIA knew about it and supported it.  
The CIA gave money and weapons to Mobutu and Kasa-Vubu.

## Britain moves faster: “The Wind of Change”

British leaders watched nationalism grow.  
They saw it in Kenya and other colonies.  
They feared more violence like in Congo.

Britain moved quickly to free colonies in Africa, the Caribbean, and Asia.

In 1960, Prime Minister Harold Macmillan visited Africa.  
He gave a speech called “The Wind of Change.”  
He said a wind of change was sweeping Africa.  
He said liberation was coming.  
He said this was true even if White Britons did not want it.

## Portugal refuses to let go

Portugal did not follow Britain, France, or Belgium.  
Portugal refused to give up its colonies.

The Second Portuguese Republic began in 1933.  
It was nationalistic and quasi-fascist.  
It treated the colonies as part of Portugal.  
It claimed Portugal brought order and civilization to Africa.

Independence movements formed in Angola, Portuguese Guinea (Guinea-Bissau), and Mozambique.  
Some groups wanted Western-style democracy.  
Others wanted communism.

In Angola, Portugal fought several groups:
- The National Liberation Front (FNLA), mostly rural and Bakongo.  
- The Marxist People’s Movement of Liberation of Angola (MPLA), mostly urban.  
- The National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), rural and mainly Ovimbundu.

In Mozambique, the Marxist Mozambique Liberation Front fought for independence.

In Guinea-Bissau, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde led the struggle.  
It was also Marxist.

### Cold War support and independence

The Cold War shaped these wars.  
The Soviet Union, China, Romania, Cuba, and Yugoslavia gave aid to independence groups.  
The United States did not.  
Portugal was a NATO ally.

In 1974, leftist military officers overthrew Portugal’s government.  
They created a democratic government.  
The new government ended the wars by granting independence to:
- Angola  
- Guinea-Bissau  
- Mozambique  
- Cape Verde  
- São Tomé and Príncipe

Independence did not end violence.  
In 1975, civil war began in Angola over control of the country.  
The United States supported UNITA and the FNLA against the MPLA.

## Rhodesia becomes Zimbabwe

Violence also erupted in Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe).

White residents rejected Britain’s plan for majority rule.  
They did not want a government led by Black Rhodesians.  
In 1965, they declared independence from the United Kingdom.  
Ian Smith became prime minister.  
Britain opposed this move.

Civil war followed.  
The White government fought two Black nationalist groups:
- ZAPU, led by Joshua Nkomo  
- ZANU, led by Robert Mugabe

The Soviet Union supported ZAPU.  
China supported ZANU.

Eventually, all three sides reached an agreement.  
Britain recognized Zimbabwe’s independence in 1980.  
Mugabe became prime minister.

After that, thousands of Nkomo’s followers were tortured, imprisoned, or killed.  
This continued until 1987.  
That year, Nkomo and Mugabe merged their political parties.

## South Africa and apartheid

In South Africa, Black Africans fought for liberation against White Africans, not a European empire.

In 1909, several areas were combined:
- British Cape Colony  
- Natal  
- The Boer republics of Transvaal and the Orange Free State

Together they formed a self-governing dominion in the British Empire.

Only the White minority could rule.  
Power struggles were between Whites of British descent and Afrikaner (Dutch) descent.

Laws denied Black Africans the right to vote.  
Laws blocked them from claiming most land.  
They could not live in some areas.  
Many were forced into separate “homelands.”

In 1948, racial segregation became official policy.  
This system was called **apartheid**.

In 1950, South Africa passed the Suppression of Communism Act.  
It banned the South African Communist Party.  
It also banned actions meant to end racial discrimination.

In 1960, Britain allowed a vote on whether to remain a dominion.  
Most South Africans could not vote.  
In 1961, South Africa became a republic.  
But the liberation struggle continued.

### Resistance and the end of apartheid

Groups like the African National Congress (ANC) and the Pan-Africanist Congress (PAC) opposed apartheid.  
At first, they used peaceful protest.

In 1960, peaceful protesters were killed in Sharpeville.  
After that, the government banned the ANC and PAC.

Many activists then used sabotage and attacks on police and military targets.  
They also used nonviolent tactics, such as strikes.

In 1976, protests began in Black townships.  
A new law required Black students to learn Afrikaans.  
Afrikaans was the language of Dutch colonizers.

In Soweto, police fired on schoolchildren.  
More than one hundred were killed.

Over decades, thousands of activists were arrested and imprisoned.  
Nelson Mandela, an ANC leader, was imprisoned.  
Many others were executed.

By the 1980s, pressure increased.  
There was continued resistance inside South Africa.  
Other countries imposed economic sanctions.  
There were boycotts of South African businesses.  
The world condemned apartheid.

In 1991, South Africa officially ended apartheid.  
In 1994, elections were held with voting rights for all races.  
The ANC won.  
The National Assembly elected Nelson Mandela president.

They wanted the right to govern themselves.

## 1. The push for self-rule after World War II

In 1941, the United Kingdom and the United States signed the Atlantic Charter.  
It promised self-determination for all peoples.  
African countries wanted that promise to become real.

In October 1945, the Fifth Pan-African Congress met in Manchester, England.

Delegates came from:  
- African colonies in Europe’s empires  
- the Caribbean  
- the United States  
- India  
- Sri Lanka  
- Central America  

They called for an end to colonialism.

---

## 2. European powers resist change

European colonial powers did not agree.

World War II had damaged their economies.  
Some believed they needed Africa’s resources and markets to rebuild.

### Example: Britain in the Gold Coast (Ghana)

Britain’s colony of Gold Coast (Ghana) received a new constitution in 1946.

It showed Britain wanted to keep control:  
- Africans could elect more members of a legislative council  
- but the council could only advise  
- real power stayed with the appointed governor  

---

## 3. Ghana wins independence

In August 1947, Ghanaians formed the United Gold Coast Convention (UGCC).  
The UGCC demanded self-government.  
Kwame Nkrumah was one of its founding members.

### Protests and arrests

In January 1948, Nkrumah and another UGCC member spoke to Ghanaian ex-service members.  
Many people were angry about unemployment and inflation.  
They planned to petition the governor.

A few days later, riots broke out.  
The government blamed the UGCC.  
It arrested several members, including Nkrumah.

### A new party and mass action

In 1949, Nkrumah formed a new party:  
- the Convention People’s Party  

In January 1950, he called for a general strike.  
He wanted Britain to allow a new constitution to be drafted.

He was jailed again.

### Election and independence

Nkrumah was still in prison when he won election in 1951.  
This was the first election in Africa with universal suffrage.

Nkrumah became Ghana’s prime minister.

On March 6, 1957, Ghana became independent.

---

## 4. Kenya and the Mau Mau uprising

After Ghana, other British colonies also gained independence.

In 1944, the Kenya African Union (KAU) was founded.  
It called for liberation from British rule.

In 1947, Jomo Kenyatta became its leader.

### Why Britain resisted

Britain did not want to grant Kenya independence.  
Many white settlers owned profitable coffee plantations.  
They controlled more land than Black Africans did.

### The Mau Mau conflict

In 1952, the Kenya Land and Freedom Army began fighting.  
People commonly called it the Mau Mau.

The Mau Mau was a nationalist movement among the Kikuyu people.  
It supported violence to reach its goal.

It attacked civilians, both white and black.  
Some victims were burned to death.  
Others were killed with machetes.  
Africans loyal to the British government were also targeted.

### Britain’s response

Britain responded harshly:  
- it banned all Kenyan political parties, including the KAU  
- thousands of people were sent to internment camps  
- whole villages were forced to move to new areas  
- British forces also killed innocent civilians  

By 1956, the uprising was mostly ended.

In 1960, Britain began talks about independence.  
Kenya became independent in 1963.  
Kenyatta became prime minister.

---

Nationalism also grew in French colonies.  
France tried moderate reforms at first.

In 1946, France proposed major reforms in its African colonies:  
- it ended forced labor  
- it ended racially discriminatory practices  
- it allowed some self-rule  
- but it did not offer independence  

Many people demanded full independence.  
They fought for it.

Examples:  
- From 1947 to 1949, the Malagasy Revolt took place in Madagascar. It cost thousands of lives.  
- In Cameroon, violence ended colonialism in 1957.  
- In Algeria, war lasted from 1954 to 1962. France granted independence in 1962. More than one million people of European descent left Algeria.

In the Belgian Congo (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), Cold War tensions increased violence.

In 1960, Belgium promised independence in thirty years.  
Nationalist groups rejected this.  
They wanted independence immediately.

These groups included:  
- the Congolese National Movement  
- the Alliance of Bakongo  

Black Congolese protested.  
Many protests turned into riots.  
People refused to pay taxes.

Many white residents formed citizens’ militias.  
They attacked Black residents.

Belgium saw how strong the nationalist movement was.  
It agreed to independence on June 30, 1960.

Independence did not end violence.

A few days after independence, Émile Janssens spoke to Black troops.  
He was the white commander of the Force Publique, the security force.  
He made clear that white officers would stay in charge.

Soldiers mutinied.

Patrice Lamumba was prime minister.  
He led the Congolese National Movement.

Lamumba responded by:  
- replacing Janssens with a Black commander  
- renaming the force the National Congolese Army  
- promoting Black soldiers  

The mutiny continued.  
White people were attacked across the country.  
Belgian forces invaded to protect them.

During the chaos, Katanga province seceded.  
Katanga was mineral-rich.  
It declared itself independent.

Lamumba asked the United Nations for help.  
The UN sent peacekeepers to restore order.  
Lamumba wanted the UN to end Katanga’s secession.  
The UN refused. It said secession was an internal political matter.

Lamumba then asked the United States for help.  
The United States refused.

Lamumba then turned to the Soviet Union.  
The Soviet Union sent weapons and military advisers.  
In Western eyes, this made Lamumba look like a communist.

Colonel Joseph-Désiré Mobutu (Mobutu Sese Seko) led the security force.  
He used the chaos to act:  
- he put Lamumba under house arrest  
- he placed Joseph Kasa-Vubu in charge  
- Kasa-Vubu led the Alliance of Bakongo  

Lamumba was later killed by Katangese troops.  
The CIA knew about it and supported it.  
The CIA gave money and weapons to Mobutu and Kasa-Vubu.

British leaders watched nationalism grow.  
They saw it in Kenya and other colonies.  
They feared more violence like in Congo.

Britain moved quickly to free colonies in Africa, the Caribbean, and Asia.

In 1960, Prime Minister Harold Macmillan visited Africa.  
He gave a speech called the wind of change.

He said:  
- a wind of change was sweeping Africa  
- liberation was coming  
- this was true even if white Britons did not want it  

---

## 8. Portugal refuses to let go

Portugal did not follow Britain, France, or Belgium.  
Portugal refused to give up its colonies.

The Second Portuguese Republic began in 1933.  
It was nationalistic and quasi-fascist.  
It treated the colonies as part of Portugal.  
It claimed Portugal brought order and civilization to Africa.

- Angola  
- Portuguese Guinea (Guinea-Bissau)  
- Mozambique  

Some groups wanted Western-style democracy.  
Others wanted communism.

### Angola: several groups

In Angola, Portugal fought several groups:  
- the National Liberation Front (FNLA), mostly rural and Bakongo  
- the Marxist People’s Movement of Liberation of Angola (MPLA), mostly urban  
- the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), rural and mainly Ovimbundu  

### Mozambique

In Mozambique, the Marxist Mozambique Liberation Front fought for independence.

### Guinea-Bissau

In Guinea-Bissau, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde led the struggle.  
It was also Marxist.

### Cold War support and independence

The Cold War shaped these wars.

The Soviet Union, China, Romania, Cuba, and Yugoslavia gave aid to independence groups.  
The United States did not.  
Portugal was a NATO ally.

In 1974, leftist military officers overthrew Portugal’s government.  
They created a democratic government.

The new government ended the wars by granting independence to:  
- Angola  
- Guinea-Bissau  
- Mozambique  
- Cape Verde  
- São Tomé and Príncipe  

Independence did not end violence.  
In 1975, civil war began in Angola over control of the country.  
The United States supported UNITA and the FNLA against the MPLA.

---

## 9. Rhodesia becomes Zimbabwe

Violence also erupted in Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe).

White residents rejected Britain’s plan for majority rule.  
They did not want a government led by Black Rhodesians.

In 1965, they declared independence from the United Kingdom.  
Ian Smith became prime minister.  
Britain opposed this move.

Civil war followed.

The white government fought two Black nationalist groups:  
- ZAPU, led by Joshua Nkomo  
- ZANU, led by Robert Mugabe  

The Soviet Union supported ZAPU.  
China supported ZANU.

Eventually, all three sides reached an agreement.  
Britain recognized Zimbabwe’s independence in 1980.  
Mugabe became prime minister.

After that, thousands of Nkomo’s followers were tortured, imprisoned, or killed.  
This continued until 1987.  
That year, Nkomo and Mugabe merged their political parties.

---

## 10. South Africa and apartheid

In South Africa, Black Africans fought for liberation against white Africans, not a European empire.

In 1909, several areas were combined:  
- British Cape Colony  
- Natal  
- the Boer republics of Transvaal and the Orange Free State  

Together they formed a self-governing dominion in the British Empire.

Only the white minority could rule.  
Power struggles were between whites of British descent and Afrikaner (Dutch) descent.

### Laws and segregation

Laws denied Black Africans the right to vote.  
Laws blocked them from claiming most land.  
They could not live in some areas.  
Many were forced into separate homelands.

In 1948, racial segregation became official policy.  
This system was called apartheid.

In 1950, South Africa passed the Suppression of Communism Act.  
It banned the South African Communist Party.  
It also banned actions meant to end racial discrimination.

In 1960, Britain allowed a vote on whether to remain a dominion.  
Most South Africans could not vote.

In 1961, South Africa became a republic.  
But the liberation struggle continued.

### Resistance and the end of apartheid

Groups like the African National Congress (ANC) and the Pan-Africanist Congress (PAC) opposed apartheid.  
At first, they used peaceful protest.

In 1960, peaceful protesters were killed in Sharpeville.  
After that, the government banned the ANC and PAC.

Many activists then used sabotage and attacks on police and military targets.  
They also used nonviolent tactics, such as strikes.

In 1976, protests began in Black townships.

Afrikaans was the language of Dutch colonizers.

In Soweto, police fired on schoolchildren.  
More than one hundred were killed.

Over decades, thousands of activists were arrested and imprisoned.  
Nelson Mandela, an ANC leader, was imprisoned.  
Many others were executed.

By the 1980s, pressure increased:  
- continued resistance inside South Africa  
- economic sanctions from other countries  
- boycotts of South African businesses  
- worldwide condemnation of apartheid

In 1994, elections were held with voting rights for all races.  
The ANC won.  
The National Assembly elected Nelson Mandela president.

## The Indian Mutiny of 1857 (Sepoy Rebellion)

The Indian Mutiny of 1857 is also called the Sepoy Rebellion.  
It was an attempt to overthrow British rule.

At first, the British East India Company preferred indirect rule.  
Later, British leaders believed they could govern India directly.  
Indian elites saw their power shrinking.  
This made more of them oppose British rule.

Many Europeans missionaries came to India.  
They tried to convert Indians to Christianity.  
This offended many people who wanted to keep their own traditions.

### The doctrine of lapse

Missionaries were only one cause of resentment.  
Lord Dalhousie was governor-general of India from 1848 to 1856.  
He created a way for Britain to take direct control of Indian states.

In Hindu custom, a ruler without a natural heir could adopt one.  
The adopted heir could inherit the kingdom.

Dalhousie introduced the doctrine of lapse.  
This gave Britain the right to approve adoptions.  
It also allowed Britain to annex states with no heirs.

Starting in 1848, Britain rejected some adoptions.  
Britain then annexed those states.

This policy mainly affected states with Hindu rulers.  
But it alarmed all of India’s aristocracy.

### British cultural changes

Britain believed its culture was superior.  
This led to changes that angered many Indians.

The British tried to end *sati* (*suttee*).  
In *sati*, some Hindu widows were expected to burn themselves alive on their husbands’ funeral pyres.  
The British also passed a law allowing widows to remarry.

The British introduced Western schooling.  
English became the language of instruction.  
This replaced Persian, which the Mughals favored.  
Persian was also a major language of literature and scholarship in many Islamic empires.

British officials preferred graduates of these schools.  
They gave them jobs in business and government.

British schools were more common in Hindu-majority areas.  
This created fear that Hindus would replace Muslims in positions of authority.  
Muslims had held many of these positions for centuries.

### The Enfield Rifle and the spark of revolt

Northern and southern independence forces both moved into the strongly royalist Viceroyalty of Peru. Their main target was Lima, the capital.

From the north came revolutionary armies led by Simón Bolívar. They came from the Viceroyalty of New Granada.  
From the south came forces led by José de San Martín. They came from the Viceroyalty of Río de la Plata and the newly independent Republic of Chile.

## San Martín takes Lima (1820–1821)

San Martín left Chile in 1820. He brought soldiers on land and sailors on ships. He was helped by Thomas Cochrane. Cochrane was a Scottish former naval officer and a mercenary. He was one of several foreigners who joined the patriots on their own initiative.

San Martín attacked royalist Peru by sea. He landed on the Peruvian coast in September 1820. The highlands stayed under royalist control. But his arrival sparked an uprising along the coast. San Martín slowly expanded his control. He eventually occupied Lima.

On July 28, 1821, Peruvian creoles in Lima were forced to declare independence. They also accepted San Martín as Protector of Peru.

## San Martín and Bolívar meet (1822)

San Martín now ruled Lima, both militarily and civilly. But royalist troops still controlled most of Peru’s interior. Many people in Lima saw San Martín and his forces as foreign invaders.

After liberating Bogotá in 1819, Bolívar moved into Ecuador. San Martín made little progress against the remaining royalists. San Martín and Bolívar were also rivals for leadership of the independence movement. They decided to meet in Guayaquil, Ecuador.

In 1821, Guayaquil’s valuable port and naval base fell under Bolívar’s control. In 1822, Bolívar entered Quito and declared Ecuador’s independence.

In July 1822, San Martín sailed to Guayaquil. He hoped to convince the city’s merchants to unite with Lima. But Bolívar arrived first. Bolívar pushed his supporters in Guayaquil to unite with Colombia. By the time San Martín arrived, control of the city was no longer the main issue.

San Martín met with Bolívar in private. Their talks were secret. Afterward, San Martín decided to leave the final liberation of South America to Bolívar. Soon after, San Martín withdrew from the struggle. He went into self-imposed exile in Europe. He never returned.

## Bolívar finishes the war in Peru (1823–1825)

Bolívar occupied Lima in 1823. In February 1824, a Peruvian congress named him dictator of Peru.

Bolívar won an important victory in August 1824. This was the Battle of Junín. In December 1824, his chief of staff, Antonio José de Sucre, defeated a much larger Spanish force. This was the Battle of Ayacucho.

In 1825, royalist troops in Upper Peru accepted a general amnesty. This happened after their defeat by Sucre. Upper Peru was renamed Bolivia in honor of *El Libertador*.

## Alliances, monarchy, and recognition

Bolívar and San Martín both thought in continent-wide terms. They supported close alliances among the new nations.

San Martín admired the British constitutional monarchy. He shared this view with Mexican conservatives. Bolívar rejected the mystical figure of a king. He believed a republican system best guaranteed stability.

## The Holy Alliance and the Monroe Doctrine (1815–1824)

Latin American independence movements wanted to end the rule of their mercantilist “parent” countries. They also wanted to end an economic system that slowed the growth of the colonies.

Many successful movements were led by well-educated elites. These leaders often faced resistance from most of the race-mixed population. Many people in this majority group supported the homeland instead.

Because they lacked broad popular support, the White creole minority had to move carefully. This group was exploitative. It also feared the oppressed mixed-race majorities. So the creole leaders often had to negotiate their gains step by step.

Liberators such as Simón Bolívar, José de San Martín, Pedro I, and Agustín de Iturbide got no major help from outside powers. They also often lacked a single, unified plan or strategy. They faced huge distances and difficult natural barriers. They also faced economic and cultural isolation between the regions they tried to unite.

Brazil’s independence followed its colonial past more than any other Latin American country. After 1822, Brazil was free of Portuguese rule. But it did not become a republic. It became an independent empire.

Brazil’s first emperor was Pedro I. He was a prince from the Portuguese royal family. He was also still an heir to the Portuguese throne.

Portuguese-born men continued to control trade. They also kept many powerful positions. These positions were in the bureaucracy, the army, and the church.

Politics in imperial Brazil was shaped by a conservative–liberal split. This division reflected conflicts between different economic groups. Independence did not bring major changes to colonial social and economic structures. The new constitutional monarchy mainly made the existing system official. It regularized the status quo.

Latin American independence created strong interest outside the region. This interest encouraged foreign travel and travel writing. Many people in the United States and Europe learned about South America through these accounts.

In the nineteenth century, European women usually did not travel for pleasure. Tourism is mainly a twentieth-century invention. Maria Dundas Graham Calcott traveled to South America in the 1820s with her husband, a navy officer. She served as governess to Pedro I’s daughter. The daughter was Princess Maria da Glória, the future queen of Portugal.

Graham kept diaries from 1821 to 1823. These diaries give a rare view of the Brazilian court during the independence process. They also show her broad interest in everyday life. She wrote about Brazil, including Salvador and Rio de Janeiro. She also wrote about Chile, including Santiago.

In Chile, Graham studied science and botany. She did this with a family friend, Thomas Cochrane. Cochrane was a former British navy officer.

Graham wrote to inform and entertain people of her time. Today, her writing helps historians in other ways. It offers insight into gender relations in the new South American nations. It also shows the elite social world in which she lived.

Graham focused on topics she saw as “suitable.” These included fashion and motherhood. These topics connected to the lives of Brazilian women.

Public life was mostly male. Her diaries show that foreign women observers like her were still outsiders. Graham was an urban elite woman. She was also Protestant. Her writing presented English customs and behavior as a model of “civilized” life.

Her views were biased. Yet, because she described private parts of women’s lives, her accounts still reveal a lot. They show details about public events in South American society. They also show her own ideas about femininity.

Her travel narrative is a window into how she believed Brazilian women shaped their lives. It is also a window into how they shaped their environment in nineteenth-century Brazil.

Some German units never made it out of Belgium. Fighting there stayed fierce for the rest of the war.

Other German units moved south. They advanced through northern France. French troops moved quickly to stop them.

In September 1914, the Battle of the Marne created new front lines. These lines soon became a stalemate. Both sides dug trenches. The trench system lasted for several years.

German armies were moving toward Paris. The French found a gap between two German divisions. The French attacked that gap.

Both sides then tried to outflank each other. They raced north in a series of moves. This became a “race to the sea.”

France called up more troops. At one point, French reserves even took Paris taxicabs. The taxis carried them to the front.

The Battle of the Marne lasted one week. In the end, the German advance was stopped. The fighting was so close to Paris that civilians could hear it.

The government censored information. Because of this blackout, rumors spread quickly. Many people feared Paris would fall. About 800,000 people left the city, expecting a German invasion.

---

In the east, Germany fought Russia sooner than expected. Russia was huge, so its military potential looked great. In reality, Russian troops were poorly equipped. They were also poorly trained.

At the Battle of Tannenberg, Russia had major problems. The high command struggled to communicate. Soldiers lacked supplies. Russia’s limited rail lines could not deliver what the army needed.

Germany crushed the Russian forces. Germany took more than 90,000 prisoners. Another 50,000 Russians became casualties during the week of fighting. German casualties were fewer than 20,000. The Russian general in command committed suicide.

---

Russia’s supply shortages also mattered in another major fight. Russia laid siege to Przemyśl, in modern-day Poland. The siege lasted from summer into fall, and then into winter.

Russian soldiers lacked coats and boots. Temperatures dropped sharply. Even so, Russia captured the city in 1915.

Austro-Hungarian forces carried most of the burden. They fought during the siege and in nearby mountains. They tried to relieve the fortress. They suffered well over 900,000 casualties. This was an astronomical number.

---

Great Britain soon used its naval power. Britain set up a blockade of German ports. This made it very hard for Germany to import needed goods.

Germany’s industrial strength helped it survive for much of the war. But in the final year, shortages hit every German family.

Germany’s navy was too small to blockade Britain in return. Still, Germany treated the North Sea as a war zone. It used mines and submarines to sink ships there.

---

In Asia, the war pushed nations to choose sides. Japan joined the Allies. Japan felt confident after defeating Russia in the Russo-Japanese War (1904–1905). Japan also saw a chance to raise its status in the world.

Japan attacked the German colonial port at Qingdao (Tsingtao). Qingdao was on the Chinese coast. Germany had held it for less than twenty years. Germany planned it as the headquarters of its Asian empire.

In mid-August 1914, Japan demanded that Germany leave Qingdao. Germany refused. Japan then blockaded the port. Japan also bombarded it.

The attacks lasted two months. Germany surrendered the city in November. Japan strengthened its relationship with Great Britain. Japan’s modernizing military also gained another victory, which increased national pride.

---

At the start of the war, the Allies rejected China’s offer of troops. By 1916, the situation had changed. Britain and France allowed Chinese laborers to come to Europe.

China had wanted to send combat troops. China hoped this would help in treaty talks after the war. China also wanted support to push Japan back from its borders.

Japan would not allow China to send combat troops. Japan had taken control of Qingdao. Japan wanted to be the unquestioned military power in Asia.

So China sent laborers instead. About 130,000 Chinese laborers went to Europe. They repaired equipment and dug trenches. They did not fight.

---

More countries entered the war after summer 1914. In October, the Ottoman Empire joined the Central powers. It did so by attacking Russia’s fleet in the Black Sea.

For the Ottomans, this was a calculated risk. The empire hoped to regain status in the world. It also hoped to gain territory. Strong ties had also grown between Ottoman leaders and German leaders in the years before the war.

Other countries followed. Bulgaria joined in 1915. It did so through a secret agreement. Bulgaria joined the Central powers. It also hoped to gain territory after the war.

Italy took a different path. When the war began, Italy declared neutrality. Many Italians disliked Austria-Hungary. The two countries had long argued over their border.

In April 1915, Italy made a secret agreement with the Allies. In May 1915, Italy declared war on the Central powers. Italy’s main goal was to regain land lost to Austria-Hungary.

---

The United States had long followed isolationism. The U.S. planned to stay out of the war. At the same time, it sold goods to both sides. It traded with Britain and France, and also with Germany and Austria-Hungary.

From the start, most American trade went to the Allies. This was partly because Britain played a major role in U.S. naval, merchant, and credit operations. It was also because the British blockade made trade with Germany difficult.

U.S. banks soon loaned money to both sides. By spring 1917, about $2 billion had gone to the Allies. Only $27 million had gone to the Central powers.

---

Most Americans did not want to enter the war. They had little interest in it. Unlike people in the warring countries, Americans were not limited by censorship. They could read about the huge casualty numbers. They could also learn about the horror of the fighting.

Many Americans felt relieved to be outside the conflict. They saw the war as insanity. They showed little desire to join it.

---

The United States also faced other problems. Its volunteer army was small. If the U.S. entered the war then, it would have little impact.

Business and banking interests leaned toward the Allies. But many Irish immigrants were strongly anti-British. This was because of ongoing conflict in Ireland. It was unclear how they would react if the U.S. fought on Britain’s side.

The U.S. also had a large German population. Many of them could oppose siding with the Allies.

Wilson was willing to intervene in Latin America. He saw it as a neighboring region. He did not take the same approach toward Europe.

However, Wilson strongly supported freedom of the seas. He also supported the rights of neutral nations during war. These commitments soon put him on a collision course with Germany.

In the eighteenth century, many philosophers wrote and talked about **natural rights**.  
Natural rights are rights that all human beings have.  
Examples include the right to life and the right to liberty.

Natural rights were seen as **fundamental** and **inalienable**.  
That means human laws cannot take them away.  
These ideas did not begin in the Enlightenment.  
They came from older traditions of justice and natural law.

For example, in ancient Persian Zoroastrianism there was the idea of *asha*.  
*Asha* means “God’s will.”  
It referred to an unchangeable law from the divine.  
This law was believed to govern the universe.

Many ancient religious and philosophical traditions developed ideas about natural law.  
But European Enlightenment thinkers did something new.  
They turned these ideas into a political system.  
In the eighteenth century, reason became more important.  
Many thinkers wanted to improve human life.  
So they imagined governments based on natural rights.  
This was different from the divine right of kings.  
It was also different from traditional Christian social hierarchies.

One early Enlightenment thinker on natural rights was the English philosopher **John Locke**.  
Locke argued that people have natural rights to **life, liberty, and property**.  
In *Two Treatises of Government*, he said people are born free.  
He also said government should exist only with the people’s consent.  
This idea is called **popular sovereignty**.

Locke and other European thinkers said all humans are inherently equal.  
But this claim was paradoxical.  
In practice, many of them supported colonialism and the Atlantic slave trade.  
These systems took natural rights away from most people.  
They denied rights to everyone except White men.

In France, Enlightenment thinkers also debated natural rights.  
**Voltaire** was a strong defender of rights and freedoms.  
His real name was François-Marie d’Arouet.  
He was a harsh critic of the Catholic Church, the aristocracy, and the French monarchy.  
He focused on religious toleration.  
He also defended freedom of speech.  
He argued for the value of reason.  
He wrote about these ideas in *Treatise on Tolerance* and *Republican Ideas*.  
In his 1759 satire *Candide*, he mocked both organized religion and secular government.

Voltaire’s contemporary **Montesquieu** also wrote about laws and rights.  
He focused on political liberty.  
He argued that government power should be separated.  
He wanted separate legislative, executive, and judicial powers.  
This separation would help keep government in check.  
He discussed this in his 1748 book *The Spirit of the Laws*.

Questions about state power and individual choice also shaped the work of **Jean-Jacques Rousseau**.  
He wrote the influential treatise *The Social Contract*.  
The idea of a **social contract** is much older than Rousseau.  
It goes back to Plato and Socrates in the fourth and fifth centuries BCE.  
It also appears in the second-century BCE Buddhist text *The Mahāvastu*.  
Social contract theory says individuals give up some natural rights to the state.  
In return, the state must protect and maintain those rights.

Rousseau argued that living in communities creates interdependence.  
So societies must balance personal freedom with state sovereignty.  
People should be free to choose their actions.  
But government must sometimes limit actions.  
It does this to protect everyone’s rights.

Rousseau also developed the idea of the **general will**.  
A state is legitimate only if it follows the will of the people as a whole.  
It should not follow the desires of a small elite minority.

Not all Enlightenment thinkers accepted natural rights.  
Some, like **Jeremy Bentham** and **Edmund Burke**, doubted that natural rights even existed.

Bentham was an English lawyer.  
He supported **utilitarianism**.  
Utilitarianism aims for the greatest good for the greatest number.  
Bentham argued that rights exist only because the state creates them.  
He said rights do not exist outside civil society.  
He also warned that challenging a government’s legitimacy could lead to chaos and lawlessness.  
This could happen even if the government ignored the general will.  
It could also happen even if the government ignored natural law.

The Irish philosopher **Edmund Burke** also rejected popular sovereignty.  
He did not deny natural law.  
But he said natural rights become irrelevant once civil society exists.  
He believed political power should be used only by people with virtue and good judgment.  
He thought such leaders would act in the people’s best interests.  
He also believed people would give up selfish desires for the good of the state.

The Enlightenment produced many different views on natural rights.  
It also encouraged people to think more critically about the state.  
It made people question when revolution might be legitimate.

Some thinkers, like Burke and Bentham, defended the supremacy of the state over individual rights.  
Others, like Locke and Voltaire, defended natural rights.  
They believed political liberty should not be interfered with.  
As these debates continued, they expanded into social contract theory.  
These discussions focused on the ethics and legitimacy of law and political order.

- **inalienable** (human laws cannot take them away)

These ideas did not begin in the Enlightenment.

---

Many ancient religious and philosophical traditions developed ideas about natural law.

One example comes from ancient Persian Zoroastrianism: **asha**.  
Asha means “god’s will.”  
It referred to an unchangeable divine law believed to govern the universe.

---

### What Enlightenment thinkers changed
Enlightenment thinkers did something new with older ideas.

They turned natural law into a political system.  
In the eighteenth century, reason became more important.  
Many thinkers wanted to improve human life.

So they imagined governments based on natural rights.  
This differed from:

- the divine right of kings
- traditional Christian social hierarchies

---

Stalin’s domestic agenda was set out in **Five-Year Plans**.  
Each plan listed economic goals the Soviet Union had to reach by the end of five years.  
The schedule was very ambitious, and often unrealistic.  
Officials still tried to meet the targets.

This was much harder to achieve.  
The policy was called **collectivization**.  
It meant replacing individual farms with large, state-run farms.  
Communist Party officials tried to meet quotas quickly.  
After the first Five-Year Plan began, quotas were raised.  
Officials pushed for results without respecting the realities of farming.  
Peasants strongly resisted government interference in their daily work.  
Some used violence as the policy was put in place.  
The revolution had promised peasants better lives.

He blamed them for problems with collectivization.  
He called them enemies of the state.

Some were blocked from certain jobs.

By 1939, over 90 percent of peasants had been forced onto collective farms.

Some poor peasants accepted collectivization because they had little property to lose.

Some killed their livestock rather than hand it over to the state.

He believed enemies surrounded him.

Collectivization caused mass death.

It was also worsened by:

- peasants slaughtering livestock  
- government policies that took food from peasants  

Ukraine, a major grain-producing region, was hit especially hard.  
Government decisions there led to mass starvation.  
Some officials entered homes and took any food they could find.

About **3.9 million** Ukrainians are estimated to have died.  
Ukrainians called this famine the **Holodomor** (“death by famine” in Ukrainian).

The problems of collectivization made some Communist Party members question Stalin’s choices.

- Russian Orthodox priests  
- ethnic minorities

- Red Army officers  
- government officials  
- prominent Soviet politicians  
- early supporters of Lenin from the first days of the Bolshevik Revolution

But anti-Semitism had existed in Europe for centuries. It never fully disappeared.

After Germany lost World War I, anti-Jewish propaganda and scapegoating increased.  
In the 1920s and 1930s, the Nazis encouraged it.

Joseph Goebbels led Nazi propaganda. His job was to convince Germans that Jewish people were an existential threat.  
Nazi messages appeared constantly in newspapers, radio, posters, and other media.

This propaganda pushed three main claims.  
1) Jewish people were a “problem.”  
2) Jewish people were like vermin. This was meant to dehumanize them.  
3) Removing them would create a better Germany and a better world.

In 1939, the Wehrmacht invaded Poland. Poland had the largest Jewish population in the world.  
This gave the Nazis the chance to begin genocide on a huge scale. This genocide is called the **Holocaust**.

Special killing squads followed the German army. They were called the *Einsatzgruppen* (“operational groups”).  
They killed “enemies” and “undesirables,” especially Jewish people.

The Nazis forced many Jewish people into ghettoes. This made them easier to control.  
They were also forced to do labor.

The largest ghetto was in Warsaw.  
By 1941, the Warsaw ghetto held 441,000 people.

In 1941, six major concentration camps were established.  
Railroad lines were built specifically to transport prisoners to these camps.

World War II, like World War I, led to major scientific and technological change.  
These changes quickly became matters of life and death.

Total war changed the relationship between governments and scientists.  
States needed new tools to fight and to protect national security.  
Governments paid for research into deadly and non-deadly technology.  
In fall 1939, British scientists quickly moved from pure research to war work.

New knowledge about radio waves led to radar.  
Radar gave early warning of enemy attacks.

Other advances improved electronics for the military.  
These included microwaves and early digital computing devices.  
These wartime tools later helped electronics spread into everyday life after the war.

Allied codebreaking helped create the first basic computers.  
British mathematician Alan Turing led a team for the British Secret Service.  
They tried to break the Nazi Enigma code.  
They built an electromagnetic device.  
It tested hundreds of thousands of possible key and letter combinations in captured messages.  
They eventually broke the code.

Another computing breakthrough was **ENIAC**.  
ENIAC stands for Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer.  
It was first built to calculate artillery trajectories for the U.S. Army.  
It worked at electronic speed, not mechanical speed.  
By 1955, ENIAC had done more calculations than humans had ever solved up to that time.

The war also brought life-saving medical advances.  
One major development improved the use and mass production of penicillin.

Another life-saving advance came from Charles Drew.  
Drew was an African American physician.  
He developed a way to process blood plasma.  
Plasma was easier to store for longer periods.  
It could also replace whole-blood transfusions in many cases.

Racial bias affected this work in 1941.  
The American Red Cross agreed with a War Department decision.  
They labeled blood and plasma as either “White” or “Negro.”  
Dr. Drew resigned from the National Blood Bank.  
He did so because the policy was racist and unscientific.

One of the most dramatic efforts was the push to build the atomic bomb.  
In December 1938, German physicists Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann split atoms by accident.  
They discovered nuclear fission.

A few months later, Germany started a secret weapons program.  
It was called the Uranium Club.  
Its goal was to create an atomic bomb.

Albert Einstein was a German-born physicist who had recently moved to the United States.  
He saw the danger of this research.  
He sent a letter to President Roosevelt.  
The letter had been written by physicist Leo Szilard.  
It warned Roosevelt and urged stronger U.S. research efforts.

By the late 1930s, British and other scientists believed an atomic bomb was possible.  
Teams of physicists formed to study nuclear chain reactions.  
Chain reactions are what drive an atomic explosion.  
Some of these scientists were refugees from Nazi Germany.

In August 1942, the U.S. government greatly expanded the work.  
It created the top-secret **Manhattan Project**.

Work took place at many sites across the United States.  
These included Los Alamos, New Mexico.  
They also included Oak Ridge, Tennessee, and Hanford, Washington.  
About 600,000 workers joined a fast, intense race to build the first atomic bomb.

Germany and Japan also tried to build atomic bombs.  
Germany faced technical and other problems.  
Some leading German scientists had fled Germany.  
Some of them helped the Manhattan Project.  
Hitler also chose to support V2 bombers for the air war with England instead of an atomic bomb.

In 1941, Japan asked physicist Yoshio Nishina to work on an atomic bomb.  
Japan called the project Ni-Go.  
Japan lacked information from Germany.  
U.S. air raids also damaged progress.  
The project did not advance much.

In July 1945, the Manhattan Project succeeded.  
The bomb was tested in the **Trinity Test**.  
The test took place at Alamogordo, New Mexico.

William L. Laurence was the project’s official historian.  
He described the first successful atomic test like this:  
“On that moment hung eternity. Time stood still. Space contracted to a pinpoint. It was as though the earth had opened and the skies split. One felt as though they had been privileged to witness the Birth of the World—to be present at the moment of Creation when the Lord Said: Let there be light.”

Vice President Harry S. Truman became president.

chapter_key: Life in the Trenches, the Mountains, and the Desert
text:
The trenches on the Western Front began after a stalemate. The Allies and the Central Powers were stuck in place in the fall of 1914. The trenches soon became a symbol of the war.

Life there was brutal. Artillery fire was constant. Mud was everywhere. Soldiers dug trenches to protect themselves from shelling. Then they became trapped in those same positions.

From the start, German troops dug deeper trenches. Their trenches were also more complex. It was as if they expected to stay a long time. Early Allied trenches were simpler. Over the years, the Allies improved them and made them more developed.

At its height, the trench system stretched nearly 500 miles.

The front line held the soldiers closest to the enemy. Soldiers usually stayed there for several days. Then they moved back to second-line support trenches. After that came third-line reserve trenches. Farther back sat the long-range artillery. Behind the trenches were field hospitals. There were also villages across the French and Belgian countryside.

Daily life in the trenches was often boring. There was little to do. But death could come at any moment, just above the parapet.

Rain fell often. Trenches filled with mud. Soldiers laid wooden planks to walk on. Even so, many still suffered from cold and wet conditions. Some developed hypothermia.

Constant wetness caused trench foot. Feet and legs could not dry. The skin split and peeled off. It was extremely painful. It was also hard to prevent.

Trenches filled with debris and trash. Soldiers lived close together. Disease spread easily in these cramped spaces.

Sometimes, the closeness of the two armies led to rare friendly contact.

One famous example happened at Christmas in 1914. German and British soldiers faced each other from their trenches. Some began calling out across no-man’s land. First one side sang Christmas carols. Then the other side joined in. After that, soldiers carefully climbed out of their trenches. They met in no-man’s land. They exchanged cigarettes, candy, and souvenirs. Many soldiers reported similar events.

This Christmas truce showed that humanity still existed in the war. But it angered commanders at headquarters. Leaders did not allow this kind of friendliness to happen again.

In other regions, armies moved more. These areas had different problems.

In the Italian Alps, Italian and Austro-Hungarian forces fought in the mountains. Soldiers fought at high altitude. Supplies were hard to deliver. Troops sometimes lived in caves. They also had to climb steep mountain heights. Snow fell often. Temperatures stayed below freezing. Frostbite was a serious danger. Avalanches were also a real threat. Poor conditions caused more than half of the casualties in this mountain fighting. The narrow Alpine passes also made retreat difficult.

Fighting in the Caucasus began in 1914. Russians fought the Ottomans there. The front was isolated. The Ottomans lacked rail lines to supply troops far from the front. Snow was many feet deep. Temperatures dropped below zero. Ottoman troops could not continue because they lacked supplies. They suffered tens of thousands of casualties.

In dry regions near the Mediterranean and in the Middle East, water was a major need. Armies had to secure enough water in the desert. It was also hard to find feed for horses. Because of this, especially in the Middle East, troops relied more on camels. Camels carried supplies and sometimes carried people too.

---

Over the years, the Allies improved them and made them more developed.

- Field hospitals

---

---

Rain fell often.  
Trenches filled with mud.

- Soldiers laid wooden planks to walk on.  
- Even so, many suffered from cold and wet conditions.

---

Constant wetness caused **trench foot**.

- Skin split and peeled off.

---

Trenches filled with debris and trash.  
Soldiers lived close together.

Soil erosion is not a widespread problem in West Africa under indigenous farming systems. However, it is a chronic problem in some places. In many areas it could become a serious hazard if farming practices change.

Soil erosion is closely linked to water control and desertification. For this reason, it is useful to discuss these issues together.

## Rainfall and water supply

In much of tropical Africa, yearly rainfall provides less water than most crops would use if they had enough moisture. Rainfall is also unreliable. It varies by season and from year to year. It is often very intense.

Because of this, conservation must focus on two needs:
- Using available moisture efficiently.
- Reducing damage from intense rainfall, such as flash floods.

This chapter includes a special section on drought in the Sahel region.

## Plant cover and mulching

Keeping plant cover, using mulch, or using both can reduce erosion. However, keeping plants that are not useful only for conservation can waste moisture. That moisture could otherwise go to the crop. This approach is only feasible where water supply is adequate for the crops being grown.

Mulching with dead plant material is also usually not practical. Materials like straw, stems, and leaves have other urgent uses. People often need them for other purposes instead of soil conservation.

Artificial mulches, such as bitumen-in-water, can work. But they are usually not economically or technically possible in the current socio-economic conditions. This is especially true in the areas where they are most needed.

## Contour ridging and tie-ridging

Contour ridging and tie-ridging can conserve water. They also reduce the speed of runoff. Using both methods together has proven effective.

These methods are simple and satisfactory ways to control water use and prevent soil erosion. Even so, soil differences must still be considered.

The importance of these measures is very high. They often require major rehabilitation schemes. These can include:
- Engineering works.
- Afforestation.
- Major changes to traditional farming practices.
- Changes to settlement patterns.
- Changes to land apportionment.

These changes require significant money and expertise. That money and expertise could otherwise be used to improve agriculture. Instead, it may be used to stop the effects of past poor practices.

## Rainfall variability and drought in West Africa

Rainfall variability and prolonged drought have been major environmental issues across Africa. In the west, the Sahel has long been known for extreme drought. However, many West African countries have also faced serious environmental challenges.

For the past thirty years, rainfall has been inconsistent and highly variable. This has harmed agriculture. Rainfall keeps soil moist and helps soil aeration. These conditions support large-scale agricultural production.

In rice production, rainfall variability has caused production fluctuations in countries such as Sierra Leone and Gambia.

The most damaging climatic condition for agriculture in West Africa has been drought. This drought has persisted since the 1960s. The 1970s and early 1980s saw the worst conditions.

The drought changed which food crops were grown. It also sharply reduced production of other crops. Examples include sorghum, millet, and rice.

## The Gambia: rainfall decline and rice production

In The Gambia, farmers reported that drought negatively changed rainfall patterns. In this country, and in other Sahelian states, rainfall is the main source of irrigation water for crops.

Agricultural production increased in the 1950s and 1960s because rains were favourable. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, rainfall declined.

In the southern part of The Gambia, farmers said June rains in the 1970s were lower than in the 1950s. They also said the rains later lasted only about a month.

Rice has been the crop most affected by these droughts. Rice is a major staple in Sierra Leone, The Gambia, and many Sahelian states.

In The Gambia, about 20–30% of land is converted to upland rice cultivation. Rice production has been dominated by women. It is a major source of income.

Since the drought began, rice production has fallen to about half of what it used to be. This has caused many people to rely on imported rice.

A key problem is reduced rainfall. Reduced rainfall also reduces runoff to the main rice plantation lands. Rivers have also dried because of the same issue.

## Other affected crops and environmental impacts

Other major staples affected by drought include:
- Millet
- Sorghum
- Groundnuts

Farming patterns for these crops depend heavily on natural rainfall. With drought, men have chosen lands that are richer and have more moisture. These lands can better sustain crop cultivation.

This has increased land degradation in places such as Burkina Faso, Mali, and The Gambia. Farming closer to water bodies has also increased water pollution.

Poor and erratic rainfall in many years since 1968 has reduced yields. It has also reduced seed germination potential. Millet and sorghum seeds have been especially affected.

## Ghana: desertification and farming systems

Ghana, like many tropical countries, is vulnerable to climate change and climate variability. About 35% of Ghana’s total land mass is desert.

Since the 1980s, desertification has increased in northern Ghana. Desertification is estimated to be advancing at about 20,000 hectares per year. This threatens water resources.

In northern Ghana, farmers commonly grow staple grains. These include maize, rice, millet, sorghum, soybean, cowpea, and groundnut. Farmers also rear small ruminants such as sheep and goats.

## 5. Rainfall variability and drought in West Africa

Rainfall variability and prolonged drought have been major environmental issues across Africa.

For the past **thirty years**, rainfall has been **inconsistent and highly variable**.  
This has harmed agriculture.

Rainfall helps:

- keep soil moist  
- support soil aeration  

These conditions support **large-scale agricultural production**.

In rice production, rainfall variability has caused production fluctuations in countries such as **Sierra Leone** and **Gambia**.

The most damaging climatic condition for agriculture in West Africa has been **drought**.  
This drought has persisted since the **1960s**, with the **1970s and early 1980s** being the worst.

- sorghum

## 6. The Gambia: rainfall decline and rice production

- June rains in the **1970s** were **lower** than in the **1950s**  
- the rains later lasted only about **a month**

## Who were the Jakhanke?

The Gambian historian Lamin Sanneh is a leading authority on the Jakhanke.  
He describes them as a “specialized caste” of Muslim clerics and educators.  

The word “caste” suggests they belonged to a larger ethnic group.  
That larger group is the Serahuli people.  
Serahuli are also called Soninke in other writings.  

Today, some people wrongly classify the Jakhanke as Mandinka.  
It is true that they speak a dialect of Mandinka.  
But their “Mandinkanization” happened mainly for a historical reason.  
Mandinka chiefs hosted them when the Jakhanke moved from present-day Mali to the Senegambia region.  

Sanneh’s phrase “clerics and educators” points to their main work.  
They were literate.  
This allowed them to teach Islam and do missionary work.  

Many Jakhanke still live in the Senegambia region today.  
They often place less emphasis on ethnic origins.  
They place more emphasis on their long role as propagators of Islam over the past 800 years.  

## Why the Jakhanke matter

The Jakhanke are important because they spread Islam peacefully in Senegambia.  
This matters even more today, because Islam is often linked to violence in many parts of the world.  

Many later methods of peaceful Islamization in Senegambia came from the Jakhanke.  
In simple terms, they set standards for missionary work.  

## Their standards and methods

Their main standard was peace.  
They did not use the sword to spread Islam.  

They used peaceful methods, including:  
- Building Koranic schools and mosques.  
- Improving and upgrading mosques.  
- Holding sessions on Koranic exegesis (interpretation).  
- Preserving holy sites where yearly Islamic gatherings take place.  
- Working as itinerant traders who shared Islam with clients and customers.  

They also used clear tactics.  

One tactic was to grow their numbers.  
They trained many talibes (disciples).  
After years of study, disciples were allowed to leave.  
They then gathered and trained new disciples themselves.  
This “massification” helped strengthen Islam.  

Another tactic was withdrawal into enclaves.  
They often chose places far from large crowds.  
They valued quiet, like a monastery.  

They were skilled at creating theocratic communities.  
Some were deep in the Senegambian savannah.  
These communities were self-sustaining.  
They focused on Islamic scholarship and religious practice.  

Examples of these religious villages still exist.  
They include Sutukuho and Sutukung in The Gambia.  
They also include Niokhlo and Suna Karantba in Casamance.  

## Alhajj Salim Suwareh

Alhajj Salim Suwareh founded the Jakhanke movement.  
He was central to its success.  

Much of his early life is unclear.  
But some details are known.  

He died around 1500.  
He reportedly made seven pilgrimages to Mecca.  
He had relatives in Mecca.  
He also lived there before moving to Africa to spread Islam.  

He settled in the Jaka region of Masina, in present-day Mali.  
This is where the name “Jakankhe” comes from.  
In Mandinka, it means “those who hail from Jaka.”  

After his seventh hajj, he returned to Africa and stayed.  
He led his people from Jaka Masina to Jaka Bambuku.  

In Bambuku, the animist ruler became hostile.  
Suwareh responded in a way compared to the Prophet of Islam.  
When Meccans threw stones at the Prophet, the Prophet fled into exile.  
Suwareh also fled.  

He led his talibes toward present-day Senegambia.  
Professor Sanneh writes that since this hijra-like flight, the Jakhanke have remained united.  
They share strong solidarity.  
This solidarity is based on loyalty to Suwareh.  

## Their rejection of violent conversion

The Jakhanke were deeply committed to peaceful Islamization.  
This commitment was tested in the 19th century.  

A Serahuli religious militant, Momodou Lamin Drammeh (1835–1887), chose war.  
He wanted to convert Bundu (eastern Senegal) to Islam by force.  

The Jakhanke rejected him.  
They disowned him.  
They fled farther, into what is now eastern Gambia.  

Drammeh’s aggressive style clashed with their orderly approach.  
Without using the sword, the Jakhanke still helped speed up the spread and reform of Islam.  
This contrasted with jihadist figures like Drammeh, Umar Taal, and Maba Jahou Bah.  

A paradox remains.  
Suwareh lived in Mecca and had relatives there.  
Yet the Jakhanke rejected uncompromising Wahhabi doctrine.  
Instead, they followed a “path of accommodation.”  

## Conclusion: the significance of the movement

The Jakhanke movement shows a peaceful, community-led spread of Islam.  
It deeply shaped the societies that received Islam.  
It presented Islam as a way of peace.  

Those who claim to spread Islam through violence today could learn from the Jakhanke.  
This movement began more than 500 years ago.

European sailors first reached sub-Saharan Africa in 1442.  
That year, Portuguese ships reached the Senegal River.

The Portuguese had sailed along the coasts of Morocco and Western Sahara since 1413.  
In 1413, they captured the Moroccan city of Ceuta.  
Ceuta is still a Spanish city today.

Between 1413 and the 1440s, the Portuguese built several fortified settlements on the Moroccan coast.  
Important sites included Arzila, Mogador (now Essaouira), Safi, and Tangier.

Portugal kept a strong presence in Morocco until 1578.  
In 1578, the Portuguese King Sebastião I was killed at the Battle of Alcácer-Quibir.  
Much of the Portuguese nobility was also killed in that battle.

By 1471, West African leaders had formed commercial and diplomatic links with Portuguese traders.  
These links were along the coast between Senegal and Ghana.  
Major early sites of trade and settlement included the Gambia River.  
They also included Bugendo on the São Domingos River in Guinea-Bissau.  
They also included Sierra Leone.

For the next 150 years, West African rulers and traders met the Portuguese more than any other European nation.  
There were also smaller trading missions led by the English and the French.  
These missions were less frequent.

At first, the Portuguese had four main motivations.

1) They wanted access to the extensive gold production of Bono-Mansu and the Akan states.  
2) They competed with the Ottoman Empire to access this gold.  
The Ottomans captured Constantinople in 1453.  
This caused a crisis in Christian Europe.  
3) They wanted to find a trade route to markets in India.  
They aimed to sail around the Cape of Good Hope.  
4) Over time, they increasingly focused on the trade in enslaved persons.

By the 1590s, the Dutch began to rival the Portuguese in Africa.  
Dutch ships were bigger and better.  
The goods they traded with African political leaders were also higher quality.

By 1650, the Dutch had captured many major Portuguese trading stations in West Africa.  
They captured Gorée in Senegal in 1621.  
They captured Elmina in Ghana in 1637.  
They captured Luanda in Angola in 1641.

At first, the Dutch were mainly interested in textiles.  
They were also interested in animal hides for the leather industry.  
They were also interested in ivory.

By the middle of the 17th century, the Dutch also turned to slave trading.

text:
After reaching the Senegal River in 1442, Portuguese voyages continued.

By 1448, some Portuguese sailors had gone up the Gambia River. They reached the major trading town of Kantora. Kantora was not far east of what is today Basse Santa Su, in the far east of the country. At that time, Kantora was a major centre for trans-Saharan trade.

By the mid-1450s, the Portuguese were trading with the Wolof state of Kajoor on the coast. The Bijagós Islands, off the coast of Guinea-Bissau, were also being discussed with European traders.

The first shared language was probably Arabic. Many Arabic speakers lived in Portugal in the 15th century. Granada was still an Islamic kingdom in Spain. Arabic was also widely spoken in many parts of West Africa.

In 1456, one sailor wrote that the Bijagós was the last place where African peoples shared a language with Portuguese sailors. This suggests it was also the southernmost reach of Arab and trans-Saharan trade at that time.

The Cape Verde Islands were probably first reached in 1456. Cape Verdean historians still debate whether the islands already had a population. Archaeological evidence is not conclusive. The islands may have been used as a salt depot for Saharan states.

Around 1471, the Portuguese reached the coastline of Ghana.

The Ghana coast was different. It was close to the gold mines of the Akan forests. Akan traders soon sold gold informally to the Portuguese.

The Portuguese state wanted a share of this trade. In 1481, Portugal sent a large fleet. They negotiated with Kwamena Ansa, the ruler at Edina (now called Elmina). The Portuguese wanted to build a fortress.

The talks ended after a very tense stand-off. The stand-off began when the Portuguese tried to build the fort at the site of a holy shrine. After the negotiations, the fortress at Elmina was built. It still remains on what became known as the Gold Coast.

In the 17th century, Elmina later changed hands and became a Dutch fortress. Over time, the Dutch and the English became the main European nations trading in Ghana.

Commerce on the Gold Coast was intense. Many Akan rulers wanted to expand their trading links.

The Portuguese built other forts along the Gold Coast. These included Axim and Komenda. Many were completed by 1500.

Later, many more forts were built. There was almost one every few miles along the Gold Coast. Some focused on the gold trade. Others focused on different exports. For example, Anishan exported corn, which European ships wanted in large amounts.

The slave trade did not dominate the Gold Coast until the 18th century.

At the same time, rulers in West and West-Central Africa were also making contact with the Portuguese.

Oba Ozolua of Benin received Portuguese visitors in 1485. Around 1490, the Atlantic trading post of Gwatón was founded.

At first, Benin sold malaguetta peppers to the Portuguese. In 1499, the sea route to India was established. After that, Benin’s peppers were less in demand in Europe.

The Portuguese tried to start a trade in enslaved people from Benin. They wanted to send them to the gold suppliers in Elmina. The Oba refused.

During the 16th century, relations between Benin and the Portuguese declined. In the early 17th century, the Obas renewed links with European traders. This was linked to Dutch demand for cloth made in Benin.

Throughout the 17th century, cloth was Benin’s main export. The “ambassy” cloths were traded regularly to Elmina. They were also traded as far away as Brazil.

Demand for this cloth fell in the late 17th century. This happened as imports of luxury cloth from India increased. By the 18th century, Benin’s Obas turned to the trade in enslaved people. They did this to preserve and renew the power of Edo and the Benin state.

The Portuguese kept sailing south after Benin. They reached the mouth of the Kongo River. They established relations with the manikongo at Mbanza Kongo, the capital of Kongo. The ruler was Nzika Nkuwu.

The island of São Tomé was settled by 1485. Many BaKongo people were taken there as enslaved workers. They worked on sugar plantations.

In 1491, Nzika Nkuwu converted to Christianity. He took the name Joao I.

This also created links between Kongo and Elmina through São Tomé. São Tomé traded with both places.

By the 1510s, traders from Benin were reported at the Kongolese port of Mpinda. This was mentioned in a letter. The letter was written in Portuguese by the new manikongo, Afonso I (1509–46).

By the 1510s, many West African peoples and rulers had links with the Portuguese. Some places, like Benin and Elmina, also had links further south to Kongo.

African rulers wanted to expand trade. They also sometimes wanted military support against rivals. This happened in Benin, which fought a major battle with Portuguese support against Nupe in 1516. It also happened during civil wars in Jolof and in Kongo.

After reaching the **Senegal River** in **1442**, Portuguese voyages continued.

## Up the Gambia River (1448)

By **1448**, some Portuguese sailors had gone up the **Gambia River**.

They reached the major trading town of **Kantora**.

Kantora was not far east of what is today **Basse Santa Su**, in the far east of the country.

By the **mid-1450s**, the Portuguese were trading with the Wolof state of **Kajoor** on the coast.

The **Bijagós Islands**, off the coast of Guinea-Bissau, were also being discussed with European traders.

## Shared language and Arabic connections

The first shared language was probably **arabic**.

Many arabic speakers lived in Portugal in the **15th century**.

Granada was still an islamic kingdom in Spain.

Arabic was also widely spoken in many parts of **west africa**.

## The southern reach of shared language (1456)

In **1456**, one sailor wrote that the Bijagós was the last place where african peoples shared a language with Portuguese sailors.

This suggests it was also the **southernmost reach** of arab and trans-saharan trade at that time.

## Cape Verde Islands (around 1456)

The **Cape Verde Islands** were probably first reached in **1456**.

Cape Verdean historians still debate whether the islands already had a population.

Archaeological evidence is **not conclusive**.

The islands may have been used as a **salt depot** for saharan states.

Around **1471**, the Portuguese reached the coastline of **Ghana**.

## Gold trade and early contact with Akan traders

The Ghana coast was different.

The Portuguese state wanted a share of this trade.

The Portuguese wanted to build a **fortress**.

---

## A tense stand-off and the building of Elmina

The talks ended after a very **tense stand-off**.

The stand-off began when the Portuguese tried to build the fort at the site of a **holy shrine**.

After the negotiations, the fortress at **Elmina** was built.

It still remains on what became known as the **Gold Coast**.

---

## Later European control (17th century)

In the **17th century**, Elmina later changed hands and became a **Dutch** fortress.
