The missionaries also greatly improved health services.

Before Christian missionaries arrived, and even well into the pre-independence period, most sick people relied on mixtures made from herbs, roots, and tree bark. Modern scientific research has confirmed that many of these mixtures had medicinal value. However, traditional medical practice had several weaknesses.

Preventive medicine was hardly known. Because of this, epidemics of different kinds were common.

Traditional doctors often could not diagnose illness accurately. They often explained natural illnesses as supernatural. They sometimes turned first to mystic cults to appease an “unknown” spirit. Only after this did they apply medicine to the sick person.

They also prescribed many taboos. In the light of modern medical science, these taboos had no real connection to the illness being treated.

Early missionaries set up medical centres. At first, these were at mission posts. Later, they spread to many other places. They treated the sick. In time, they also built leprosariums and orphanages to support their medical work.

In Nigeria, one of the first missionary groups to introduce organised medical services was the Roman Catholic Church. Father Jean Marie Coquard worked in and from Abeokuta for forty years. In the second half of the nineteenth century, the Egba knew him as both a priest and a surgeon.

In 1892, the Church Missionary Society opened the Iyi Enu Hospital in Onitsha. Today, it is a leading hospital in Anambra State. In 1902, the Methodists opened a clinic at Igbo-Ora.

The Scottish missionary Mary Slessor became well known in the Cross River area as a nurse. Through hard work and persuasion, she helped stop the practice of killing twins.

Another important missionary doctor was J. R. Stephen. For many years, he led a missionary hospital at Ilesha.

As in other West African countries, many more mission-sponsored hospitals were founded during the twentieth century.

In Ghana, Christian missionaries were also very active in starting medical services. Roman Catholic Sisters provided medical care in the Upper and Northern Regions. They did this before the government began providing hospitals and clinics in regional and district headquarters.

In the Western Region, Catholic Sisters ran a hospital at Eikwe. It specialised in maternity cases. Like Slessor in Nigeria, they also helped end the practice of killing twins at birth.

Other Roman Catholic hospitals were built across all nine regions of the country. These included hospitals at Asikuma and Foso (Central Region), Akyem Swedru (Eastern Region), Berekum (Brong-Ahafo), Maase (Asante Region), and Anfoega (Volta Region).

The Presbyterians also opened hospitals in several parts of Ghana. This included the hospital at Agogo in Asante-Akyem.

Other long-standing and well-known missionary hospitals included those run by the Methodists at Wenkyi in the Brong-Ahafo Region. Another was run by the Seventh Day Adventists at Kwahu Atibie in the Eastern Region.

World War II (WWII) sped up the growth of nationalism.  
It also weakened the foundations of imperialism.

The war had a huge economic impact on West Africa.  
Its effects were wide and long-lasting.

## 1) West Africa became more important to the world economy
Europe depended more on tropical Africa for key products.  
These included rubber, cotton, cocoa, palm produce, and groundnuts.

Because of this, West African colonies increased production of cash crops.

In Nigeria, export values rose sharply.  
They went from **10,300,00 pounds in 1931** to **24,600,00 pounds in 1946**.  
Imports also rose.  
They went from **6,800,00 pounds** to **19,800,00 pounds** in the same period.

## 2) Workers developed strong grievances
Colonial governments introduced price controls.  
They also controlled the marketing of export crops.  
They set wage ceilings.  
They pressured workers and farmers to produce more.

At the same time, African businessmen were excluded from import and export trade.  
This trade was reserved for European firms.

## 3) Trade unions grew quickly
The cost of living rose.  
Wages did not rise in the same way.

This pushed workers to organize.  
It increased labor activism.

In Nigeria, trade unions grew from **5 to 70**.  
The **Nigerian Trade Union Congress (1943)** became the central coordinating body.

Trade unions worked closely with nationalist leaders.  
Together, they pressed for the end of colonialism.

## 4) Cities grew fast and became overcrowded
The war created new jobs.  
Many people moved into cities to find work.

Many West African cities more than doubled in population.

- **Lagos** grew from **100,000 in 1939** to **230,00 in 1950**.  
- **Accra** grew from **70,000 in 1941** to **166,00 in 1948**.

Towns became overcrowded.  
Many job-seekers and workers were unhappy.

They saw white people living in comfortable European reservations.  
These areas had paved streets, lawns, and gardens.  
Meanwhile, many Africans lived in slums.

Because of this, many people became open to nationalist messages.  
They became early and willing recruits for militant nationalist movements.

## 5) Education expanded
The war brought an economic boom.  
This increased prosperity for some families.

More parents could afford to send children to school.  
Literacy spread.  
Newspaper readership increased.

Newspapers became a powerful tool for nationalists.  
They used them to push for political, economic, and social development.

## 6) Unemployment still increased among school-leavers
Even with more job opportunities, many school-leavers could not find work.  
Thousands remained unemployed.

For the first time, cities developed a new class of unemployed people.  
They became angry and frustrated.

They blamed the colonial government and European firms.  
Nationalist agitators could easily win them over.

## 7) Returning ex-servicemen had the biggest impact
The most decisive factor was the return of ex-servicemen.

Over **176,000** men from British West Africa served in the British colonial army.  
After the war, many survivors returned.

About **100,000** returned to Nigeria.  
About **65,000** returned to Ghana.  
They came back from the Middle East, East Africa, Burma, and India.

These ex-servicemen had seen life in more developed countries.  
They had experienced higher living standards in the army.

They had also seen strong nationalist movements in Asia.  
They fought alongside Europeans.  
They saw European weaknesses.

This challenged the myth of European racial superiority.

They returned home wanting a better life for themselves and their people.  
They demanded that Africa receive the freedom they had fought for.  
Many joined militant nationalist groups.

chapter_key: METHODS USED IN GATHERING/COLLECTING INFORMATION FOR THE WRITING OF AFRICAN HISTORY
text:
To collect data for the reconstruction of African history, a historian must not rely only on written sources. The historian must also use non-documentary sources. The historian must use several methods. This helps to check bias, prejudice, and exaggeration.

## Methods of collecting data

### 1) Personal enquiry and interview
A historian can interview people who know about the past.  
These may include:
- Eye-witnesses  
- Traditional historians (for example, court linguists)  
- Older court officials  
- Elderly people  

The historian can record the interviews.  
Later, the historian can replay them, write them out, and analyze the information.

### 2) Inter-disciplinary approach
A historian can work with experts in other fields.  
This cooperation can provide useful information for African history.

The historian may work with:
- Linguists  
- Archaeologists  
- Botanists  
- Ethnographers  
- Other specialists  

The researcher and these scholars gather information together.  
They use it to draw valid conclusions.

### 3) Reviewing written sources
A historian can also collect information by reviewing written sources.  
These include:
- Books  
- Newspapers  
- Journals  
- Broadcasts  
- Diaries  
- Manifestoes  
- Private letters  

The historian reviews both primary and secondary sources.  
The historian examines them and cross-checks them.  

Written records can have shortcomings.  
Even so, reviewing them helps the historian reflect the past more accurately.  
This supports a more unbiased history that is backed by evidence.

### 4) Questionnaire
A historian can use a carefully prepared questionnaire.  
It should cover:
- Political life  
- Economic life  
- Social life  
- Religion  
- Technology  

The historian gives a set of well-structured questions to people who know about the past.  
The historian collects the responses.  
Then the historian analyzes them to reach a reasonable conclusion.

### 5) Personal observation and records
A historian can visit places of historical importance.  
Examples include:
- Slave sites  
- Castles  
- Forts  

A historian can also observe and record events, such as:
- Festivals  
- Funerals  

This can produce important findings.  
These details are first-hand information.  
They are eye-witness accounts of events seen directly.

The historian can compare different accounts.  
The historian can ask questions about them.  
This helps the historian form a more reliable view of what happened in the past.

---

## Reliability of sources for African history

Both written and unwritten sources have weaknesses.  
Even so, they can be described as adequately reliable.  
This is because historians use historical methods.  
They use scientific methods when drawing conclusions.

### Reliability of written sources
Written records are often precise.  
They can be very reliable.

Documentary sources include:
- Newspapers  
- Personal letters  
- Diaries  
- Journals  
- Manifestoes  

These sources can be reviewed and cross-checked.  
This helps reduce prejudice and bias.  
It supports truthfulness.

When written records are compared with other evidence, the historian can reach a more objective conclusion.

### Reliability of unwritten sources
Unwritten sources can also be reliable.  
They often involve scientific methods in research.

For example, the Ghanaian linguist Professor Abena Dolphyne researched the Bono, Asante, and Fante people.  
She reached an important conclusion.  
She found that the Asante language is less related to Fante.

Archaeology is also a major source for African history.  
It uses scientific methods such as:
- Reconnaissance  
- Stratification  
- Radiocarbon dating  
- Potassium-argon dating  
- Data analysis  

These methods help archaeologists reach accurate and reliable conclusions for historical writing.  
Reconnaissance is the process of discovering sites and plotting them for digging.

---

## Weaknesses of some non-documentary sources

### Problems with archaeology
Archaeology has flaws as a non-documentary source.

There is no fully conscious system for preserving archaeological knowledge.  
Some preservation may be accidental.  
This means archaeologists may depend on chance.

Archaeological remains can suffer:
- Wear and tear  
- Weathering  
- Disfigurement  

This can make it hard for historians to get very reliable information.

Radiocarbon dating is also very expensive.  
This can hinder effective research.

### Problems with oral tradition
Oral tradition can include exaggeration.  
Narrators may shape information to suit their interests.

Sometimes oral accounts:
- Leave out parts that do not support the narrator’s interest  
- Lack specific details because of real memory loss  

Oral tradition may also focus too much on personalities and major events, such as wars.  
It may play down social and economic aspects of the past.  
This can make information scanty.  
This harms scholarship and posterity.

---

## Conclusion
Both documentary and non-documentary evidence must be used together to write African history.  
Each type of source supports the other.

Both types are created or passed on by human beings.  
Because people can be subjective, biased, and impressionistic, no single type of source is always more reliable than the other.

chapter_key: Origins and Timeframe of Early Trade
text:
West Africa has had links with the Mediterranean world for a very long time.  
These links began long before Islam rose in the late 6th century CE.

Several centuries before the Roman Empire, the Greek historian Herodotus (c. 484–425 BCE) wrote about peoples in Africa.  
He wrote many times about the peoples of the Nile Valley.  
He stressed that many of them were Black Africans.  
He also suggested links with people farther west.

Rock art from this period, and later, suggests contact with the Mediterranean world.  
Some images suggest wheeled chariots south of what is now the Sahara.

## The Sahara was once greener

In ancient times, the Sahara was not as harsh as it later became, and as it is today.  
Rock art in the Sahara is abundant.  
Some of it is up to 12,000 years old.

One important site is Tassili n’Ajjer.  
It is north of Tamanrasset in the Algerian Sahara.  
It is one of the oldest examples of rock art in the Sahara.

Another important site is the Tibesti Massif in Chad.  
It also has rock art from around this time.

These paintings show places that are desert today as fertile land.  
They show many animals that cannot live in the Sahara now.  
These include buffalo, elephants, rhinoceros, and hippopotamus.

This fertile period in the Sahara happened during the European Ice Age.  
The Ice Age was not a problem in Africa.  
In fact, this seems to have been a time of plenty.

## Desertification and continued contact

The Sahara seems to have started desertifying faster around 3000 BCE.  
Even so, strong links with the Mediterranean continued for a long time.

One example is the Carthaginian general Hannibal.  
Carthage was an empire based in Libya.  
It was the most powerful empire in the Mediterranean until Rome rose.

Around 220 BCE, Hannibal attacked Roman forces in Europe.  
His campaign included crossing the Alps.  
His supplies were carried by elephants.  
These were African elephants, linked to peoples and places south of the Sahara.

Over time, desertification increased.  
The Sahara became harder to cross.  
By the rise of Islam in the early 7th century CE, there were fewer connections.

## Islam and the rise of caravan trade

Islam rose in the early 7th century CE.  
This began around c. 610 CE, with the early Caliphs.

Later, powerful Islamic kingdoms grew in Morocco.  
Centres of learning also grew in Cairo, Tripoli, and the Middle East.  
These changes supported the growth of caravan trade across the Sahara.

By the 9th century CE, the empire of Ghāna (also called Awkar) had formed.  
It was in what is now Mauritania.

text:
The trans-Saharan trade grew from the 10th to the 15th century.  
This growth changed West Africa in deep ways.  
Many major changes happened in the 15th century.  
They happened across the whole region, from west to east and from north to south.

These changes were political, economic, and social.  
They helped drive globalization.  
They also shaped Europe’s later role.  
Europe did not cause these West African changes.  
West Africa’s changes came first.

A clear example comes from what is now Nigeria.  
In Borno, the gold trade from Bono-Mansu grew.  
This helped push the capital away from the old centre of Kanem.  
The capital moved south to Gazargamo (Ngazargamu) in Borno, around 1470.  

In Kano, a new system was established.  
It was called the Sarauta system.  

In Yorubaland, large earthworks were built around Ijebu.  
They are called “Eredos.”  
They are about 10 metres deep.  
The archaeologist Gérard Chouin has dated them to 1370–1420.

Similar changes happened in other regions.  
In Mali, the Dogon people of the Bandiagara escarpment probably moved there in the 15th century.  

Also in the 15th century, the Mossi kingdom rose in what is now Burkina Faso.  
This rise was linked to profits from taxing the onward gold trade.  
Al-Sa’dī describes Mossi attacking the town of Mâssina in this period.  

At this time, Bono-Mansu rose to prominence.  
The gold-trading centre of Bighu was also important.  
Bighu was on the Gold Coast.  
It later became very important in the 17th and 18th century.  
Al-Ouazzan mentions it in the 1520s, calling it “Bito.”  
This suggests it rose to prominence in these decades.

In Senegambia, major changes also took place.  
A military leader named Koli Tenguela rose at the end of the 15th century.  
This likely connected to efforts to control the gold trade.  
That gold came from the kingdom of Wuuli.  
Wuuli was on the north bank of the Gambia River.  

Tenguela was a Fula.  
He later led an army south across the Gambia River.  
He went to the Fuuta Jaalo mountains in Guinea-Conakry.  
He established a new polity there.  
This then helped lead to the establishment of Fuuta Tooro on the Senegal River.

Across West Africa, political change was already happening.  
This was true from Borno to Fuuta Tooro.  
It happened before trade with Europe had begun.  

West African mining technology grew.  
Economic change grew.  
Political reorganization grew.  
These developments helped create the framework for later European exploration.  
In the 15th century, European powers began sailing along the West African coast.  
They sought to expand their knowledge of the world.

A striking example comes from northern Nigeria.  
Kano grew very rapidly in the 15th century.  
It sent military expeditions to the south.  
It became a regional hub.  
It linked trade networks from southern Nigeria to what is now Mali and beyond.  
The Kano Chronicle gives details of these changes.

During the reign of Kano’s Sarkin Dauda (c. 1421–38), the Chronicle describes links with Nupe.  
Between Kano and Nupe, the major power was Zaria.  
Zaria conquered a large area.  
The Kano Chronicle says:

“At this time, Zaria, under Queen Amina, conquered all the towns as far as Kwararafa and Nupe. Every town paid tribute to her. The Sarkin Nupe sent forty eunuchs and ten thousand kolas to her…in time the whole of the products of the west were brought to Hausaland [of which Kano was the capital].”

So, as European power began to expand along the West African coast in the 15th century, the trans-Saharan trade was reaching its peak.  
The 15th century was not only a time of European expansion.  
It was also a time of wider global expansion in networks, trade, and production.  
In West Africa and beyond, this power showed itself in more complex states.

## Ghana Empire

Ghana was one of the earliest and most famous empires in West Africa.  
It existed from the 5th century to the 13th century.  
It was located in areas that are now Mali and Mauritania.  
Ghana was closely linked to the Trans-Saharan trade.

The Ghana Empire had its capital at Kumbi Saleh, in Mauritania.  
This empire is not the same as modern Ghana.  
Modern Ghana has its capital at Accra.  
Modern Ghana was named after the older Ghana Empire.

The main people of the Ghana Empire were the Serahuli.  
They were also called the Soninke.  
They were part of the Mande-speaking peoples.

Ghana became strong because of its role in trade.  
It was in a strategic position on the Trans-Saharan trade routes.  
British historian Kevin Shillington said Ghana grew powerful because of trade.  
He said trade made Ghana’s rulers rich.  
He also said trade was likely important from the very beginning.

Ghana was located halfway between two key trade goods.  
Salt came from the desert in the north.  
Gold came from Bambuk in the east.  
Ghana acted as a middleman between these regions.

The camel was later introduced as a carrier of goods.  
This greatly increased trade across the Sahara.  
It also boosted trade between Ghana and desert peoples, such as the Berbers.

We know about Ghana’s wealth because Arabic traders wrote about it.  
In the 11th century, an Arab geographer named al-Bakari visited Kumbi Saleh.  
He described great wealth there.  
He also described a well-developed system of government under the Ghana ruler.

Al-Bakari said Kumbi Saleh had two separate wards.  
One ward was for foreigners.  
Arab traders lived there.  
The other ward was the main town.  
The king and his people lived there.

Al-Bakari also described the king’s appearance.  
He said the king was richly dressed in gold.  
He said the king could raise an army of 200,000 men.  
He also said the king allowed both Islam and animism in Kumbi Saleh.

Arabic writers mostly met royals, nobles, and traders.  
They were mainly interested in gold.  
They wrote little about ordinary people.  
However, their writings suggest that ordinary people fished and farmed.  
They lived along the banks of the River Senegal.

Ghana’s success depended on trade.  
Its collapse also related to trade.

The Almoravids began to wage war against other Berber tribes.  
This made the trade routes to Ghana unsafe.  
Trade was disrupted.

Dry weather also caused problems.  
It reduced Ghana’s ability to feed its people and its large army.  
This weakened the state.

By the 12th century, some vassal states began to rebel.  
Mali was one of them.  
They wanted freedom from Ghana’s control.

---

## Songhay Empire

Songhay lasted from the 11th century to the 16th century.  
It rose to prominence because of the Trans-Saharan trade.

By the 14th century, Muslim traders had settled in Gao.  
Gao was Songhay’s main trade town.  
Gao became a hub for Trans-Saharan trade.  
It served the central and eastern Sahara.

Songhay’s farmers and fishermen supported the trade towns.  
They helped ensure that traders had enough food.

Songhay earned most of its revenue from taxes.  
These taxes were placed on trade caravans.

One great emperor was Muhammad Ture.  
He was also called Askia Muhammad.  
He introduced Islam into Songhay.  
He also expanded the empire.

Like Mansa Musa of Mali, Askia Muhammad made a pilgrimage to Mecca.  
On this journey, he showed how rich and powerful his kingdom was.

The Trans-Saharan trade helped make Songhay rich and prosperous.

text:
For dan Fodio, the main reason for the jihad was to purify Islam.  
This took place in territories that were already Muslim in the early nineteenth century.  
He believed Muslim leaders had practiced an impure form of Islam until then.  
Because of this belief, he saw his struggle as legitimate.

Some historians describe the Sokoto jihad as a revolution.  
They point to socio-economic inequalities in the Hausa kingdoms at the start of the nineteenth century.  
Dan Fodio gained support because he favored equality.  
He also said he was fighting corruption.  
In 1804, he began his fight against the king and aristocracy of Gobir.  

The social side of the jihad matters, but it should not be overstated.  
Dan Fodio himself said the main causes were religious.  
He stated this in *Kitab al-Farq*.  

Letters from the 1800s also help explain his aims.  
After trying to invade Borno, a kingdom that had existed since the ninth century, he wrote to its leader.  
He tried to convince Mohammed el-Kanemi of the religious and legal merits of his struggle.  
For dan Fodio, the jihad was mainly, but not only, a way for “pure” Muslims to reform “lax” Muslims.

In the 1970s, some historians emphasized an ethnic dimension.  
They argued that dan Fodio, a descendant of Fulanis settled in Hausa regions since the fifteenth century, set Islam against the Hausas.  
Most leaders of the Sokoto jihad were Fulani.  
Even so, it is hard to claim the jihad was based only on ethnicity.  
The Fulani were fewer in number than the Hausas.  
It is unlikely they thought they could overthrow Hausa kings on ethnic grounds alone.  
Dan Fodio also wrote against ethnic discrimination in *Bayan Wayan Wujub al-Hijra*.

Scholars also argue that the jihad was not entirely new in West Africa.  
Debates about Islam’s role in society existed before dan Fodio’s jihad.  
These debates included food bans, marriage laws, and women’s clothing.  
Women’s clothing especially drew the attention of Shaikh Jibril b. ’Umar.  
He was one of dan Fodio’s teachers.  

Other jihads had already happened in West Africa.  
Examples include Bundu in the late seventeenth century.  
They also include Futa Jallon in 1725 and Futa Toro in 1776.  
So, some Muslim scholars had already become reformers and conquerors before Usman dan Fodio.

Because of this, the religious questions raised by dan Fodio were not completely original.  
What made him stand out was his lasting political victory.  
He defeated opponents across a vast territory.  
This political success helped secure his long-term impact.

chapter_key: The structure and economy of the caliphate
text:
The first six years of the jihad (1804–1810) were crucial.  
They created the political and religious base for a new state.

This state was not an empire.  
It was a group of territories under the authority of the caliph in Sokoto.

The Sokoto Caliphate was highly decentralised.  
The caliph ruled, but local areas had wide freedom.

The caliphate was new in the Hausa regions.  
It gave moral and political authority to dan Fodio and his successors.

The caliph’s companions were Fulani scholars who became jihadists.  
They were appointed as emirs.  
Each emir led a territorial subdivision.  
Each emir answered directly to the caliph.

Because the caliphate was so large, it was split in practice.  
Western emirates were under Sokoto’s authority.  
Eastern emirates stayed more or less autonomous.

Dan Fodio’s successors had to fight to enforce their authority.  
Because of this, jihad continued with few breaks until the mid-nineteenth century.

Mohammed Bello was dan Fodio’s son and direct successor.  
He took the title of sultan.  
He led many military campaigns.  
He compared these campaigns to the seventh-century Muslim conquest of the Arabian Peninsula.

Bello’s policy had several parts.  
He appointed family members to lead frontier towns.  
He settled Fulani nomadic groups in villages.  
He built fortified villages to watch some borders.

Security was needed at the caliphate’s borders.  
Security was also needed in buffer zones between emirates.

Sokoto recruited soldiers during the dry season.  
These troops could crush rebellions.  
They could also stop Tuareg incursions from the north.

The caliph’s authority depended on what he could do.  
He had to control borders.  
He had to redistribute spoils from campaigns.  
He also redistributed taxes to allies and family members.

Hausa rulers had used their own taxes.  
The caliphate replaced these with Islamic taxes, such as zakat.  
In theory, revenue was then governed by Islamic law.

In practice, taxes depended on each emirate.  
For example, Kano or Zaria had a property tax.  
This existed outside the emirate of Sokoto.

Sokoto’s efforts to centralise power were limited.  
They were limited by pre-jihadic structures in Hausa cities.  
They were also limited by the difficulty of reaching many rural people.

The Sokoto Caliphate followed the original aims of the jihad.  
It tried to establish Islamic law in courts across the caliphate.

This created a need for educated men.  
Schools grew in urban centres.  
At first, there were not enough qualified personnel.

A key feature of the caliphate was its literate staff.  
These men worked in the administration of each emirate.  
Some were born free.  
Some were born into slavery.  
Together, they formed a working bureaucracy.

A lack of labour led to many expeditions.  
These expeditions aimed to capture slaves.  
Slaves were sold or used for work in plantations and other production sites.

Slave labour supported the salt mines in the north of the caliphate.  
Slave labour also supported industries in the central regions.  
These included iron, cotton, indigo, and leather.

The state’s wealth depended on a servile economy.  
This economy was fuelled by wars and raids.

In Kano in the 1820s, North African merchants supplied many slaves.  
In the city, for every freeman there were thirty slaves.

Islam entered the Hausa regions in the fourteenth century.  
It came through travellers and traders.  
These people came from neighbouring Borno and from regions north of the Sahara.

Islam spread further through the jihad.  
Pre-Islamic religions, often called “traditional” religions, continued.  
But Islamic culture spread across the region.

Books helped this spread.  
Some were written by dan Fodio’s family.  
Others were sold through the Sahara.

The Hausa regions became more connected to the Muslim world.  
This happened through pilgrimage to Mecca.  
It also happened through trade.  
It also happened through the spread of brotherhoods.

Some integration may have existed before.  
The jihad greatly accelerated the process.

## The first six years (1804–1810)

The first six years of the jihad (1804–1810) were **crucial**.  
They created the political and religious base for a new state.

---

## What kind of state was created?

This state was **not an empire**.  
It was a group of territories under the authority of the caliph in Sokoto.

The Sokoto caliphate was **highly decentralised**.  
The caliph ruled, but local areas had wide freedom.

The caliphate was new in the Hausa regions.  
It gave moral and political authority to **dan Fodio** and his successors.

---

## Leadership and emirates

The caliph’s companions were Fulani scholars who became jihadists.  
They were appointed as **emirs**.

Each emir led a territorial subdivision.

- Western emirates were under Sokoto’s authority.  
- Eastern emirates stayed more or less autonomous.

---

## Continued conflict and enforcement of authority

Dan Fodio’s successors had to fight to enforce their authority.  
Because of this, jihad continued with few breaks until the mid-nineteenth century.

---

## Mohammed Bello and military expansion

Mohammed Bello was dan Fodio’s son and direct successor.  
He took the title of **sultan**.

He led many military campaigns.  
He compared these campaigns to the seventh-century Muslim conquest of the Arabian peninsula.

---

Bello’s policy had several parts:

- He appointed family members to lead **frontier towns**.  
- He settled Fulani nomadic groups in **villages**.  
- He built **fortified villages** to watch some borders.

Security was needed at the caliphate’s borders.  
Security was also needed in buffer zones between emirates.

---

## Recruitment and border defence

Sokoto recruited soldiers during the dry season.

These troops could:

- Crush rebellions.  
- Stop Tuareg incursions from the north.

---

## What the caliph’s authority depended on

The caliph’s authority depended on what he could do.

He had to:

- Control borders.  
- Redistribute spoils from campaigns.  
- Redistribute taxes to allies and family members.

---

## Taxes and revenue in theory and practice

Hausa rulers had used their own taxes.  
The caliphate replaced these with Islamic taxes, such as **zakat**.

In theory, revenue was governed by Islamic law.

In practice, taxes depended on each emirate.  
For example, Kano or Zaria had a property tax.  
This existed outside the emirate of Sokoto.

---

## Limits on centralisation

Sokoto’s efforts to centralise power were limited.

They were limited by:

- Pre-jihadic structures in Hausa cities.  
- The difficulty of reaching many rural people.

---

## Law, courts, and education

The Sokoto caliphate followed the original aims of the jihad.  
It tried to establish **Islamic law** in courts across the caliphate.

This created a need for educated men.  
Schools grew in urban centres.  
At first, there were not enough qualified personnel.

---

## Administration and bureaucracy

A key feature of the caliphate was its **literate staff**.  
These men worked in the administration of each emirate.

Some were born free.  
Some were born into slavery.

Together, they formed a working bureaucracy.

---

## Labour, slavery, and production

A lack of labour led to many expeditions.  
These expeditions aimed to capture slaves.

Slaves were sold or used for work in plantations and other production sites.

Slave labour supported the salt mines in the north of the caliphate.  
Slave labour also supported industries in the central regions, including:

- Iron  
- Cotton  
- Indigo  
- Leather

The state’s wealth depended on a **servile economy**.  
This economy was fuelled by wars and raids.

In Kano in the 1820s, North African merchants supplied many slaves.  
In the city, for every freeman there were **thirty slaves**.

---

Islam entered the Hausa regions in the fourteenth century.  
It came through travellers and traders from neighbouring Borno and from regions north of the Sahara.

Islam spread further through the jihad.  
Pre-Islamic religions, often called “traditional” religions, continued.  
But Islamic culture spread across the region.

Books helped this spread.  
Some were written by dan Fodio’s family.  
Others were sold through the Sahara.

The Hausa regions became more connected to the Muslim world through:

- Pilgrimage to Mecca  
- Trade  
- The spread of brotherhoods

Some integration may have existed before.  
The jihad **greatly accelerated** the process.

chapter_key: AL HAJJ UMAR TAL AND THE OMARIEN DYNAMIC IN WEST AFRICA
text:
Alhaji Salim Suwareh did not raise the sword to spread Islam.  
Al Hajj Umar Tal (1797–1864) did.  
He did so with as much success as the Jakhanke missionaries.

Before looking at his full life, it helps to start with his jihads.  
These took place in present-day Mali and Guinea Conakry.  
They lasted from 1848 to 1864.

His first targets were the gold states of Bambuk and Bure.  
At that time, they were ruled by, and inhabited by, animist Malinke.

Between 1848 and 1854, he moved quickly.  
In six years, he conquered and forcibly converted the Malinke of Bandjogou, Bougary, and Farabana.  
All three places are in the present-day Republic of Guinea Conakry.

He raised the flag of the Tijaniyya sect of Islam.  
He set up his first capital at Jalafara.

His success pushed him to expand his attacks.  
He attacked the Bambaras of Kaarta and Segou.  
He also attacked the animist Fulani of Macina.  
These areas are in the present-day Republic of Mali.

By 1854, Tal had built a large Muslim state.  
It included Kaarta, Segou, Macina, and Khasso.  
He brought the Bambara into submission under his Tijaniyya sect.  
The Bambara were the only well-organized fighting force in this part of the Sahel.

The Malian historian Sekene Mody Cissokho wrote:  
“Al hajj Umar brought Islam to the Western Sudan.”  
This is high praise for a scholar who became a jihadist and empire builder.

His later success was already visible in his early years.  
In 1820, at age 23, he finished his studies.  
He received the title “alfa,” meaning scholar.

In the same year, he made a pilgrimage to Mecca.  
He stayed in Arabia for 13 years.  
During this time, he was ordained as the Kalifa, or emissary, of the Tijaniyya sect in West Africa.

This gave him recognition and approval to lead jihads in the Sahel.  
He briefly passed through Kanem-Borno and Sokoto.  
In those places, jihads had just been completed.  
He likely learned lessons on how to prepare his own jihads in the Sahel.

Cissokho says Umar’s aim was not mainly to destroy existing states.  
Instead, his goal was to convert rulers and people.  
He wanted them to move from animism to Tijaniyya Islam.  
He also wanted some to move from Qadiriyya to Tijaniyya.

His success was not only due to the sword.  
His form of Tijaniyya was also pro-poor and socially uplifting.  
In conquered territories, he quickly freed slaves.  
He also helped the poor and downtrodden meet basic needs.

He remained popular until his death.  
He died at Dinguiray in 1864.  
This followed a bloody encounter with the French.

After his death, his son Amadou Seku replaced him.  
Amadou Seku struggled to hold together the vast Imamate his father had created.

European sailors first reached sub-Saharan Africa in 1442.  
That year, Portuguese ships reached the Senegal River.

The Portuguese had sailed along the coasts of Morocco and Western Sahara since 1413.  
In 1413, they captured the Moroccan city of Ceuta.  
Ceuta is still a Spanish city today.

Between 1413 and the 1440s, the Portuguese built several fortified settlements on the Moroccan coast.  
Important sites included Arzila, Mogador (now Essaouira), Safi, and Tangier.

Portugal kept a strong presence in Morocco until 1578.

text:
After reaching the Senegal River in 1442, Portuguese voyages continued.

By 1448, some Portuguese sailors had gone up the Gambia River. They reached the major trading town of Kantora. Kantora was not far east of what is today Basse Santa Su, in the far east of the country. At that time, Kantora was a major centre for trans-Saharan trade.

By the mid-1450s, the Portuguese were trading with the Wolof state of Kajoor on the coast. The Bijagós Islands, off the coast of Guinea-Bissau, also entered discussions with European traders.

At first, the main language used for communication was probably Arabic. Many Arabic speakers lived in Portugal in the 15th century. Granada was still an Islamic kingdom in Spain. Arabic was also widely spoken in many parts of West Africa.

In 1456, one sailor wrote that the Bijagós was the last place where African peoples shared a language with Portuguese sailors. This suggests it was also the southernmost reach of Arab and trans-Saharan trade at that time.

The Cape Verde Islands were probably first reached in 1456. Cape Verdean historians still debate whether the islands already had a population. Archaeological evidence is not conclusive. The islands may have been used as a salt depot for Saharan states.

Around 1471, the Portuguese reached the coastline of Ghana.

---

The Ghana coast was different. It was close to the gold mines of the Akan forests.

Soon, Akan traders sold gold informally to the Portuguese. The Portuguese state wanted a share of this trade. In 1481, Portugal sent a large fleet. The Portuguese negotiated with Kwamena Ansa, the ruler at Edina (now called Elmina), to build a fortress.

The negotiations were tense. The conflict began when the Portuguese tried to build the fort on the site of a holy shrine. After the negotiations ended, the fortress at Elmina was built. It still remains today. The area became known as the Gold Coast.

In the 17th century, Elmina later changed hands and became a Dutch fortress. Over time, the Dutch and the English became the main European nations trading in Ghana.

---

Because commerce on the Gold Coast was so strong, many Akan rulers wanted to expand their trading links.

The Portuguese built other forts along the Gold Coast. These included Axim and Komenda. Many were completed by 1500.

Later, many more forts were built. There was almost one every few miles along the coast. Some focused on the gold trade. Others focused on different exports. For example, Anishan exported corn, which European ships wanted in large amounts.

The slave trade did not dominate the Gold Coast until the 18th century.

---

At the same time, rulers in West Africa and West-Central Africa also made contact with the Portuguese.

Oba Ozolua of Benin received Portuguese visitors in 1485. Around 1490, the Atlantic trading post of Gwatón was founded.

At first, Benin sold malaguetta peppers to the Portuguese. In 1499, the sea route to India was established. After that, Benin’s peppers were less in demand in Europe.

The Portuguese tried to start a trade in enslaved people from Benin. They wanted to send them to the gold suppliers in Elmina. The Oba refused.

During the 16th century, Benin’s relations with the Portuguese declined. In the early 17th century, the Obas renewed links with European traders. This was because the Dutch wanted cloth made in Benin.

Throughout the 17th century, cloth was Benin’s main export. The “ambassy” cloths were traded regularly to Elmina. They were also traded as far away as Brazil.

Demand for Benin cloth fell in the late 17th century. This happened as imports of luxury cloth from India increased. By the 18th century, Benin’s Obas turned to the trade in enslaved people. They did this to preserve and renew the power of Edo and the Benin state.

---

After Benin, the Portuguese sailed further south.

They reached the mouth of the Kongo River. They established relations with the manikongo at Mbanza Kongo, the capital of Kongo. The manikongo was Nzika Nkuwu.

The island of São Tomé was settled by 1485. Many BaKongo people were taken there as enslaved workers. They worked on sugar plantations.

In 1491, Nzika Nkuwu converted to Christianity. He took the name Joao I.

This also created links between Kongo and Elmina through São Tomé. São Tomé traded with both places.

By the 1510s, traders from Benin were reported at the Kongolese port of Mpinda. This was mentioned in a letter written in Portuguese. The letter was written by the new manikongo, Afonso I (1509–46).

---

By the 1510s, many West African peoples and rulers had connections with the Portuguese.

Some places, like Benin and Elmina, also had links further south to Kongo.

African rulers wanted to expand trade. They also sometimes wanted military support against rivals. This happened in Benin, which fought a major battle with Portuguese support against Nupe in 1516. It also happened during civil wars in Jolof and Kongo.

Diplomacy and royal exchanges shaped the first decades of West Africa’s relationships with Portugal.

It was common for princes from Benin, Jolof, and Kongo to spend time in Portugal to study.  
Some were also sent by their royal elders as ambassadors to the Portuguese court.

This continued into the 17th century.  
Kongo sent ambassadors to the Dutch colonial court in Brazil.  
Kongo also sent ambassadors to the Vatican, the home of the Catholic Church.  
Kongo also sent ambassadors to Portugal.

In the 1650s, Allada sent ambassadors to the Spanish court.  
Later, Dahomey sent ambassadors five times to the Portuguese in Brazil and Portugal.  
These missions took place between 1755 and the 1810s.

When Brazil declared independence from Portugal in 1811, Dahomey was the first state to recognise Brazil’s independence.

## Portugal also treated these ties as diplomacy

Under King João II (1481–95), Portugal sent ambassadors to several African royal courts.  
They went to Benin.  
They went to Kongo.  
They also went to the court of the Mandimansa, the emperor of Mali.

One envoy was sent as far as Timbuktu.  
It is not certain that he arrived.

Letters from Portuguese kings to West African rulers described them as fellow monarchs.  
In both Africa and Portugal, kingship was seen as a divine gift.  
This created a sense of shared status.

## A surviving portrait

Some portraits of these ambassadors still exist.

The most important were painted in Brazil by a Dutch artist, probably Jasper Beckx.  
They show Dom Miguel de Castro.

Miguel de Castro was an ambassador of the manikongo’s court.  
The manikongo was Garcia II Ncana a Luquini nzenze atumba.  
He sent Miguel de Castro as an envoy to the Dutch court in Brazil, probably in 1643.

## Why were these embassies sent?

The aims of these embassies varied.  
They can be grouped into three main categories.

### 1) Seeking a military alliance

Two examples show this clearly.

**Example 1: Jolof, 1488**  
In 1488, the Jolof prince Bumi Jeléen came to Portugal.  
He said he was the rightful ruler of Jolof.  
He had been removed from power by his brothers and rivals.  
He asked Portugal for help.

João II received him at court.  
João II sent a military fleet to support Bumi Jeléen on his return to the Senegal River.

When they reached West Africa, Bumi Jeléen was treacherously murdered.  
He was killed by the leader of the fleet, Pero Vaz de Cunha.  
Pero Vaz de Cunha claimed he suspected Bumi Jeléen of betraying them.

This was an ignominious episode.  
João II had many leaders of the plot put to death.  
Bumi Jeléen’s followers and relatives moved to the Cape Verde islands.  
By then, the islands were under Portuguese control.

**Example 2: Kongo and the Dutch, 1640s**  
In the 1640s, the Kingdom of Kongo allied with the Dutch against the Portuguese.  
The Dutch seized Luanda in 1641.  
Kongo armies then fought Portuguese troops at forts in the interior of Angola.  
These forts included Ambaca and Massangano.

Dom Miguel de Castro’s embassy was part of this alliance.  
He was sent to discuss military strategy.  
The goal was to drive the Portuguese out of West-Central Africa for good.

This alliance was defeated in 1648.

### 2) Interest in Christianity

Another reason for embassies was interest in Christianity.

Princes from Benin studied in Portuguese missions.  
Princes from Kongo did the same.

In Benin, interest in Christianity later weakened.  
In Kongo, it did not.  
Kongo sent ambassadors to the Vatican repeatedly.  
They asked for more priests and missionaries.  
This continued long into the 17th century.

In the 1670s, more than a dozen members of the Ndongo royal family studied in Portugal.  
They spent many years in monasteries and convents.  
New research by the historian José Lingna Nafafé is showing this.

Allada also asked Spain for missionaries in the mid-17th century.  
At that time, the climate was becoming unpredictable.  
Floods were frequent.  
The king of Allada hoped Christian priests could intercede with divinities and prevent floods.

### 3) Commercial activity

Trade was often a key motivation.

Access to Atlantic trade helped rulers increase supplies of money.  
In the past, many types of money were used in West Africa.  
These included cowries, iron bars, and strips of cloth.

These currencies existed before Europeans arrived.  
Atlantic trade later expanded the money supply.  
This also helped market exchange grow.

West African rulers negotiated with European monarchs to increase access to currency.  
They hoped this would increase tax revenue.  
They also hoped it would strengthen the state.

Different currencies were used in different regions:

1. **Gold**, especially on the Niger Bend and in the Akan kingdoms of the Gold Coast.  
2. **Cowries**, in Benin, Oyò, on the Niger Bend, and later in Hueda and Dahomey.  
3. **Copper rods**, on the Gold Coast and in Calabar.  
4. **Iron bars**, in Senegambia and on the Gold Coast.  
5. **Strips of cloth**, widely used in Senegambia, Sierra Leone, and parts of the Gold Coast and Oyò.

In the 1620s, smaller kingdoms along the Gold Coast sent embassies to the Dutch.  
Commercial goals were also a clear motive for Allada’s embassies in the 1650s.  
Dahomey’s five embassies to Brazil and Portugal in the late 18th and early 19th century also had commercial aims.

## Dahomey’s embassies and elite life

By this time, Dahomey’s royal family had become experts in fine living in Brazil and Portugal.

The embassies sent in 1795 show this.  
The two ambassadors travelled first to Salvador, in Brazil.  
They spent large sums on fine silk and damask clothing and hats.  
All of this was paid for by the Portuguese crown.

Later that year, they travelled on to Lisbon.  
After arriving, they visited the theatre and the opera every night.

## Conclusion

These diplomatic exchanges show that African–European relations operated at the level of grand politics.  
They also operated at a local level.

West African rulers pursued goals common to leaders everywhere.  
They wanted commercial success.  
They wanted military success.  
They also acted from religious belief.

Portugal also sent many embassies at first.  
But by the 1530s, the European presence was becoming increasingly “informal”.  
Small-scale traders began to take over.

- the court of the **Mandimansa**, the emperor of **Mali**

One envoy was sent as far as **Timbuktu**. It is not certain that he arrived.

Letters from Portuguese kings to West African rulers described them as fellow monarchs.

In both Africa and Portugal, kingship was seen as a divine gift. This created a sense of shared status.

---

## 3. A surviving portrait

Some portraits of these ambassadors still exist.

The most important were painted in **Brazil** by a **Dutch** artist, probably **Jasper Beckx**. They show **Dom Miguel de Castro**.

Miguel de Castro was an ambassador of the **Manikongo’s** court. The Manikongo was **Garcia II Ncana a Luquini Nzenze Atumba**.

He sent Miguel de Castro as an envoy to the **Dutch court in Brazil**, probably in **1643**.

---

## 4. Why were these embassies sent?

The aims of these embassies varied. They can be grouped into three main categories:  
1. military alliances  
2. Christianity  
3. commercial activity  

---

### 4.1 Seeking a military alliance

Two examples show this clearly.

#### Example 1: Jolof, 1488

In **1488**, the Jolof prince **Bumi Jeléen** came to Portugal.

He said he was the rightful ruler of Jolof. He had been removed from power by his brothers and rivals. He asked Portugal for help.

**João II** received him at court. João II sent a military fleet to support Bumi Jeléen on his return to the **Senegal River**.

When they reached West Africa, Bumi Jeléen was treacherously murdered. He was killed by the leader of the fleet, **Pero Vaz de Cunha**. Pero Vaz de Cunha claimed he suspected Bumi Jeléen of betraying them.

This was an ignominious episode. João II had many leaders of the plot put to death.

Bumi Jeléen’s followers and relatives moved to the **Cape Verde Islands**. By then, the islands were under Portuguese control.

#### Example 2: Kongo and the Dutch, 1640s

In the **1640s**, the kingdom of **Kongo** allied with the **Dutch** against the Portuguese.

The Dutch seized **Luanda** in **1641**. Kongo armies then fought Portuguese troops at forts in the interior of **Angola**. These forts included **Ambaca** and **Massangano**.

Dom Miguel de Castro’s embassy was part of this alliance. He was sent to discuss military strategy.

The goal was to drive the Portuguese out of West-Central Africa for good.

This alliance was defeated in **1648**.

Another reason for embassies was interest in Christianity.

Princes from **Benin** studied in Portuguese missions. Princes from **Kongo** did the same.

In Benin, interest in Christianity later weakened. In Kongo, it did not.

**Allada** also asked **Spain** for missionaries in the **mid-17th century**.

At that time, the climate was becoming unpredictable, and floods were frequent. The king of Allada hoped Christian priests could intercede with divinities and prevent floods.

---

### 4.3 Commercial activity

Trade was often a key motivation.

Access to Atlantic trade helped rulers increase supplies of money.

In the past, many types of money were used in West Africa. These included **cowries**, **iron bars**, and **strips of cloth**. These currencies existed before Europeans arrived. Atlantic trade later expanded the money supply. This also helped market exchange grow.

West African rulers negotiated with European monarchs to increase access to currency. They hoped this would:  
- increase tax revenue  
- strengthen the state  

Different currencies were used in different regions:  
1. **Gold**, especially on the **Niger Bend** and in the **Akan** kingdoms of the **Gold Coast**  
2. **Cowries**, in **Benin**, **Oyò**, on the **Niger Bend**, and later in **Hueda** and **Dahomey**  
3. **Copper rods**, on the **Gold Coast** and in **Calabar**  
4. **Iron bars**, in **Senegambia** and on the **Gold Coast**  
5. **Strips of cloth**, widely used in **Senegambia**, **Sierra Leone**, and parts of the **Gold Coast** and **Oyò**

In the **1620s**, smaller kingdoms along the **Gold Coast** sent embassies to the **Dutch**.

Commercial goals were also a clear motive for Allada’s embassies in the **1650s**.

Dahomey’s **five** embassies to **Brazil** and **Portugal** in the **late 18th** and **early 19th century** also had commercial aims.

---

## 5. Dahomey’s embassies and elite life

By this time, Dahomey’s royal family had become experts in fine living in Brazil and Portugal.

The embassies sent in **1795** show this.

The two ambassadors travelled first to **Salvador**, in Brazil. They spent large sums on fine **silk** and **damask** clothing and hats. All of this was paid for by the Portuguese crown.

Later that year, they travelled on to **Lisbon**.

After arriving, they visited the theatre and the opera every night.

---

## 6. Conclusion

These diplomatic exchanges show that African–European relations operated at the level of grand politics. They also operated at a local level.

West African rulers pursued goals common to leaders everywhere:  
- commercial success  
- military success  
- religious belief  

Portugal also sent many embassies at first.

But by the **1530s**, the European presence was becoming increasingly informal. Small-scale traders began to take over.

chapter_key: IV: European Trading Communities in West Africa
text:
There were two main types of European trading community in West Africa.

**1) Informal communities**  
- Europeans settled in West Africa.  
- They married local women.  
- They formed African families.  
- These families often became important in local trade networks.

**2) Fortified trading-post communities**  
- These grew around fortified trading posts on the coast.  
- These posts were also called **factories** (from the Portuguese word **feitoria**).  
- They were especially common on the **Gold Coast** and in **Hueda**.  
- They were also found on rivers around **Gambia** and **Bissau**.  
- Key rivers included the **Gambia**, **Casamance**, **São Domingos**, **Corubal**, **Nunez**, and **Pongo**.

## Forts and the early gold trade
The fortified factories were often modelled on **Elmina**.  
Elmina was the first, oldest, and biggest of these trading posts.  
It was built in the **1480s**.  
This shows how important the **gold trade** was at the start.

However, in the **1500s**, informal trade was more common than forts.  
This was true apart from Elmina and smaller forts on the Gold Coast.

## Informal traders as intermediaries
In the 1500s, male Portuguese traders went to places such as:  
- **Senegambia**  
- the rivers of **Guinea-Bissau**  
- **Sierra Leone**  
- **Benin**

They married local women.  
They often acted as trading intermediaries with local rulers.  
They could do this because they, their wives, and their children could speak both African and European languages.

## “Ganagoga” in Senegambia
One trader became famous in Senegambia in the 16th century.  
He was known as **“Ganagoga.”**  
His original name was **João Ferreira**.  
He married the daughter of the ruler of **Fùùta Tòòro** (on the Senegal River).  

“Ganagoga” meant **“he who speaks all the languages”** in the **Biafada** language of Guinea-Bissau.  
This shows how valuable language skills were.

Relationships with daughters of ruling families were not unusual.  
In the early 17th century, a **Dutch Jewish trader** got into trouble.  
He had an affair with the daughter of the **Buur of Kajoor** in Senegal.

## Religious roles and the term “tangomão”
Some historians think these early traders also took on religious roles.

In the 1500s, the Portuguese called settlers in Africa **“tangomãos.”**  
The word came from the name of a shrine in Sierra Leone: **tunguma**.

One writer in **1506** described an early Portuguese settler in Sierra Leone.  
This man had settled there in the **1480s**.  
He had officiated at the tunguma shrine at the request of the **Temni** peoples.

Sierra Leone’s communities changed a lot in the 16th century.  
A wave of Mande-influenced warriors called the **Manes** arrived.  
They defeated the warriors of existing communities.  
By **1600**, they had intermarried with them.

So, “tangomão” meant a European who:  
- settled in West Africa, and  
- adopted West African beliefs and practices.

## Women’s central role in trade
In many of these communities, African women ran the trading networks.  
They were married to male European traders.

Many European men became ill with malaria and other diseases.  
They had no physical resistance to these diseases.  
They often looked very unwell.  
They spent much of their time in bed.  
Many died young.

The women usually spoke African languages much better.  
They could build networks with their home communities.  
They managed the day-to-day business.

Some historians think this strong role for women traders mattered later.  
They suggest it influenced women’s powerful place in some 20th-century independence movements.  
They point especially to **Guinea-Bissau** and parts of **Nigeria**.

## Cacheu: Crispina Peres and Bibiana Vaz
A clear example comes from **Guinea-Bissau** in the mid-17th century.

In the factory of **Cacheu**, the most powerful traders in the **1660s, 1670s, and 1680s** were:  
- **Bibiana Vaz**  
- **Crispina Peres**

Peres was married to a Portuguese trader.  
He was so ill that she ran their business.

Peres made many enemies because she was so effective in business.  
She was eventually captured by the **Portuguese Inquisition**.  
She was deported to **Lisbon**.  
She was tried in **1664** for **“fetishism”** as a crime against Catholic Christianity.

Vaz was also extremely powerful.  
In the **1690s**, she kept the Portuguese Governor of Cacheu prisoner.  
She held him in the passageway of her house in **Farim** for **18 months**.

## African influence and inheritance rules
These mixed communities were more influenced by African practices than European ones.

European languages and writing were still important.  
They helped people get better trade terms with Europeans.

But marriage and inheritance followed local rules.  
They followed the rules of the place where the European had settled.

This encouraged Portuguese settlement in **matrilineal** societies.  
In matrilineal societies, inheritance passed through the female line.  
Examples included **Guinea-Bissau** and the **Gold Coast**.

In these places, children of a European man and an African wife could inherit:  
- rights  
- social status  
- property  
They inherited according to local law.

In **patrilineal** societies, inheritance passed through the male line.  
In those places, children of these marriages inherited no social or property rights.  
This was because their fathers were Europeans, and had been born with none in that society.

A key example is **Senegambia**.  
Very few European men settled there after the **1550s**.

## What informal communities did
These informal communities focused on trade.  
They helped African rulers expand trading connections.

They could negotiate with European traders and ships.  
Many ships stopped only briefly.  
These families helped get the best price.

Some families kept links to Europe.  
They sent children to study in Europe into the **18th century**.  
They became rich merchants in coastal towns.

Most families largely let go of their European past.  
They became fully integrated into African societies.  
Their European male ancestors had settled as stranger-guests of African landlord kings.

## Growth of forts in the late 1500s and 1600s
Informal settlements were the majority in the **16th century**.  
But by the late 16th century and early 17th century, forts became more common.  
This was especially true on the **Gold Coast** and in **Hueda**.

In **Casamance** and **Guinea-Bissau**, forts formed in places such as:  
- **Cacheu (1589)**  
- **Ziguinchor (1645)**  
- **Bissau (1687)**

The 17th century also saw the fort at **James Island (1651)**.  
It was at the estuary of the **Gambia River**.

On the Gold Coast, the Dutch built more castles.  
The most famous was **Cape Corso (Cape Coast)**.  
It was built in **1610** and expanded in **1652**.  
Other forts included **Sekondi (1642)**, and those at **Axim** and **Elmina**.

## Slave trade expansion and fortified ports
The Atlantic slave trade expanded hugely in the late 17th century.  
This helped the fortified model grow.

European factories at **Offra (1660)** and in **Hueda** were fortified.  
Offra was the port for **Allada**.

By the middle of the **18th century**, fortified communities were more important than informal ones.  
By then, many informal-community families had fully integrated into their host African societies.

## Dependence on African intermediaries and local ceremonies
Even with military protection, these forts relied heavily on African intermediaries.  
They needed them for trade.

Military captains often attended royal ceremonies in local African states.  
This often happened in **Dahomey**, for example.

They also sent gifts for funeral rites of important people.  
In practice, this meant they had to accept and take part in African religious practices linked to funerals.

## How fortified communities differed
Communities around forts were different from informal communities.

The military aspect was central.  
Europeans rented land for their posts.  
But they were also occupiers, not just tenants.

They had armed militias.  
They often allied with one local ruler against another.  
This could create problems.

By the 18th century, **guns** were one of the largest imports from Atlantic trade to Africa.  
This was a major change from earlier centuries.  
Earlier, **copper**, **iron**, and **cloth** had also been important.

European traders were accustomed to slavery.  
They brought racial animus that became especially strong in Europe from around **1650** onwards.

They used **“castle slaves.”**  
This idea came from Europe.  
It was shaped by experience in New World plantation societies.  
It influenced local practices of service and dependence.

## Families and continuity, but also major change
Many European officials in forts had families with African women.  
Their children often became traders.  
Their dual heritage gave them access to both African and European worlds.

Some of these families became important in local politics.  
In this way, there was continuity with earlier informal communities.

However, by the 18th century, the military presence and the growth of slavery made these communities very different in many important ways.

- property

### Patrilineal societies
In patrilineal societies:  
- inheritance passed through the male line  

In those places, children of these marriages inherited no social or property rights.  
- This was because their fathers were Europeans, and had been born with none in that society.

A key example is Senegambia.  
- Very few European men settled there after the 1550s.

---

## 9. What informal communities did

These informal communities focused on trade.

They:  
- helped African rulers expand trading connections  
- could negotiate with European traders and ships  

Many ships stopped only briefly.  
- These families helped get the best price.

Some families kept links to Europe.  
- They sent children to study in Europe into the 18th century.  
- They became rich merchants in coastal towns.

Most families largely let go of their European past.  
- They became fully integrated into African societies.  
- Their European male ancestors had settled as stranger-guests of African landlord kings.

---

## 10. Growth of forts in the late 1500s and 1600s

Informal settlements were the majority in the 16th century.

But by the late 16th century and early 17th century:  
- forts became more common  
- this was especially true on the Gold Coast and in Hueda  

In Casamance and Guinea-Bissau, forts formed in places such as:  
- Cacheu (1589)  
- Ziguinchor (1645)  
- Bissau (1687)  

The 17th century also saw the fort at James Island (1651).  
- It was at the estuary of the Gambia River.

On the Gold Coast, the Dutch built more castles.  
- The most famous was Cape Corso (Cape Coast).  
- It was built in 1610 and expanded in 1652.

Other forts included:  
- Sekondi (1642)  
- those at Axim and Elmina  

---

## 11. Slave trade expansion and fortified ports

The Atlantic slave trade expanded hugely in the late 17th century.  
- This helped the fortified model grow.

European factories at Offra (1660) and in Hueda were fortified.  
- Offra was the port for Allada.

By the middle of the 18th century:  
- fortified communities were more important than informal ones  
- by then, many informal-community families had fully integrated into their host African societies  

---

## 12. Dependence on African intermediaries and local ceremonies

Even with military protection, these forts relied heavily on African intermediaries.  
- They needed them for trade.

Military captains often attended royal ceremonies in local African states.  
- This often happened in Dahomey, for example.

They also sent gifts for funeral rites of important people.

In practice, this meant they had to accept and take part in African religious practices linked to funerals.

---

## 13. How fortified communities differed

Communities around forts were different from informal communities.

- The military aspect was central.  
- Europeans rented land for their posts.  
- But they were also occupiers, not just tenants.  
- They had armed militias.  
- They often allied with one local ruler against another.  
- This could create problems.

By the 18th century:  
- guns were one of the largest imports from Atlantic trade to Africa  
- this was a major change from earlier centuries  
- earlier, copper, iron, and cloth had also been important  

European traders were accustomed to slavery.  
They brought racial animus that became especially strong in Europe from around 1650 onwards.

They used “castle slaves.”  
- This idea came from Europe.  
- It was shaped by experience in New World plantation societies.  
- It influenced local practices of service and dependence.

---

## 14. Families and continuity, but also major change

Many European officials in forts had families with African women.  
- Their children often became traders.  
- Their dual heritage gave them access to both African and European worlds.  
- Some of these families became important in local politics.

In this way, there was continuity with earlier informal communities.

However, by the 18th century:  
- the military presence  
- and the growth of slavery  

made these communities very different in many important ways.

Europeans came to Africa mainly to trade.  
Trade was almost the only reason they came.  

Most Europeans expected to stay for a short time.  
They hoped to get rich and then leave.  

Some later found other kinds of value in Africa.  
Some stayed and formed families.  
These families became part of local communities.  
Even then, trade stayed central.

## What African rulers wanted from trade

For African rulers, trade created many opportunities.  
In the first two centuries, they especially wanted currency materials.  
These were goods that could be used as money.

### Cloth
Cloth was one of the biggest imports.  
It came from India and Europe.  

In the early 1600s, some Dutch ships carried almost only cloth.  
They shipped it to Senegambia and the Gold Coast.  

Cloth stayed important in the 1700s and 1800s.  
One key cloth was the *pièce de guinée*.  
It was an indigo-dyed blue cloth made near Pondichéry in India.  
The French imported it to Senegambia.  
It was used as currency on the Upper Senegal River for a long time.  

Cloth was used as money in Senegambia.  
It was also used as currency in parts of Angola and the Gold Coast.

### Copper, iron, and cowries
Copper was another major import.  
It was especially important in Benin and the Gold Coast.  

Iron bars were also important in the Gold Coast and Senegambia.  
These iron bars had to be branded with the mark of a European company.  
Examples were OWIC (Dutch West Indian Company) and RAC (English Royal African Company).  
If the bars were not branded, African traders valued them less.  

Cowries were also imported.  
They came from the Maldives.  
They reached Benin from as early as 1505.

## Other imports, and how “money goods” worked

This period also included imports of jewels.  
It also included some manufactured goods, like mirrors and basins.  

But most cargo value was still in goods that could become currency.  
Evidence suggests metals were imported in set sizes for trade.  

Copper often came as rings, called manillas.  
Iron often came as bars of a set length, especially in Senegambia.  
People used these as mediums of exchange.  

Local smiths then melted the metals down.  
They used them for farm tools, weapons, and art.  
In Benin, this included the Benin bronzes.  
Bronze production rose sharply in the 1500s when copper imports grew.  
Bronzes were important before that, but production expanded then.

## A major shift in the late 1600s

In the second half of the 1600s, a shift happened.  
Currency imports declined.  

They were replaced by luxury consumption goods.  
These included alcohol and tobacco, especially from Brazil.  
They also included guns and gunpowder.  

The Nigerian historian Joseph Inikori links this change to slower African economic growth.  
He argues that fewer currency imports showed a market that had stopped growing.  
It needed less money to keep exchange working.

## Trade was more balanced before the late 1600s

Until the second half of the 1600s, trade between Africa and Europe was fairly balanced.  
African rulers wanted more currency supplies.  
Europeans did not focus only on enslaved people yet, as they later did.  
Europeans also wanted gold and ivory.

Several places exported cloth.  
These included Allada, Benin, Cape Verde, Loango, and the rivers of Cameroon and Gabon.  

Some of this cloth was sold far away.  
In the 1600s, it reached Brazil, Curaçao, and the United States.  
(Curaçao is a Caribbean island near Venezuela, and it belonged to the Dutch.)  

Oyò cloth was traded to Yorubà communities in Brazil through the 1700s and into the 1800s.  
In Salvador, Brazil, marketwomen of Yorubà ancestry worked as cloth sellers.  
They were called *vendedoras de panos*.  
They continued into the 1800s.

In 1630, the Dutch invaded Portuguese colonies in Brazil.  
The Portuguese colonists formed an army.  
It included many Africans from the Gold Coast and Angola.  
The Gold Coast group demanded specific cloth as part of their pay and clothing.  
That cloth was sent specially from the Dutch fortress at Elmina.

## African goods also found markets in Europe

West African textiles were not the only exports with overseas markets.  
Basketwork from Gold Coast communities was highly valued in Holland in the early 1600s.  

Ivory carvings made by the Sape peoples of Sierra Leone were found across Europe.  
Europeans turned them into everyday objects.  
These included salt cellars and candle holders.  
They were part of the export trade from that region.  

In the 1900s colonial era, some European art historians thought these ivories came from Benin.  
The American art historian Peter Mark later established they came from Sierra Leone.

Europeans who settled in Africa did so as part of business.  
Their early trading presence in West Africa was mostly between equal partners.  

Diplomatic embassies show mutual recognition.  
Each side saw the other as kings and rulers by divine power.  

Each side also imported “money” from the other.  
Europeans imported gold.  
Africans imported copper, cowries, cloth, and iron.

The Atlantic slave trade existed, but it was not yet as important as it later became.  
In West Africa, it stayed quite minor until the 1640s.  
It expanded greatly in Angola after 1580, with trade to Brazil and Latin America.  
That was in West-Central Africa.  
In West Africa, only Senegambia had a slave trade that mattered much before the 1640s.  
After the 1640s, it began to grow in Allada and Calabar.

The slave trade became dominant.  
Europeans settled in fortified trading posts.  
They did not settle informally with African hosts as much.  
Trade became less equal overall.  
This remained true through the 1700s.

## 1. Why Europeans came to Africa

Europeans came to Africa mainly to trade.  
Trade was almost the only reason they came.

Most Europeans planned to stay for a short time.  
They hoped to get rich and then leave.

Some later found other kinds of value in Africa.  
Some stayed and formed families.

These families became part of local communities.  
Even then, trade stayed central.

---

## 2. What African rulers wanted from trade

Trade gave African rulers many opportunities.

In the first two centuries, rulers especially wanted currency materials.  
People could use these goods as money.

### 2.1 Cloth

Cloth was one of the biggest imports.  
It came from India and Europe.

In the early 1600s, some Dutch ships carried almost only cloth.  
They shipped it to Senegambia and the Gold Coast.

Cloth stayed important in the 1700s and 1800s.  
One key cloth was the *pièce de guinée*.

This was an indigo-dyed blue cloth made near Pondichéry in India.  
French traders imported it to Senegambia.

People used it as currency on the upper Senegal River for a long time.

People used cloth as money in Senegambia.  
People also used it as currency in parts of Angola and the Gold Coast.

### 2.2 Copper, iron, and cowries

Copper was another major import.  
It mattered especially in Benin and the Gold Coast.

Iron bars also mattered in the Gold Coast and Senegambia.  
European companies branded these bars with their marks.

For example, traders used marks like OWIC (Dutch West Indian Company) and RAC (English Royal African Company).  
African traders valued unbranded bars less.

Traders also imported cowries.  
They came from the Maldives.  
They reached Benin as early as 1505.

---

## 3. Other imports, and how “money goods” worked

Traders also brought jewels.  
They also brought some manufactured goods, like mirrors and basins.

But most cargo value still came from goods that could become currency.  
Evidence suggests traders imported metals in set sizes for trade.

Copper often arrived as rings called manillas.  
Iron often arrived as bars of a set length, especially in Senegambia.

People used these items as a medium of exchange.

Local smiths then melted the metals down.  
They made farm tools, weapons, and art.

In Benin, artists made the Benin bronzes.  
Bronze production rose sharply in the 1500s as copper imports grew.  
Bronzes already mattered before that, but production expanded in this period.

---

## 4. A major shift in the late 1600s

In the second half of the 1600s, trade patterns shifted.

Currency imports declined.  
Luxury consumption goods replaced them.

These luxury goods included alcohol and tobacco, especially from Brazil.  
They also included guns and gunpowder.

The Nigerian historian Joseph Inikori links this change to slower African economic growth.  
He argues that fewer currency imports showed a market that had stopped growing.  
In his view, the market needed less money to keep exchange working.

---

## 5. Trade was more balanced before the late 1600s

Until the second half of the 1600s, trade between Africa and Europe stayed fairly balanced.

African rulers wanted more currency supplies.  
Europeans did not yet focus mainly on enslaved people, as they later did.  
Europeans also wanted gold and ivory.

Several places exported cloth.  
These included Allada, Benin, Cape Verde, Loango, and the rivers of Cameroon and Gabon.

Traders sold some of this cloth far away.  
In the 1600s, it reached Brazil, Curaçao, and the United States.  
Curaçao is a Caribbean island near Venezuela, and it belonged to the Dutch.

Oyò cloth reached Yorubà communities in Brazil through the 1700s and into the 1800s.  
In Salvador, Brazil, marketwomen of Yorubà ancestry sold cloth.  
People called them *vendedoras de panos*.  
They continued into the 1800s.

In 1630, the Dutch invaded Portuguese colonies in Brazil.  
The Portuguese colonists formed an army.  
It included many Africans from the Gold Coast and Angola.

The Gold Coast group demanded specific cloth as part of their pay and clothing.  
The Dutch then sent that cloth specially from the Dutch fortress at Elmina.

---

## 6. African goods also found markets in Europe

West African textiles were not the only exports with overseas markets.

In the early 1600s, people in Holland highly valued basketwork from Gold Coast communities.

Ivory carvings made by the Sape peoples of Sierra Leone also spread across Europe.  
Europeans turned them into everyday objects, such as salt cellars and candle holders.  
These ivories were part of the export trade from that region.

In the 1900s colonial era, some European art historians claimed these ivories came from Benin.  
The American art historian Peter Mark later showed they came from Sierra Leone.

---

## 7. Summary: from equal partners to a new pattern

Europeans who settled in Africa did so for business.  
In early West African trade, Africans and Europeans often dealt as equal partners.

Diplomatic embassies show mutual recognition.  
Each side treated the other as kings and rulers with divine power.

Each side also imported “money” from the other:

- Europeans imported gold.  
- Africans imported copper, cowries, cloth, and iron.  

The Atlantic slave trade existed, but it did not yet dominate.  
In West Africa, it stayed quite minor until the 1640s.

In Angola, the trade expanded greatly after 1580, with trade to Brazil and Latin America.  
This was in west-central Africa.

In West Africa, only Senegambia had a slave trade that mattered much before the 1640s.  
After the 1640s, the trade began to grow in Allada and Calabar.

In the later 1600s, the pattern changed.  
The slave trade became dominant.

Europeans built and used fortified trading posts more often.  
They relied less on informal settlement with African hosts.

Trade became less equal overall.  
This remained true through the 1700s.
