text:
The first half of the 17th century brought many changes.  
These changes were very important in West Africa.  
They were also part of wider global changes.  
Wars and revolutions happened in many places.  
They happened in China, Europe, and Africa.

Two main forces drove these transformations:

1) Environmental pressure caused by the “mini ice age” (peaking in the 1640s).  
2) Political competition linked to the rise of the capitalist world system.

## 1) Environmental pressure: the “mini ice age”

The environmental pressure came from a major climate shift.  
This shift is often called the “mini ice age.”

From the 1570s onward, global temperatures fell.  
This cooling created serious climate problems.

In Africa, different regions faced different disasters:

- Angola had droughts from around 1600.  
- Senegambia had droughts from around 1640.  
- Yorubà-speaking areas of Nigeria and Benin had floods in the early 17th century.  
- Morocco had heavy snow.

In the 1650s, the King of Allada sent ambassadors to Spain.  
He said one reason was to try to stop the terrible storms Allada was facing.

Other parts of the world also suffered.  
Freezing temperatures reduced harvests of wheat and other crops.  
Food prices rose.

Some of the coldest temperatures occurred around 1640.  
This was also when major revolutions began.

- In China, a civil war began. It led to the overthrow of the Ming dynasty.  
- In Europe, Portugal declared independence from Spain in 1640. A war followed and lasted until 1668.  
- In England, a civil war began in 1641. The King was deposed and executed.  
- France also experienced civil conflict.

### Why did temperatures fall, and why did crises grow?

European historians have often pointed to changes in the sun.  
A team of archaeologists based in Colombia offers a different explanation.

In the 16th century, Europeans conquered the Americas.  
This conquest is usually linked to a huge population collapse among Indigenous Americans.

Recent estimates suggest about 90% died from disease and war.  
That may have been 10–15% of the entire world population.

This population collapse led to two key changes:

a) Forests spread into former settlements and farmland.  
b) There was less deforestation and less burning.

More forest growth absorbed more carbon dioxide.  
Less burning produced less carbon dioxide.  
This matches today’s understanding of climate change as a balance between carbon emissions and carbon capture.

According to the Colombian archaeologists, these changes helped lower global temperatures.

## 2) Political competition and the growth of trade

Political competition increased as trade grew.  
States that could control trade became more powerful.

In West Africa, trade with European partners became more important.  
States that built these trading relationships could prosper.  
But there could also be costs.

In larger kingdoms, coastal provinces gained power.  
Some broke away from central control.

- In Jolof, Kajoor broke away by the 1550s.  
- In Kongo, Nsoyo broke away in the early 17th century.

At the same time, rival rulers tried to open trading stations.  
They struggled for the best access to international trade.

This created conflict.  
It also increased demand for European trade.

It helped drive the building of many fortified trading posts.  
These were built along the Gold Coast.  
They were also built along the coasts of Hueda and Allada.  
This happened in the second half of the 17th century.

## European competition in West Africa

Europeans also competed with each other for access to African trade.  
This competition was intense.

However, it did not lead to direct military confrontations between European nations in Africa during this period.  
European wars were fought in Europe.  
In Africa, European traders competed within a shared, cooperative trade structure.

By the second half of the 17th century, many groups were active in West Africa.  
Danish, Dutch, English, French, and German trading companies all sought a foothold.  
They brought popular and fashionable trade goods.  
They also negotiated with each other.  
They exchanged goods to create the best “assortment.”

## Effects on African rulers and growing pressure

European competition could benefit African rulers.  
Rulers could play one trader against another.  
This helped them get better prices.

But rulers also faced pressure.  
They had to meet traders’ demands.  
If they did not, traders could move elsewhere.  
Traders looked for captives, ivory, and gold.

Mutual dependence grew between African rulers and European traders.  
At the same time, the environment became more fragile.  
This happened in Africa and in other parts of the world.

Food and resources became less reliable.  
Shortages could lead to conflict more often.

Reparation is the idea of paying compensation to a group that has been oppressed in a society. Many societies around the world have suffered subjugation by more powerful societies or classes. Examples include colonialism, the Jewish Holocaust during the Second World War, and the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade (TAST).

After oppressed people free themselves from these conditions, they often demand reparation. Reparation can be given in different forms. It can be in kind, or it can be material compensation.

One of the most well-known and controversial cases is reparation for slavery in Africa. The argument is that compensation should be paid to the descendants of Africans who were enslaved during the TAST.

The Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade displaced Africans to the New World. In this trade, humans were treated as commodities, instead of goods like gold or ivory. After the discovery of the New World, European merchants transported Africans across the Atlantic Ocean. They did this to supply labour for plantations.

This trade devastated African society at home. It also harmed Africans in the diaspora. Enslaved Africans were obtained in several ways. They were captured through warfare. They were taken through kidnapping. They were also sold in markets, among other sources.

Enslaved people suffered severe conditions. They suffered during the Middle Passage. They suffered under the plantation system. They also experienced psychological trauma after emancipation.

Because of these injustices against enslaved people and their descendants in the Americas, African-Americans and members of the Caribbean diaspora are increasingly demanding reparation.

## what is reparation?

many societies around the world have experienced subjugation by more powerful societies or classes. examples include:

- colonialism  
- the jewish holocaust during the second world war

after oppressed people free themselves from these conditions, they often demand reparation.

reparation can be given in different forms, such as:

- **in kind** (support or resources provided directly)

chapter_key: 6 - Christian Missionary Activities in West Africa
text:
The missionary movement expanded into Africa because many Europeans believed Christians had a duty to renew and improve African societies. The fight against slavery also mattered. Humanitarian concern increased European interest in Africa. It also encouraged mission work.

This period also opened Africa to new forces of change. These forces included “legitimate commerce” (trade that was not based on slavery). They also included Christianity, “civilization,” and colonization.

## Costs and early challenges

Christian missions achieved some of their goals. But the work came with serious costs.

Many missionaries died young. The tropical climate was dangerous for them.

In West Africa, missionaries tried to move beyond the coast to reach inland communities. At the same time, Islam was expanding southward. This created a challenge for Christian mission work.

At first, missionary work had little success. Many people reacted with indifference. Early success happened more often in coastal areas. These areas included mulatto communities and European trading settlements.

## Early European contact and later mission efforts

The first Europeans arrived on the West African coast at the end of the fifteenth century. For many years, they focused more on the slave trade than on evangelization.

By the start of the nineteenth century, churches in Christian Europe began more systematic mission work. Anglicans, Methodists, and Baptists were active in Sierra Leone. Presbyterians worked in Nigeria, along with others. Methodists also set up missions in Ghana, Gambia, and Dahomey.

In the nineteenth century, Afro-Brazilians returned to Benin and Nigeria. They brought Catholicism with them.

## A new era of missions

A new era began in Sierra Leone in 1787. Black Christians from Nova Scotia settled there.

Another major change began in southern Africa. Missionary work moved inland from Cape Town. This advance began with the arrival of J. T. van der Kemp in 1799.

New missionary societies started work in many parts of Africa. These included the LMS, the CMS, the Holy Ghost Fathers, and the White Fathers.

## Early mission stations and early successes

The CMS began work in freed-slave villages in Sierra Leone in 1804. The Methodists began there in 1811.

Early missionary success included Freetown and nearby villages. There was also early success along the Liberian coast. Afro-Americans and freed slaves were converted there.

Other early successes happened in French trading posts. These included Grand Bassam and Assinie in Ivory Coast. They also included Libreville in Gabon.

## The interior and the Evangelical Revival

Except for the extreme south and the Horn of Africa, Europeans had little contact with the interior before the last quarter of the nineteenth century.

In the late eighteenth century, the Evangelical Revival began. It brought many missionaries to Africa. Their work produced the first lasting results of Christian presence in Sub-Saharan Africa.

## Catholic missions and the “reprise” idea

In the later nineteenth century, Catholic priests focused strongly on the African interior.

From 1867 until his death in November 1892, Cardinal Lavigerie planned to plant churches in Africa south of the Sahara.

Modern Christian mission history in Africa is often dated from the late eighteenth century. However, Catholics had been in Africa earlier. This was especially true during the first Portuguese ventures in the early centuries of the Christian era. Because of this, the late nineteenth-century rise of Christianizing missions is sometimes described as a “reprise,” or a return.

## Missionary societies and Bible work

The late eighteenth century saw the rise of Christian groups in Europe that aimed to evangelize Africa.

On 2 October 1792, the Baptist Missionary Society was formed. In 1795, the interdenominational London Missionary Society was established.

In 1804, the British and Foreign Bible Society was founded. Its task was to promote translation and printing of the Holy Bible.

At first, most missionary journeys were made by English-speaking Protestants. In the 1820s and 1830s, they were joined by Protestants from Germany, Switzerland, and France. Related organizations also developed in Scandinavia, Holland, and the USA.

## Religion and education in West Africa

West Africa owes Christian missionaries more than a new religious faith. Christianity changed the beliefs and lives of millions of people. Missionaries also laid the foundation of Western education.

The Portuguese were the first to introduce Christianity into West Africa. After they left the West Coast in the mid-seventeenth century, Christianity survived mainly in Upper Guinea. A bishop remained in the Cape Verde Islands. He also served part of the mainland.

Christianity was not firmly established in West Africa until the nineteenth century.

## Focus of this chapter

This chapter examines how Christianity and Western-style education influenced West African values, attitudes, and lifestyles.

chapter_key: EVANGELICAL MOVEMENTS AND MISSIONARY SOCIETIES IN THE ENGLISH COLONIES
text:
From the second half of the eighteenth century, a strong evangelical movement grew. It spread in the United Kingdom, Europe, and the New World. It inspired many men and women to become missionaries.

They formed religious societies. Members travelled to Africa and other lands. Their goals were clear. They wanted to spread the Gospel message. They also wanted to provide social services. They aimed to help suppress slavery and the slave trade.

These movements saw this work as a form of reparation. They believed Europe owed something to Africans. This was because of centuries of exploitation. The Trans-Atlantic slave trade had caused great harm to African society.

Several early Protestant evangelical societies were founded in Great Britain. These included the Baptist Missionary Society. They also included the Church Missionary Society for the Propagation of the Gospel. Another was the Wesleyan Missionary Society. There was also what became known as the Presbyterian Missionary Society of the Church of Scotland.

Similar organizations were formed in other European countries. The Basel Missionary Society was founded in Switzerland. The Breman Mission was formed in Germany.

Evangelical societies were also founded in the Americas. These included the Baptist Missionary Board. They also included the Nova Scotian Methodists. Their members went to work among the Maroons. The Maroons had settled mainly in Liberia.

At the same time, the Roman Catholic Church promoted similar movements in Europe. These efforts were supported by the Propagation of the Faith within the Vatican. Its Cardinal Secretary later became Pope Gregory XVI.

With this support, several Roman Catholic missionary societies were founded. These included the Congregation of the Holy Ghost. It was commonly known as the Holy Ghost Fathers. Another was the Society of African Missions (SMA). Another was the Society of Missionaries of Africa. People often called them the White Fathers. This was because they wore white, Muslim-like clothing. Another group was the Society of the Divine Word (SVD). The initials come from its Latin name.

These missionary societies laid the foundations of the Roman Catholic Church in West Africa. This continued through the independence period. Later, African clergy replaced the white pastors.

text:
During the early Portuguese contact with Nigeria, Catholic priests set up missionary stations in Benin and nearby areas. Portuguese missionaries worked from the island of Sao Tome. Later, Spanish missionaries also worked in Benin. Even so, Christianity was not firmly established in Nigeria until the nineteenth century.

Christianity first grew among Yoruba recaptives. These were people freed from slave ships by the British Royal Naval Squadron. Many of them became Christians while in Sierra Leone. They returned home between 1839 and 1845.

Pastors of the Church Missionary Society (C.M.S.) visited these new Christian communities. They came from Badagry and later from Sierra Leone. They visited Abeokuta and other towns.

One of the first missionaries was Rev. Henry Townsend. He travelled from Sierra Leone to Badagry in 1842. Rev. Ajayi Crowther was with him.

The pioneer missionaries had success. C.M.S. churches were established in several important towns. These included Abeokuta (1846), Lagos (1851), Ibadan (1853), and Oyo (1856).

After this, C.M.S. branches were founded in south-eastern Nigeria. The main centres were Bonny and Brass. Bishop Ajayi Crowther did important work in this region. He was assisted by an Igbo recaptive, Rev. J. C. Taylor. The effects of their work in southern Nigeria can still be seen today.

Other missionaries also opened mission stations in Nigeria. Baptist missionaries began work under the American evangelist Thomas Bowen. They started from Ogbomosho in 1855.

Around the same period, the Church of Scotland (Presbyterian) began work in Calabar. The mission was led by Rev. Hope Waddell. This pioneering work started in 1846. Later, Rev. Hugh Goldie and William Anderson joined him.

Another well-known missionary was Mary Slessor. She arrived in Nigeria in 1876. She worked for many years as a missionary nurse. She helped stop the killing of twins in the areas where she served.

The story of Christianity in Nigeria is not complete without Father Berghero. He was an Italian Roman Catholic priest. He worked from Whydah, in what is now the People’s Republic of Benin (formerly Dahomey). In 1860, he visited Abeokuta and Lagos. Freed Catholic slaves from Brazil welcomed him warmly.

A permanent Catholic station was established in Lagos in 1868. Other stations soon followed. These were at Lokoja, Abeokuta, and Ibadan.

Within ten years of Father Berghero’s visit, the Roman Catholic Church in Nigeria was strongly established. It was no longer administered from Dahomey. By 1885, the church had spread further inland.

This inland growth was helped by Father Joseph Lutz. He began work around Onitsha in 1886. He spread the gospel in many parts of what are now Imo and Anambra States. Another important Catholic missionary in this area was Bishop Shanahan, an Irishman.

Lokoja had a small C.M.S. station in 1858. However, missionaries did not enter Hausaland until 1889. Hausaland was predominantly Muslim. For many years, most converts were people from southern Nigeria who lived in the north. Converts also came from the large non-Muslim population of the north.

chapter_key: I: Immediate Causes of Portuguese Sailings to Africa
text:
Europe in the 14th century was in serious trouble.

Between 1346 and 1353, the Plague spread across Europe.  
It is estimated to have killed 30 to 50% of the European population.

Some archaeologists think the Plague also affected West Africa.  
The evidence for this is still debated.  
The archaeologist Gérard Chouin has argued for this idea most strongly.

After the population collapse, countries like Portugal faced many problems.

The workforce in Portugal fell by more than half.  
With fewer workers, much farmland was abandoned.  
Forests and wild plants took over this land.

One of the earliest sources about West Africans in Portugal comes from 1471.  
It is from the Portuguese Cortes (parliament) at Évora.  
It says African labourers were vital for clearing wastelands.  
This suggests Europe had a major labour shortage after the Plague.  
It also shows African labour helped address that shortage.

Many nobles lost their labourers, called serfs.  
Portugal also experienced civil wars in the 1380s.

There was a shortage of wheat for making bread.  
At the same time, the Portuguese currency, the escudo, suffered very high inflation.

These problems increased Portuguese interest in Morocco.

Portugal was interested in Morocco for two main reasons.  
First, Morocco was fertile and grew wheat.  
Second, Portugal hoped to protect its currency by gaining access to gold.  
Portuguese leaders believed that sailing along the West African coast could help them reach West African gold supplies.

West Africa in the 15th century looked very different from Europe.  
Many West African states were expanding and growing.

Mossi was established in the 15th century in what is now Burkina Faso.  
Kano became a major power.  
Songhay rose and took power from the Mali Empire.

Much of this growth was linked to increased gold production.  
This gold came especially from the Akan states in Ghana.

So much gold was produced that trade across the Sahara could not keep up.  
At Kano, there were not enough goods to exchange for the gold.  
Many gold traders left with nothing to buy.  
This is reported by the early 16th-century Muslim traveller known as Leo Africanus, from southern Spain.

The Portuguese learned about West African growth in several ways.

One important source was the Catalan Atlas, made around 1375.  
It was drawn by Abraham Cresques, a Jewish mapmaker from Majorca.  
The map showed the power of Mali and its gold production in detail.

The Atlas also showed strong trade links between Spain and West Africa through the Sahara.  
These journeys were often made by Jewish traders.

These traders shared news about West Africa in Spain and Portugal.  
Jewish communities existed in Saharan settlements such as Tuat.

In 1391, riots targeted Spanish Jews.  
After this, more Jewish people settled in Morocco.  
Many worked in the carpet and textile trade connected to the Mali Empire.

Because they knew something about Africa, Portuguese leaders wanted direct links to West African gold producers.  
Portugal also had a large Jewish population.

Portuguese leaders also hoped to find a Christian king called Prester John.  
They believed he lived somewhere in Africa.  
They wanted a Christian alliance against the Islamic Ottoman Empire, which was growing in power.  
They also wanted to divert part of the gold supply.

Prester John probably referred to the Christian king of Ethiopia.  
But people in Portugal did not know this at the time.

All these factors shaped Portuguese voyages to West Africa.  
They help explain why the Portuguese reached the Senegal River in 1442.

europe in the 14th century was in serious trouble.

between 1346 and 1353, the plague spread across europe.  
it may have killed 30 to 50% of the population.

some archaeologists think the plague also reached west africa.

the evidence is still debated.  
the archaeologist gérard chouin argues strongly for this view.


## portugal after the population collapse

after the population collapse, portugal faced many problems.

the workforce fell by more than half.  
with fewer workers, much farmland was abandoned.  
forests and wild plants spread over this land.


## early evidence of west africans in portugal

one early source dates to 1471.

it comes from the portuguese cortes at évora.  
it says african labourers were vital for clearing wastelands.

this suggests two things.

- europe had a major labour shortage after the plague.  
- african labour helped reduce that shortage.  


## social and political strain in portugal

many nobles lost their labourers, called serfs.

portugal also faced civil wars in the 1380s.


## economic pressure: food and money

there was a shortage of wheat for making bread.

at the same time, the escudo faced very high inflation.

these problems increased portuguese interest in morocco.

portugal had two main reasons.

1) morocco was fertile and grew wheat.  
2) portugal hoped to protect its currency with gold.  

portuguese leaders thought coastal sailing could help.  
they hoped it would lead to west african gold supplies.

west africa in the 15th century looked very different.

many west african states were expanding and growing.

examples include:

- mossi, formed in the 15th century in today’s burkina faso  
- kano, which became a major power  
- songhay, which rose and took power from mali

much of this growth linked to increased gold production.

this gold came especially from the akan states in ghana.

so much gold was produced that saharan trade could not keep up.

at kano:

- the power of mali

Jerusalem is a holy city for Jews, Christians, and Muslims.

- Jews believe King Solomon built the Temple there in the tenth century BCE.  
- Christians believe the Romans crucified Jesus there in 33 CE. They also believe he rose to heaven from there and promised to return.  
- Muslims believe Muhammad traveled from Jerusalem to heaven in 621. They believe he received instructions about prayer.

Because of this, many people feel strongly about Jerusalem. Claims to the area go back a long time. Even so, there is evidence that the three religions lived in harmony for centuries.

In 1095, this changed. European Christians decided to take Jerusalem from its Muslim rulers. They also wanted to conquer the “Holy Lands.” This area stretched from modern-day Turkey in the north, down the Mediterranean coast, to the Sinai Peninsula. Muslims controlled this whole region. This was the start of the Crusades.

Many knights joined the Crusades because of religious zeal. Others wanted adventure. Some hoped to win land and a title. Many were also motivated by the Church’s promise of full forgiveness of sins.

Most Crusaders were French knights. They captured Jerusalem in June 1099. The capture included horrific slaughter. A French writer who was there gave this eyewitness account:

“On the top of Solomon’s Temple, to which they had climbed in fleeing, many were shot to death with arrows and cast down headlong from the roof. Within this Temple, about ten thousand were beheaded. If you had been there, your feet would have been stained up to the ankles with the blood of the slain. What more shall I tell? Not one of them was allowed to live. They did not spare the women and children.”

A Muslim eyewitness also described what happened. The conquerors stripped the temple of its wealth. They also looted private homes.

In 1187, Muslim forces took back Jerusalem. Their leader was the legendary Saladin. Europe reacted quickly. King Richard I of England, called the Lionheart, joined others to fight again.

The struggle for the Holy Lands lasted a long time. It did not end until 1291. That year, the Crusaders lost their Mediterranean stronghold at Acre (in present-day Israel). The last Christians left the area a few years later.

The Crusades had lasting effects. Some were negative. Some were positive.

Negative effects:
- Large-scale persecution of Jews began.  
- Christians grouped Jews with Muslim “infidels.” They called Jews “the killers of Christ.”  
- In later centuries, kings expelled Jews from their kingdoms. Or they forced Jews to pay heavy tributes to stay.  
- Hatred between Muslims and Christians grew. Intolerance increased.

Positive effects:
- Sea trade between East and West expanded.  
- Crusaders encountered silk, spices, and porcelain. They wanted more of these goods. This created new markets for merchants.  
- Venice, an Adriatic port city, grew very rich from trade with Islamic merchants.

Merchants’ ships carried valuable goods between western Europe and the East. This trade existed from the tenth century onward. The routes were later called the Silk Road.

Venetian sailors traveled widely. From the time of the early adventurer Marco Polo, they sailed to ports on the Black Sea. They also set up colonies along the Mediterranean coast.

But the old Silk Road had major problems. Transport was costly and slow. It was often unprofitable. Muslim middlemen collected taxes as goods changed hands. Robbers attacked caravans carrying treasure.

Because of this, Europeans wanted a direct water route to the East. They wanted to avoid the land part of the journey. Sailors also wanted a route to the Spice Islands in modern-day Indonesia. These islands were exotic and wealthy. Muslim rulers kept their location secret.

Venice had long been a rival of Genoa and Florence. Merchants from Genoa and Florence also began to look west.

Prince Henry the Navigator led Portugal’s exploration of Africa and the Atlantic in the 1400s.  
With his support, Portuguese sailors found an eastward sea route to Africa.  
They gained a foothold there.  
This foothold became the base of Portugal’s trade empire in the 1400s and 1500s.

Portuguese sailors built an Atlantic empire by colonizing islands.  
These included the Canary Islands, Cape Verde, the Azores, and Madeira.  
Merchants used these islands as stopping points for later voyages.

From these strategic outposts, Portugal expanded its reach.  
It moved down the west coast of Africa to the Congo.  
It also traveled along the west coast of India.  
Eventually, it reached Brazil on the east coast of South America.  
Portugal also set up trading posts in China and Japan.

Portugal did not control a huge land empire.  
But it held key islands and coastal ports.  
These locations gave Portugal near-unmatched control of sea trade routes.  
By the 1400s, Portugal had a global empire of trading posts.

When Portuguese traders reached West Africa, they encountered the African slave trade.  
This trade was already active among African states.  
The Portuguese saw that enslaved labor could help grow sugar on their Atlantic islands.  
Soon, they began exporting enslaved Africans.  
They also exported African ivory and gold.

Sugar helped drive the Atlantic slave trade.  
The Portuguese islands quickly developed sugar plantations.  
The Portuguese also traded enslaved people to other European nations.  
This provided labor that those nations wanted.

As European exploration expanded, slavery expanded too.  
Over time, much of the Atlantic World became a vast sugar-plantation system.  
Africans were forced to labor to produce sugar.  
European consumers bought this highly profitable product.

The most famous Spanish explorers left stories that shaped how many people in the West viewed the Americas. These stories often suggested that Europeans were superior. They also often described Native Americans as savage.

But many of these stories were not neutral reports. Conquistadors often wrote to impress the Spanish Crown. They wanted rewards and status. They used a type of document called *probanzas de méritos*. This means “proofs of merit.”

Below are excerpts from Columbus’s 1493 letter to Luis de Santángel. The letter shows how dramatic reports from explorers helped create myths about the Spanish conquest and the “New World.”

> “This island, like all the others, is most extensive. It has many ports along the sea-coast excelling any in Christendom—and many fine, large, flowing rivers.  
>   
> The land there is elevated, with many mountains and peaks incomparably higher than in the centre isle. They are most beautiful, of a thousand varied forms, accessible, and full of trees of endless varieties, so high that they seem to touch the sky. I have been told that they never lose their foliage.  
>   
> There is honey. There are many kinds of birds. There is a great variety of fruits.  
>   
> Inland there are numerous mines of metals and innumerable people. Hispaniola is a marvel. Its hills and mountains, fine plains and open country, are rich and fertile for planting and for pasturage, and for building towns and villages.  
>   
> The seaports there are incredibly fine. The rivers are magnificent. Most of them bear gold.  
>   
> The trees, fruits and grasses differ widely from those in Juana. There are many spices. There are vast mines of gold and other metals in this island.  
>   
> They have no iron, nor steel, nor weapons. Nor are they fit for them. Although they are well-made men of commanding stature, they appear extraordinarily timid.  
>   
> The only arms they have are sticks of cane, cut when in seed, with a sharpened stick at the end. They are afraid to use these.  
>   
> Often I have sent two or three men ashore to some town to converse with them. The natives came out in great numbers. As soon as they saw our men arrive, they fled without a moment’s delay, although I protected them from all injury.”

Farther west, the Spanish in Mexico wanted to expand their empire. They looked north to the land of the Pueblo peoples.

King Philip II ordered Juan de Oñate to explore the American Southwest for Spain. Oñate explored in the late 1590s. The Spanish hoped the area we now call New Mexico would produce gold and silver. It produced little that was valuable to them.

In 1610, Spanish settlers founded Santa Fe. Its original name was **La Villa Real de la Santa Fe de San Francisco de Asís**. This means “Royal City of the Holy Faith of St. Francis of Assisi.” Many Pueblo villages were in the area.

Santa Fe became the capital of the Kingdom of New Mexico. This kingdom was an outpost of the larger Spanish Viceroyalty of New Spain. New Spain was governed from Mexico City.

As in other Spanish colonies, Franciscan missionaries tried to convert the Pueblo to Catholicism. They wanted a “spiritual conquest.”

At first, the Pueblo accepted parts of Catholicism that fit with their own beliefs. But Spanish priests demanded that the Pueblo give up their old ways completely. The priests also focused on converting young people. This pulled children away from their parents. The Pueblo saw this as a deep insult.

In the 1670s, the region faced more problems. There was a long drought. Apache and Navajo attacks increased. Many Pueblo people believed these troubles were connected to the Spanish presence.

Because of this, the Pueblo decided to drive out the Spanish and their religion. A Pueblo leader named Popé called for a return to native ways. He believed this would end the hardships. To him and many others, it seemed clear that “when Jesus came, the Corn Mothers went away.” They believed removing the Spanish would bring back prosperity and a pure native way of life.

In 1680, the Pueblo organized a coordinated rebellion against the Spanish. The Pueblo Revolt killed more than four hundred Spaniards. It forced the remaining settlers to flee south toward Mexico. The number of settlers who fled may have been as many as two thousand.

After the revolt, drought and attacks by rival tribes continued. The Spanish saw a chance to return. In 1692, they came back and took control again.

Some Spanish people explained the Pueblo victory in 1680 in religious terms. They said it was the work of the Devil. They believed Satan had pushed the Pueblo to fight God’s chosen people, the Spanish. They also believed the Spanish, and their God, won in the end.

chapter_key: THE DIVERGING CULTURES OF THE NEW ENGLAND AND CHESAPEAKE COLONIES
text:
People in England promoted colonization in North America. Many of them never crossed the Atlantic. They wrote about the riches the English would find there.

These promoters wanted to make money. They hoped to import raw materials to England. They also wanted new markets for English goods. Many also wanted to spread Protestantism.

The English people who actually migrated often had different goals.

## The Chesapeake: Virginia and Maryland
In the Chesapeake Bay region, English migrants founded Virginia and Maryland. These colonies were mainly commercial.

Early settlers at Jamestown hoped to find gold. They did not. Settlers in Virginia and Maryland soon learned that tobacco was the best way to make money.

Thousands of young Englishmen came to these colonies. Many were unmarried, unemployed, and impatient. A few Englishwomen came too. They hoped tobacco farming would give them a better life.

## New England: Puritan migration
A very different group went to New England. The climate was cold. The soil was rocky. Many migrants still chose this region for religious reasons.

Many Puritans crossed the Atlantic with their families. They brought children. They often followed their ministers “beyond the seas.”

They imagined a “new English Israel.” They wanted reformed Protestantism to grow and thrive there. They hoped it would be a model for the Christian world. They also wanted a counter to what they saw as a Catholic menace.

In Virginia and Maryland, settlers focused on expanding tobacco fields. In New England, settlers built towns centered on the church. Each congregation decided what was best for itself.

The Congregational Church grew out of this Puritan effort in America.

Many historians think later divisions between the North and South began here. They point to the deep differences between the Chesapeake colonies and the New England colonies.

## Why the regions became so different
These differences began with problems in England.

In the early 1600s, the Church of England demanded conformity. The Church of England had been established in the 1530s. Conformity meant following the church’s required practices.

Puritans wanted more reform. By the 1620s, the Church of England viewed leading Puritan ministers and their followers as outlaws. The church saw them as a national security threat because they opposed its power.

As pressure increased, many Puritans chose to leave England. They moved to New England. By 1640, New England’s population reached twenty-five thousand.

At the same time, many loyal members of the Church of England moved to Virginia. They wanted economic opportunity. Many of them also mocked and ridiculed Puritans, both in England and in New England.

## Civil war and its effects
In the 1640s, England’s troubles grew worse. Civil war broke out.

Royalists supported King Charles I and the Church of England. Parliamentarians opposed them. The Parliamentarians included Puritan reformers and their supporters in Parliament.

In 1649, the Parliamentarians won. In an unprecedented act, they executed Charles I.

In the 1650s, England became a republic. It was a state without a king.

English colonists in America followed these events closely. Many Puritans left New England and returned to England. They wanted to join the struggle against the king and the national church.

Other English men and women in the Chesapeake and elsewhere were horrified. They believed the Parliamentarians, led by Puritan insurgents, were unleashing chaos in England.

This turmoil made it hard to govern the colonies. It also made imperial oversight difficult. During this time, the Chesapeake and New England regions developed in different ways. They formed divergent cultures.

In the early **1600s**, the **Church of England** demanded **conformity**.  
The Church of England had been established in the **1530s**.

Conformity meant following the church’s **required practices**.

Puritans wanted **more reform**.

By the **1620s**, the Church of England viewed leading Puritan ministers and their followers as **outlaws**.  
The church saw them as a **national security threat** because they opposed its power.

As pressure increased, many Puritans chose to leave England.  
They moved to **New England**.

By **1640**, New England’s population reached **twenty-five thousand**.

At the same time, many loyal members of the Church of England moved to **Virginia**.  
They wanted **economic opportunity**.

Many of them also mocked and ridiculed Puritans, both in England and in New England.


## Civil war and its effects

In the **1640s**, England’s troubles grew worse.  
**Civil war** broke out.

Royalists supported **King Charles I** and the **Church of England**.

Parliamentarians opposed them.  
The Parliamentarians included **Puritan reformers** and their supporters in Parliament.

In **1649**, the Parliamentarians won.  
In an unprecedented act, they executed **Charles I**.

In the **1650s**, England became a **republic**.  
It was a state without a king.

English colonists in America followed these events closely.

Many Puritans left New England and returned to England.  
They wanted to join the struggle against the king and the national church.

Other English men and women in the Chesapeake and elsewhere were **horrified**.  
They believed the Parliamentarians, led by Puritan insurgents, were unleashing **chaos** in England.

This turmoil made it hard to govern the colonies.  
It also made imperial oversight difficult.

text:
The shift from indentured servitude to slavery as the main labor system happened first in the West Indies.

On Barbados, colonized in the 1620s, English planters first grew tobacco for export. In the 1640s, they switched to sugarcane. They also began to rely more and more on enslaved Africans.

In 1655, England took Jamaica from Spain. England quickly turned Jamaica into a profitable sugar island. It was run on forced labor as part of England’s growing empire.

Slavery spread more slowly in the Chesapeake colonies. But by the end of the 1600s, Virginia and Maryland had adopted chattel slavery as the main labor system for growing tobacco. Chattel slavery legally defined Africans as property, not as people. Chesapeake colonists also enslaved Native people.

When the first Africans arrived in Virginia in 1619, slavery was not yet an established institution in colonial America. Slavery did not exist in England. Many Africans worked as servants. Like White servants, some could gain land of their own. Some Africans who converted to Christianity became free landowners. Some even had White servants.

In the Chesapeake, Africans’ status changed in the last decades of the 1600s. More and more, they were treated as enslaved people.

Bacon’s Rebellion sped up this shift toward African slavery in the Chesapeake. The rebellion included both White people and Black people. Many believed the Virginia government blocked their access to land and wealth. They also believed the government did too little to take land from Native Americans.

The rebellion was named for Nathaniel Bacon. He was a wealthy young Englishman who arrived in Virginia in 1674. At first, he was friendly with the royal governor, William Berkeley. But Bacon was later shut out of the governor’s inner circle of powerful friends and advisers.

Bacon wanted land on the Virginia frontier. Governor Berkeley refused to allow more expansion. He feared war with nearby Native tribes.

Bacon gathered supporters. Many were former indentured servants. They believed the governor limited their economic chances. They also believed he denied them the right to own tobacco farms.

Bacon’s followers said Berkeley’s frontier policy did not protect settlers. They were also angry that Berkeley tried to keep peace. He did this by signing treaties with local Native peoples.

Bacon and his followers saw all Native peoples as obstacles to getting land. They supported a policy of extermination.

Tensions between English settlers and Native peoples led to open war. In 1675, Susquehannock warriors attacked frontier settlements in Virginia. They killed English planters. They destroyed plantations, including one owned by Bacon.

In 1676, Bacon and other Virginians attacked the Susquehannock. They did this without the governor’s approval. Berkeley then ordered Bacon’s arrest.

Bacon responded by marching to Jamestown with his followers. He forced the governor to flee to Virginia’s eastern shore. Bacon’s forces then burned Jamestown.

A civil war followed. It was a brutal fight between Berkeley’s supporters and Bacon’s supporters. News of the rebellion reached England. King Charles II sent royal troops and English commissioners to restore order in the tobacco colonies.

By the end of 1676, Berkeley’s supporters had the advantage. They executed several rebel leaders. Bacon did not die by hanging. He died of dysentery.

The rebellion faded in 1676. But Virginia remained divided. Many Bacon supporters still had grievances about access to Native land.

Bacon’s Rebellion helped push the Chesapeake toward a system of racial slavery. At the time, indentured servants were most of the region’s labor force. Wealthy White people feared this large group of workers. They worried about the freedom servants still had. They also feared the alliance that Black and White servants formed during the rebellion.

Planters saw Black slavery as a way to reduce these risks. It reduced reliance on White indentured servants, who were often unhappy and difficult to control. It created a racially defined labor caste. This caste had tightly controlled movement. It also reduced the chance of future alliances between Black and White workers.

Racial slavery also eased some conflict between rich and poor White people. White people could unite as members of a “superior” racial group.

Slavery was already legal in the tobacco colonies before Bacon’s Rebellion. But new laws after the rebellion sharply limited Black freedom. These laws helped build the foundation of racial slavery.

In 1680, Virginia passed a law that did several things. It banned free Black people and enslaved people from carrying weapons. It banned Black people from gathering in large groups. It set harsh punishments for enslaved people who assaulted Christians. It also set harsh punishments for enslaved people who tried to gain freedom.

Two years later, Virginia passed another law. It said that all Africans brought to the colony would be enslaved for life.

As a result, tobacco planters relied more on enslaved labor. The colonies also created strict laws to control enslaved people. These changes helped planters meet labor needs. They also reduced English fears of more uprisings. And they eased class tensions between rich and poor White people.

chapter_key: Robert Beverley on Servants and Enslaved People
text:
Robert Beverley was a wealthy planter in Jamestown. He also enslaved people.  
In 1705, he published a book called *The History and Present State of Virginia*.  
In this excerpt, he explains how Virginia treated White servants and enslaved Black people differently.

## Beverley’s description (rewritten in clear, short sentences)

He says there were two groups of workers.

### 1) “Slaves for life”
These were Black people (“Negroes,” in his words).  
He says their children were also enslaved.  
A child’s status followed the mother’s status.  
He uses the Latin phrase *partus sequitur ventrem*.  
This means “status follows the womb.”  
He says they were enslaved for life.

### 2) “Servants for a time”
These were people who served for a limited number of years.  
Their service time was set by a contract (an indenture).  
If they had no contract, local custom and law decided the length.

The law worked like this:

- If a servant was under 19, the court decided their age.  
  Then they had to serve until age 24.
- If a servant was judged to be 19 or older, they served 5 years.

### Work and daily treatment
Beverley says male servants and enslaved people (men and women) often did the same field work.  
They tilled soil and spread manure.  
They planted tobacco and corn.

He says there were some differences in clothing and food.  
But he says the work itself was similar to what overseers, free workers, and planters did.

### Women’s work
He says White women servants were rarely made to work in the fields.

New England was the second major region the English colonized in the first half of the 1600s.  
It was very different from the Chesapeake tobacco colonies, which focused on commerce.  

New England was settled mainly by Puritan families in the 1630s.  
From the beginning, the region had a strong religious purpose.  

In England, reform-minded men and women had called for bigger changes in the national church since the 1580s.  
These reformers followed the teachings of John Calvin and other Protestant reformers.  
They were called Puritans.  
They wanted to “purify” the Church of England.  
They believed the church still had un-scriptural elements.  
They especially opposed Catholic elements that remained in church institutions and practices.  

Many early leaders in New England were educated ministers.  
They had studied at Cambridge or Oxford.  
But they questioned the practices of the Church of England.  
Because of this, the king and his officials blocked their careers.  
The goal was to silence dissenting voices.  

Other Puritan leaders came from the English gentry.  
One example was John Winthrop.  
He was the first governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony.  

These well-to-do Puritans, and many thousands more, left England.  
They did not leave to create religious freedom for everyone.  
They left so they could practice their own religion without persecution.  

Puritan New England gave them a place to live as they believed the Bible required.  
In their “New” England, they tried to build a model of reformed Protestantism.  
They aimed to create a new English Israel.  

Puritanism created conflict in English society.  
Puritans demanded reforms that challenged traditional festive culture.  
For example, they condemned bear-baiting.  
Bear-baiting was a popular pastime where dogs attacked a chained bear.  
These events often happened on Sundays, when people had a few free hours.  

Puritans also attacked the theater.  
This was the same culture in which William Shakespeare wrote his plays.  
Puritans wanted playhouses closed.  
They said theaters were places of decadence.  

The Bible itself became part of the conflict.  
James I led the Church of England.  
Soon after he became king, he ordered a new Bible translation.  
He wanted to weaken Puritan use of the Geneva Bible.  
The Geneva Bible followed John Calvin’s teachings.  
It placed God’s authority above the monarch’s.  

The new translation was the King James Version.  
It was published in 1611.  
It emphasized the majesty of kings.  

In the 1620s and 1630s, the conflict grew worse.  
The state church banned Puritan ministers from preaching.  
Church leaders saw Puritans as a national security threat.  
They believed Puritan demands undermined the king’s authority.  
Puritans wanted cultural, social, and religious reforms.  

Many Puritans refused to conform to the Church of England.  
They sought refuge in the New World.  
But the emigrants were not all the same.  
Some wanted a complete break with the Church of England.  
Others still wanted to reform the national church.

European settlement in America caused many changes in the environment. These changes affected animals and people.

In Europe, beaver-trimmed hats became very popular. At the same time, many Native Americans wanted European weapons. These two demands led to heavy hunting of beavers in the Northeast.

Soon, beavers disappeared from New England, New York, and other areas. When beavers were gone, beaver ponds also disappeared. These ponds had been homes for fish. They also provided water for deer, moose, and other animals.

Europeans also brought pigs to America. They often let the pigs roam and forage in forests and other wild areas. The pigs ate foods that deer and other native animals needed. This reduced the amount of game that Native peoples had traditionally hunted.

European ideas about land ownership also caused conflict. Many Native peoples did not believe land should be privately owned. They saw land as a shared resource, held in common for the good of the group.

A European idea called “usufruct” is similar to this view. Usufruct means the right to use and enjoy common land. However, colonists did not widely practice usufruct in America.

Instead, colonizers marked land as private property. They created fields, built fences, and set boundaries. Native peoples often moved with the seasons to use different resources. Now they found some areas closed to them. Colonizers claimed these places because they insisted on private-property rights.

Parliament passed the Tea Act of 1773 for economic reasons.  
It was not meant to punish the colonists.  
It was not meant to prove Parliament’s power.  
It was not meant to raise money.

The act was meant to protect a British tea company.  
That company was the East India Company.  
The company was close to bankruptcy.

In the colonies, tea was still taxed.  
It was the one consumer good still under the Townshend duties.  
Many colonists hated these duties.

Protest leaders told people not to buy British tea.  
Their followers avoided it too.  
Instead, they drank smuggled Dutch tea.  
They did this to show patriotism.

The Tea Act gave the East India Company new advantages.  
It could ship tea straight to the colonies.  
It did not have to pay import or export duties.  
It also did not have to use middlemen in Britain or in the colonies.

Because of these changes, the company could sell tea more cheaply.  
This was true even with the Townshend tax still added.  
The price could be lower than smuggled Dutch tea.  
That would hurt the smuggling trade.

Many people in British North America disliked the act.  
They were already unhappy with earlier imperial policies.

The act gave the East India Company a monopoly.  
This shut out colonial merchants who wanted to sell tea themselves.  
It also cut into profits from smuggled foreign tea.

These merchants were powerful and influential.  
So their anger mattered.

The Townshend tea tax stayed in place.  
Because of that, tea became a strong symbol.  
It stood for the idea of “no taxation without representation.”

chapter_key: COLONIAL PROTEST: THE DESTRUCTION OF THE TEA
text:
The 1773 act brought back the colonists’ worst fears. To the Sons and Daughters of Liberty, and to their supporters, the act seemed like clear proof. They believed a small group of corrupt members of Parliament was breaking the British Constitution. Many protest leaders had learned to expect the worst from Britain. So they saw the 1773 act as part of a larger conspiracy against liberty.

As they had done with earlier acts and taxes, colonists answered the Tea Act with a boycott. The Committees of Correspondence helped organize resistance in colonial port cities. Up and down the East Coast, ships carrying British tea could not come ashore to unload. In Charlestown, Boston, Philadelphia, and New York, tea worth the equivalent of millions of dollars was held hostage. It sat locked in warehouses. Or it spoiled in ship holds as ships were forced to sail back to Great Britain.

In Boston, Thomas Hutchinson was now the royal governor of Massachusetts. He promised that radicals like Samuel Adams would not stop the ships from unloading. He urged merchants to stand firm. He wanted them to accept the tea once it was unloaded.

In November 1773, the Dartmouth sailed into Boston Harbor. It had twenty days to unload its tea and pay the duty. If it did not, it had to return to Great Britain. Two more ships arrived soon after. They were the Eleanor and the Beaver. Samuel Adams and the Sons of Liberty tried to stop the captains from paying the duties. They also posted groups around the ships. Their goal was to make sure the tea was not unloaded.

On December 16, the Dartmouth’s deadline was close. Townspeople gathered at the Old South Meeting House. They were determined to act. After the meeting, a group of Sons of Liberty and their followers went to the three ships. Some wore disguises as Mohawks. A crowd watched and protected them. The group dumped all the tea into the harbor. They destroyed goods worth almost $1 million in today’s dollars. This was a major loss.

The event soon inspired more resistance along the East Coast. But not all colonists supported the tea dumping. Not even all Patriots supported it. The large-scale destruction of property shocked people on both sides of the Atlantic.

In colonial America, women carried heavy responsibilities at home. They did most domestic work. They also raised children.

The war for independence increased their workload. It also reinforced their usual roles. Rebel leaders expected women to make supplies for the war. These supplies included clothing and food. Women also had to keep their farms and households running. This was difficult when husbands and sons were away fighting.

Women were also expected to help the army directly. They provided food and lodging for soldiers. They nursed wounded soldiers.

The Revolution also created some new opportunities. Some women took on public roles that were usually reserved for men.

One example was the Daughters of Liberty. This was an informal group formed in the mid-1760s. It opposed British revenue-raising measures. The group worked hard to support the war effort.

Another example was Esther DeBerdt Reed of Philadelphia. She was the wife of Governor Joseph Reed. She formed the Ladies Association of Philadelphia. She led a fundraising drive to get badly needed supplies for the Continental Army.

In 1780, she wrote “The Sentiments of an American Woman.” She urged other women to act. She reminded them of earlier sacrifices. She wrote that women had given up tea rather than accept it from their persecutors. She said they treated former necessities as luxuries when liberty was at stake. She described women spinning flax and making linen for soldiers. She also described supporting exiles and fugitives, despite the hardships of war.

Reed and other women in Philadelphia raised almost $300,000 in Continental money for the war.

Before the Revolution, several colonies had official churches.  
These churches were supported by taxes.

After the Revolution, some people questioned these systems.  
They questioned state-approved churches.  
They questioned rules that limited public office to one faith.  
They questioned paying taxes to support churches.

In other states, especially in New England, church and government stayed closely connected.  
This was influenced by the older Puritan tradition.

## Virginia
In colonial Virginia, the official church was the Church of England.  
It did not tolerate Catholics, Baptists, or people of other religions.

In 1786, Virginia passed the **Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom**.  
This was a revolutionary response to the special power of the Church of England.  
The law ended the Church of England’s privileged position.  
It protected religious liberty.

Under this statute:  
- No one could be forced to attend a specific church.  
- No one could be forced to support a specific church.  
- No one could be prosecuted for their religious beliefs.

## Pennsylvania
Pennsylvania’s first constitution had a religious test for state legislators.  
It allowed only people who believed in both the Old and New Testaments.

This rule kept Jews from holding that office.  
The New Testament is not part of Jewish belief.

In 1790, Pennsylvania removed this requirement from its constitution.

## New England
The New England states changed more slowly.  
In the former Puritan colonies, the **Congregational Church** remained dominant.  
This church had been established by seventeenth-century Puritans.

Massachusetts, Connecticut, and New Hampshire required public support for Christian churches.

In Massachusetts, **Article III** of the state constitution linked republican government with promoting Protestant Christianity.  
It said that good government depends on piety, religion, and morality.  
It said these values spread through public worship and public instruction.  
It gave the legislature power to require towns and religious groups to pay for:  
- public worship of God  
- the support of Protestant teachers of piety, religion, and morality  
This applied when people did not provide such support voluntarily.

At the same time, Article III also promised legal protection for all Christian denominations that behaved peacefully.  
It said no Christian sect would be legally placed under another.

Even though the Revolution ended British rule in the United States, many supporters of the 1787 federal Constitution still believed in a British-style social hierarchy. These supporters were called Federalists.

At first, the Federalists were not a political party. Instead, they shared certain beliefs.

They believed political participation should be tied to property rights. This kept many citizens from voting or holding office.

Federalists did not think the Revolution changed traditional roles between women and men. They also did not think it changed the roles between White people and other races.

They believed there were clear differences in rank and intelligence. To them, the idea that everyone was equal seemed ridiculous.

They argued that women, Black people, and Native people had to accept a lower place than White male citizens. They feared that trying to force equality would destroy the republic.

They also believed the United States was not created to be a democracy.

The people who designed the Constitution expected to lead the new republic. They held a majority in the new national government. Many of them took the new executive jobs created by the first Congress.

George Washington appointed Alexander Hamilton, a leading Federalist, as secretary of the treasury. Washington chose Thomas Jefferson as secretary of state. He appointed Henry Knox as secretary of war. Knox had served with Washington during the Revolutionary War.

Edmond Randolph, a Virginia delegate to the Constitutional Convention, became attorney general.

Congress passed its first major law in the 1789 Tariff Act. This law placed a duty on imports. The goal was to raise money to deal with the nation’s economic problems.

The act was a victory for nationalists. Nationalists wanted a strong federal government. They had tried, and failed, to pass similar measures in the 1780s under the Confederation Congress.

As production became mechanized and moved into factories, workers’ lives changed a lot.

Before factories, farmers and artisans controlled their own work.  
They chose the pace of the day.  
They also chose the order of tasks.

An artisan could take an afternoon off if he wanted.  
A farmer could rebuild a fence on Thursday instead of Wednesday.

People talked while they worked.  
They often drank during the workday.  
Journeymen were often promised alcohol as part of their wages.

Sometimes one person read a book or newspaper out loud to the others.  
In warm weather, doors and windows could be opened.  
Work often stopped when it became too dark to see.

Factory work was very different.

Workers had to arrive at a set time, usually early in the morning.  
They had to work all day.  
They could not leave when they felt tired.  
They could not take breaks except at set times.

If a worker arrived late, their pay was reduced.  
Being five minutes late could cost several hours of pay.  
If someone was late many times, they could be fired.

Many factory jobs were repetitive.  
This made the days feel long.

Hours depended on the factory.  
But most workers labored 10 to 12 hours a day.  
They worked six days a week.

In winter, the sun set early.  
Factories used oil lamps for light.  
Workers strained their eyes to see.  
They coughed as smoke filled the rooms.

In spring, days grew longer.  
Factories held “blowing-out” celebrations.  
These marked the time when oil lamps were no longer needed.  
The “blow-outs” often included processions and dancing.

Freedom in factories was limited.

Drinking was not allowed.  
Some factories did not allow workers to sit down.

Doors and windows were kept closed.  
This was especially true in textile factories.  
Breezes could disturb the fibers.

In summer, mills were often extremely hot and humid.  
In winter, workers often shivered from the cold.  
In these conditions, workers’ health suffered.

Factories were also dangerous.

In textile factories, cotton bales sat near oil used on machines.  
This made fires common.

Injuries were common too.  
Hands and fingers could be crushed or cut off in machines.  
Sometimes limbs were crushed.  
In some cases, entire bodies were crushed.

Workers who survived these injuries usually lost their jobs.  
They also lost their income.

Corporal punishment was common in factories.  
This happened to both children and adults.  
In the worst places, children sometimes died.  
They died from injuries caused by an overseer.

Over time, conditions got worse in many mills.

Workers were told to manage more machines at once.  
Owners also made the machines run faster.

Many factories cut wages.
